Isaac had his servants dig more wells because after his father died, the Philistines filled in all the wells he inherited. Isaac gave the wells the same names that his father had given them.
So Isaac's servants dug wells in the Gerar valley where they found a freshwater spring.
The other herdsmen in Gerar fought with Isaac's herdsmen and said, "This is our water," so Isaac named the well Esek because they were hostile toward his herdsmen.
Isaac's servants dug another well that he named Sitnah, and he fought with the Gerar herdsmen about that well too.

So he left and went to another place and dug another well that they did not fight over, and he named that place Rehoboth. Then he said, "Now the Lord has made room for us, and we will be prosperous here."
And he left and went to Beersheba.
And the Lord appeared to him that night and said, "I am the God of your father Abraham, fear not, because I am with you, I will bless you and multiply your descendants for my servant Abraham's sake.
Isaac set up camp in Beersheba, his servants dug a well, and he built an altar in the place where he called on the Lord's name.
Then Abimelech, Phichol the chief captain of his army, and his friend Ahuzzath left Gerar, and they went to visit Isaac.
And Isaac asked them, "Why have you come to see me? I know you hated me because you sent me away?"
And they said, "We saw that the Lord was with you, and we said, 'We need to make an oath between us, and we want to make a covenant with you.
We do not want you to harm us, because we haven't touched you, and we've done nothing but good to you, we let you leave here in peace, and now you're blessed by the Lord.'"
Isaac prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank.
They got up early the next morning and swore an oath to each other, then Isaac sent them away, and allowed them to leave in peace.
One day Isaac's servants came and told him they had found water in the well they had dug.
He called that well Sheba, and that's why the city is still named Beersheba to this day.
Esau was forty years old when he married two wives, Judith who was Beeri the Hittite's daughter, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite.
This caused great distress to Isaac and Rebekah.
When Isaac was old his eyes grew dim, and he could not see, he asked to see his oldest son Esau and when he came to him, he said, "My son, I am here.
I am old, and I do not know when I am going to die.
That's why I want you to take your hunting weapons, your bow and arrows, and your quiver, and go out to the fields, and find some venison.
When you return, I want you to make that savory meat recipe I love to eat, so I can bless you in front of the Lord before I die."
Isaac's wife Rebekah heard Isaac talking to Esau before he went hunting.
Rebekah told her youngest son Jacob what Isaac had said to Esau.
And she said, "Isaac told Esau to bring him some venison and to make a savory meat recipe for him to eat. Then he said he would bless Esau in front of the Lord before he dies."
And Rebekah said to Jacob, "That's why I want you to do what I tell you.
Go out to the herd and fetch two kid goats, and I will make a savory meat recipe that your father loves.
Then, I want you to take it to your father, and he will give you his blessing before he dies."
And Jacob said to his mother, "Esau is a hairy man, and I am not.
If father touches me, he will think I am trying to deceive him, and he will curse me instead of blessing me."
And Jacob's mother said, "The curse will be on me, so do what I say, and go fetch the goats."
Jacob went and fetched the goats, and brought them to his mother, and she prepared the savory meat stew, that Isaac loved.
Rebekah had some of her oldest son Esau's clothes in her house, and she put them on her youngest son Jacob.
Then she put the goat skins on Jacob's hands and neck.
She gave Jacob the bread and stew she had prepared.
Jacob brought them to his father and said, "Father, I am back," and Isaac asked, "Who are you, my son?"
And Jacob said, "I am Esau, I did what you asked me to do, I brought you some venison, sit up so you can eat, and give me your blessing."
And Isaac asked his son, "How did you find it so quickly?" And he said, "It was because your Lord God brought it to me."
And Isaac said to Jacob, "Come here my son, so I can feel you, and then I will know whether or not, you are my son Esau."
Jacob went over to his father, and Isaac felt his arm and said, "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau."
He did not recognize Jacob, because his hands were hairy, just like his brother Esau's hands, so Isaac blessed Jacob.
And he asked, "Are you my son Esau?" And Jacob said, "I am."
And he said, "Bring me your venison so I can eat it, and my soul will bless you," and Jacob brought it to him, and he ate it and drank wine.
And he said to Jacob, "Come here, and give me a kiss."
Jacob kissed him, and he smelled Esau's clothes that Jacob was wearing, and he blessed him and said, "My son smells like the fields which the Lord has blessed.
That's why God will give you heaven's dew, and the fat of the earth, with plenty of wheat and wine.

People will serve you, and nations will bow down to you. You will be Lord over your brothers, and your mother's sons will bow down to you. Anyone that curses you will be cursed, and anyone that blesses you will be blessed."
As soon as Isaac finished blessing him, Jacob left, and his brother Esau returned from hunting.
He made a savory meat stew and brought it to his father. Then Esau said to his father, "Get up father, and eat the venison I brought you, so your soul may bless me."
And Isaac said, "Who are you?" And he said, "I am your firstborn son, Esau."
That's when Isaac started trembling and said, "Who brought me the venison that I ate before you got here, because I already blessed him, and he will be blessed."
When Esau heard what his father said, he started crying bitterly and said, "Bless me too father."
And Isaac said, "Your brother snuck in here, and he's stolen your blessing."

And he said, "There's a reason his name is Jacob because this is the second time he's taken advantage of me. He schemed to take my birthright, and now he's stolen my blessing. Do not you have any kind of blessing for me?"

And Isaac said to Esau, "I have made him your lord, and I have given all his brothers to him for servants, and I blessed him with wheat and wine to sustain him. I have nothing left for your blessing."
And Esau said to his father, "Do not you have just one blessing for me? Please give me a blessing father," and Esau started weeping very loudly.
Then Isaac said, "Behold your home will be the fat of the earth and the dew from heaven above.
You will live by your sword, and you will serve your brother until you have taken control, then you will break the yoke he has placed around your neck."
After that Esau hated Jacob for stealing his father's blessing from him, and Esau said in his heart, 'My father is close to death, and after I have finished mourning him, I will kill Jacob'.
Someone heard what Esau said and told Rebekah, and she sent for Jacob, and said to him, "Your brother Esau, is very upset, and he's planning to kill you.
I want you to leave and flee to my brother Laban's house in Haran.
Stay there until your brother's fury calms down.
When your brother's anger subsides, I will send for you after he forgets what you've done. Why should I be deprived of both sons on the same day?"
Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "The daughters of Heth make me weary. If Jacob marries one of Heth's daughters, I will have nothing left to live for."
Isaac called for Jacob; he blessed him and told him not to take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.

And he said, "Get up and go visit Bethuel in Padan-Aram. Your uncle Laban has daughters that you can marry, and you will find a wife there." Betheul was Rebekah's father, and Laban was Rebekah's brother.
"Furthermore," Isaac said, "Let God Almighty bless you, and make you fruitful, and multiply you into a multitude of people.
God will give you and your descendants Abraham's blessing, because God promised to give Abraham a land, where you are a stranger, for your inheritance."
Then Isaac sent Jacob away, and he went to visit Laban in Padan-Aram. Laban was Bethuel the Syrian's son, Rebekah's brother, and Jacob's Uncle. Rebekah was Esau and Jacob's mother.
When Esau heard that Isaac blessed Jacob and told him not to take a wife from the daughters of Canaan, and sent him to Padan-Aram, to find a wife.
When he saw that Jacob had obeyed his father and mother and went to Padan-Aram.
And when he saw that the daughters of Canaan did not please his father.
He went to visit Ishmael and married Ishmael's daughter Mahalath. Ishmael was Abraham's son, and Nebajoth was Mahalath's sister.
Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran.
He stopped at a certain place where he stayed all night. After the sun set, he made a pillow from some stones, and he lay down and went to sleep.
He dreamed about a ladder that reached from heaven to the earth, and the angels of God were using it to ascend and descend from heaven to earth.

He saw the Lord standing above the ladder and heard the Lord say, "I am the Lord God of your grandfather Abraham, and the God of your father Isaac, and I will give you and your descendants the land where you lie.
Your descendants will be like the earth's dust, and they will spread north, south, east, and west. All the families on the earth will come from you and your descendants, and they will be blessed.
And, behold I am with you, and I will protect you everywhere you go, and I will bring you back to this land because I will not leave you until I've kept all the promises I made to you."
Jacob awakened from his sleep and said, "I did not know the Lord was in this place, but he surely is."
Jacob was afraid and he said, "This place is dreadful! This is truly the house of God, and this is the gate to heaven."
Jacob got up early that morning, and he took the stone that he'd used for his pillows and built a column with it, and then he poured oil on top of it.
He named that place Bethel, but at first the city was known as Luz.
Jacob made a promise to the Lord and said, "If God is with me, and protects me everywhere I go and gives me bread to eat, and clothes to wear.
When I peacefully return to my father's house, then the Lord will be my God.
I have built a column with this stone, and it will be God's house, and I will return to you 10% of everything that you have given me."
Then Jacob traveled to the land of the people in the east.
When he looked up, he saw a well out in the field covered by a large stone and nearby were three herds of sheep because they were watered there.
The shepherds would bring all their sheep to the well, then they would roll away the stone and water the sheep. When they were finished, they would put the stone back on top of the well.
And Jacob asked them, "Where are you from my brothers?" and they said, "We are from Haran."
And then he asked them if they knew Laban and they said, "Yes we know Laban, he is Nahor's son."
And he asked them if he was well and they said, "Yes, he's doing well." Then they saw Rachel coming towards them with her sheep, and Rachael was Laban's daughter.
Then Jacob said, "The sun is still high in the sky, and it's not time to gather the cattle, go feed and water your sheep."
And they said, "We cannot, water our sheep until all the herds are gathered together, and they roll the stone away from the well."
While he was still talking to them, Rachel came with her father's sheep, because she was a shepherd, and she took care of her father's sheep.
When Jacob saw Laban's daughter Rachel with her father's sheep he went and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well, and she watered the herd. Laban was Jacob's mother's brother.
Jacob kissed Rachel, and he began to weep out loud.
Jacob told Rachel that he was her father's nephew and her aunt Rebekah's son, then she ran to her father and told him.
When Laban heard that his sister's son Jacob was there, he ran out to meet him. He embraced him, kissed him, and brought him back to his house, and Jacob told him why he was there.
And Laban said to him, "You are my flesh and blood relative."
After Jacob had been there for a month Laban said to him, "Because you are my relative, you should not have to serve me for nothing, so tell me, what should I pay you for your labor?"
Laban had two daughters, the oldest one was named Leah, and the younger one was named Rachel.
Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel was very beautiful.
Jacob loved Rachel and he said, "I will serve you for seven years if you let me marry your younger daughter."
And Laban said, "It would be better for me to give her to you than to let her marry another man."
Jacob served Laban for seven years, but to him, it seemed like it was only a few days, because he loved Rachael.
And Jacob said to Laban, "I have finished my seven years of servitude to you, and now it is time for me to marry my wife.
Laban prepared a great feast and invited all the men there to the celebration.
But in the evening, Laban took his daughter Leah to Jacob, and he made love to her.
Laban gave his maid Zilpah to his daughter Leah for a housemaid.

The next morning Jacob was surprised to see Leah in his bed. Jacob went to Laban and said, "What have you done to me? I served you for seven years so I could marry Rachel, and now, you have deceived me."
And Laban said, "The custom in our country is for the firstborn daughter to marry before the younger daughter.
If you spend the first week with Leah as your wife, and then work for me for another seven years, I will let you marry Rachael too.
Jacob and Leah consummated their first week of marriage, and then Laban gave Rachel to him as his second wife.
Then Laban gave Bilhah his housemaid to his daughter Rachel.
Jacob made love to Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than he loved Leah. And he served Laban another seven years.
When the Lord saw that Leah was hated, he made her fertile, but Rachel was barren and had no children.
Leah conceived and gave birth to a son, and she named him Reuben. She said it was because the Lord had seen that Jacob did not love her, and maybe now he would love her too.
She conceived again and gave birth to another son that she named Simeon, and she said, "The Lord heard that I was hated, and he has given me another son."
Leah conceived again and gave birth to a third son that she named Levi, and she said, "Now Jacob will love me because I have given him three sons."
Then she conceived again and gave birth to a son that she named Judah, and she said, "Now I will praise the Lord."
Rachel was envious of her sister because Leah had children and she did not. And she said to Jacob, "If I do not have any children I will die."
Jacob was angry with Rachel and he said, "Am I, God? Because he is the one who has prevented you from having children."
And she said, "Go to my maid Bilhah, and she will bear my children for me."
She gave Bilhah to Jacob for a wife, and Jacob slept with her. Bilhah was Rachael's housemaid.
Bilhah conceived and gave birth to a son for Jacob.
And Rachel said, "God has judged me, and he has heard my prayers, and he has given me a son," and she named him Dan.
Then Bilhah conceived again and gave birth to a second son for Jacob.
And Rachel said, "I have wrestled with my sister Leah, and I have won," and she named her second son Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she had stopped bearing children, and she gave her maid Zilpah to Jacob for a wife.
And Zilpah gave birth to another son for Jacob.
And Leah said, "A troop of sons is coming," and she named her son Gad.
And Zilpah gave birth to a second son for Jacob.
And Leah said, "I am happy, because the other women will say that I am blessed," and she named her son Asher.

When it was time to harvest the wheat, Reuben went out into the fields and found some aphrodisiac mandrake roots and brought them to his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes."

And Leah said to her, "Is it not enough that you have taken my husband, and now you want to take my son's mandrakes too?" Then Rachel said, "Very well, I will let him spend the night with you tonight for some of your son's mandrakes."

In the evening Jacob was coming in from the fields, and Leah went out to meet him. And she said, "I have hired you from Rachael for tonight with some of my son's mandrakes," and Jacob slept with Leah that night.
God heard Leah's prayers, and she conceived and gave birth to a fifth son for Jacob.
And Leah said, "God has answered my prayers because I gave my young servant to my husband, and she named her son Issachar.
Leah conceived again and gave birth to a sixth son for Jacob.
And Leah said, God has given me a gift, now my husband will live with me, because I have given him six sons, and she named her son Zebulun.
Then she gave birth to a daughter, whom she named Dinah.
God remembered Rachel and he heard her prayers, and she conceived.
She got pregnant and gave birth to a son, and she said, "God has taken away my shame."
She named her son Joseph and she said, "I pray the Lord will give me another son."
After Rachel had given birth to Joseph, Jacob went to Laban and said, "Let me go my own way, so I can have a place, in my own country.
You know I have served you well, so give me my wives and children, and let me go."
Laban answered Jacob and said, "If you love me, I beg you to stay, because I have learned by experience, that the Lord has blessed me because of you."
Laban said, "Tell me how much you need in wages to stay, and I will give it to you."
Jacob answered him and said, "You know how well I have served you, and how I have cared for your cattle.
Before I came here you had very little, now your herds have multiplied abundantly. The Lord has blessed you since I have been here, but when will I be allowed to provide for my own house and family?"
And Laban said, "What do you want me to give you to stay?" And Jacob said, "You will not be giving me anything, but if you pay me what I want, I will stay to feed and take care of your herd.
I will sort through your herds today, and remove all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown sheep, and all the speckled and spotted goats, and that's the payment I will require to stay.
So, in the future, if you find any goats that are not speckled and spotted, or any brown sheep mixed in with my herd, you will know that I have stolen them from you."
And Laban said, "Your word is good, and I agree to your terms."

That day Jacob removed all the striped and spotted male goats, all the speckled and spotted female goats, and every goat that had some white on it, plus all the brown sheep, and gave them to his sons.
Jacob's sons moved three days away, and Jacob stayed and fed the rest of Laban's herds.
Jacob took green poplar, hazel and chestnut tree limbs, and peeled bark strips from them, which exposed the white wood underneath.
He set the peeled tree limbs in front of the watering troughs, so that when Laban's herds came to drink, they would conceive, because that's when they would breed.
The herds conceived near the tree limbs, and they gave birth to striped, speckled, and spotted cattle.
Jacob separated the lambs from Laban's herd and mixed the rest of the herd with the striped and brown cattle, and he separated his own herd from Laban's herd, and did not let them mix together.
Whenever the stronger cattle conceived, Jacob laid the tree limbs in front of the cattle by the troughs, so that they would conceive.
But when the cattle were feeble, he put them in with Laban's stock, and he kept the strongest ones for himself.
Jacob's wealth increased immensely, and he had many cattle, servants, camels, and donkeys.
One day Laban's sons said, "Jacob has taken everything that our father owned, and he has used it to enrich himself."
Jacob noticed that Laban's frame of mind had changed and his opinion of him was not what it was before.
And the Lord said to Jacob, "Return to your father's land where your family lives and I will be with you."
Jacob called Rachel and Leah out to the fields where he was tending his herd.
And he said to them, "I can see that your father's opinion of me has changed, and things are not as they were before, but my father's God has been with me the whole time.
You know that I have served your father well and with all my strength.
Your father deceived me, and he has changed my wages ten times, but God has not allowed him to hurt me.

If your father Laban had said that my wages would be all the speckled cattle, then nothing but speckled cattle would have been born. But if he had said, all the striped cattle will be your wages, then nothing but striped cattle would have been born.
Therefore, God has taken away your father's cattle and given them to me.
And at that time, I saw in a dream, that all the male breeding cattle were either striped, speckled, or spotted.
Then God's angel spoke to me in a dream and said, "Jacob," and I said, "Here I am."
And the angel said, "Look up and see, all the male breeding cattle are either striped, speckled, or spotted because I have seen every bad thing that Laban has ever done to you.
I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the column and made a promise to me. Now get up and leave this land and return to your family's land."
Then Rachel and Leah answered him and said, "There is no inheritance left for us here from our father's house.
He looks at us as if we were strangers, because not only did he sell us to you, but he also spent all of our money.
For God has taken away all our father's wealth and given it to us, so you should do what God told you to do."
Then Jacob got up and put all his wives and children on the camels.
He took everything he owned, including all his cattle and property, plus the goods and cattle he had acquired in Padan-Aram because he was going back to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan.
Laban went to shear his sheep, and Rachel had stolen the idols that belonged to her father.
Laban the Syrian was unaware that Jacob had left without telling him that he was leaving.
So Jacob fled with everything he had and crossed the river and turned towards Mount Gilead.
On the third day after he left, someone told Laban that Jacob was gone.
Laban and his brothers pursued Jacob for seven days before they caught up with him on Mount Gilead.
That night God came to Laban in a dream and said, "Do not speak either good or bad to Jacob."
When Laban and his brothers caught up with Jacob, he was camped on Mount Gilead, and Laban's men were camped there too.
And Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done, I did not even know you were leaving. Why have you carried away my daughters like they were prisoners captured with a sword?
Why did you sneak away without telling me? I could have had a celebration, and sent you away with music, songs, harps, and tambourines.
Why did you leave and not even give me the chance to kiss my grandchildren goodbye? You have done a very foolish thing.
I have the power to hurt you, but the God of your father spoke to me last night and said, 'Do not say anything good or bad to Jacob.'
And now, you left because you longed for your father's house. But why did you steal my gods' idols?"
Jacob answered and said, "I left without telling you because I was afraid of you. I thought you would take your daughters away from me by force."

Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen her father's idols, and he said, "If you find someone here who has stolen your idols, let them be put to death. If our brothers find something here that belongs to you, take it with you."
Laban searched Jacob's tent, Leah's tent, and the two female servants' tents, but he found nothing. Then he entered Rachel's tent.
Rachel had hidden her father's idols in the camel's saddle where she was sitting, and Laban searched her entire tent, but he found nothing.

While her father was searching her tent she said, "Please do not be angry with me if I do not get up, because it is that time of the month for me," and he searched her tent, but he did not find his idols.
Jacob chided Laban because he was angry, and that's when he said, "What have I done to you, what is my sin, how have I trespassed against you? Why have you chased after me with such anger?
Now that you have searched everything I own, what have you found? If you found something I have stolen put it here in front of our brothers and let them judge us.
I have been with you for twenty years, your ewes and goats never had a miscarriage, and I have not eaten any of the rams from your herds.

I never brought you any of the animals that were ripped apart by predators, and I absorbed all those losses myself. You made me to pay for everything that was ever lost or stolen in broad daylight or at night.
I have suffered droughts, freezing temperatures, and many sleepless nights.

I have been in your house for twenty years; I served you for fourteen years so I could marry your daughters. I served you for six years for the cattle that were my wages, and you have changed my wages ten times.

If my father's God, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac had not been with me, you would have sent me away empty handed. God saw my labor, and the way that you have treated me, and that's why he rebuked you last night."

Laban answered Jacob and said to him, "These are my daughters, these are my grandchildren, these are my cattle, and everything here is mine. So, what can I do today to cause my daughters or their children to suffer?
That's why I want us to make a covenant, as a witness between me and you."
So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a column.
Then Jacob said to his brothers, "Gather some stones." So, they made a pile of stones and used it as a dinner table to eat.
Laban called it Jegar-Sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.
Laban said, "This pile of stones is a witness between me and you on this day, and that's why I named it Galeed.
It was also called Mizpah, because Laban said, "The Lord will keep watch over us while we are separated.
If you abuse my daughters, or you take other wives beside my daughters, and even if we do not see each other, God is a witness between me and you."
And Laban said to Jacob, "Look at this pile of stones and the stone column we have built together.
This pile of stones and the stone column will be a border between us and a reminder that we will not cross it to cause harm to each other.
Let the God of Abraham, the God of Nahor, and the God of their father judge any slight between us." So, Jacob swore an oath based on his father's fear of God.
Then Jacob offered a sacrifice on the side of the mountain. He told his brothers to eat some bread, so they ate and stayed on the mountain all night.
Laban got up early the next morning, kissed his grandchildren, blessed them, and left to return to his home.
Jacob met God's angels on the road after he resumed his journey.
When Jacob saw them, he said, "This is God's multitude," and he named the place Mahanaim.
Jacob sent messengers to his brother Esau, in Seir in the country of Edom.
And he said, "When you speak to Esau, tell him you are one of his brother Jacob's servants, who has been traveling with Laban.
And Jacob has acquired oxen, donkeys, herds, and male and female servants. Jacob has sent me to tell you that he is coming, and he hopes you will meet him with grace and kindness."
When the messengers returned to Jacob, they told him that they went to see his brother Esau, and that his brother was coming to meet him with 400 men.
Jacob was distressed and terrified when he heard this news, so he divided his people, flocks, herds, and camels into two separate companies.
Then he said, "If Esau defeats one of our companies, the other one may be able to escape."
And Jacob said, "God of my grandfather Abraham, God of my father Isaac, and the Lord who said to me, 'Return to your country and your relatives, and I will deal favorably with you.'
I do not deserve your mercies or the truths that you have shown me because when I crossed the river Jordan, I had nothing but my staff. Now I have divided my camp into two companies.
Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, because I am afraid that he will defeat me, and destroy my children and their mothers.
You said you would be good to me and multiply my descendants like the sand of the sea, which are too numerous to be counted."
Jacob stayed there that night, and the next morning he prepared a gift for his brother Esau.
Jacob sent 200 female goats, 20 male goats, 200 ewes, and 20 rams.
Plus thirty milk camels with their colts, forty cows, ten bulls, twenty female donkeys, and ten foals.

Jacob separated them into herds and divided each separate group of animals among his servants, and Jacob said to them, "Go meet Esau before he gets here, and keep each group separated and at safe a distance from each other."
Jacob said to his second in command, "When you meet Esau, and he asks who you are, where you are going and who owns these herds?
Tell him that they belong to his brother Jacob, who he has sent a gift to my Lord Esau, and that his brother Jacob is behind us."
Then Jacob spoke to his second and third in command, plus all the other servants that were driving the herds and said, "When you find Esau, speak to him with respect.
Tell my brother Esau that I sent my servant ahead of me with a present, because I am hoping that he will welcome me."
So Jacob sent the gifts ahead, and that night he stayed with his company.
Jacob got up in the middle of the night, and took his two wives, his two female servants, and his eleven sons and crossed over the flowing Jabbok stream.
He sent them across the brook, along with all his possessions.
When Jacob was alone, he wrestled all night long with a man he met there.
When the man saw that he could not win the wrestling match, he dislocated Jacob's thigh and pulled it out of joint.
And the man said, "Let me go, because it is daybreak." But Jacob replied and said, "I will not let you go unless you bless me."
And the man asked Jacob, "What is your name?" And he said, "My name is Jacob."
And the man said, "Your name is not Jacob anymore, but you will be called Israel because you have been as victorious with God and men as a prince."
And Jacob asked him, "Tell me your name," and he said, "Why do you want to know my name?" And then he blessed Jacob.
Jacob named the place Peniel and he said, "I have seen God face to face, and that is why my life is protected."
He crossed the Peniel as the sun was rising, but he had to stop because of his injured thigh.
That's why, to this day, the children of Israel do not eat the shrunken sinew from the hollow of the thigh, because God's angel touched Jacob's thigh and injured it.
Jacob looked up and saw Esau coming his way with 400 men, and he divided his children between Leah, Rachel, and their two housemaids.
He put the housemaids and their children out front, with Leah and her children behind them, then Rachel and Joseph behind Leah.
Jacob approached his brother and bowed down to him seven times.
Esau ran out to meet him, embraced him, hugged his neck, then kissed him and they both began to weep.
Esau looked up and saw the women and children with Jacob and he asked, "Who are all these people with you?" And Jacob answered and said, "These are the children which God has graciously given me".
Then Jacob's housemaids moved closer with their children, and they bowed to Esau.
Leah approached with her children, and they bowed to Jacob's brother, then Joseph and Rachel approached and they bowed to Esau.
And Esau asked, "Why are you bringing these herds, and this crowd of people for me to meet?" And Jacob said, "I have brought these gifts to find grace in my Lord's sight."
And Esau said, "Jacob my brother, I have enough of everything, keep what you have for yourself."
And Jacob said, "You have received me with grace and goodwill, I have seen the face of God in you, and you were pleased to see me. So, I ask you to please accept my gifts.
I ask you to accept my blessing, and the gifts I have brought you because God has dealt generously with me, and I have more than enough," so Esau accepted Jacob's gifts.
Then Esau said, "Let's travel together, and I will lead the way."

Jacob answered and said, "My Lord, you know that my children are young and they are still being nursed by their mothers. My flocks and herds are still nursing their young ones too. If the men push them too hard, they will all die.
Why do you not go on ahead of me, and I will follow behind you at a pace that is safe for the children and cattle. I will catch up with you when I arrive in Seir."
And Esau said, "Let me leave some of my men with you." Jacob answered and said, "Why do you need to do that, you know I have come and shown you grace, so why do not you trust me?"
Then Esau left, and he returned to Seir with his men.
Jacob traveled to Succoth, where he built a house and sheds for his cattle, so he named the place Succoth.
When Jacob left Padan-Aram, he traveled to the Shechem city of Shalem in the land of Canaan, and he camped outside the city.
Jacob bought a parcel of land from Hamor's son Shechem. He paid Shechem 100 silver shekels for the field, and he pitched his tent there.
Jacob built an altar there and called it Elelohe-Israel.
Leah and Jacob's daughter Dinah, left and went to visit some of the women that lived in her new country.
When Hamor's son Shechem saw Dinah, he defiled her and slept with her. Hamor was a Hivite, and his son Shechem was a prince in that country.
Shechem fell in love with Jacob's daughter, and he whispered sweet nothings in her ear.
Shechem asked his father Hamor to talk to Jacob to ask him if he could marry Jacob's daughter.
Jacob heard about what happened to his daughter, his sons were out in the field tending his cattle when they heard what had happened to Dinah. Jacob held his temper until they came in from the field.
Shechem's father Hamor, went to talk to Jacob about Dinah.

Jacob's sons came in from the field when they heard what happened. The men were angry and upset when they heard about it because prince Shechem had convinced Jacob's daughter to have sex with him, while she was in Israel.
And Hamor said to them, "The soul of my son longs for your daughter, and I have come to ask you to allow her to marry Shechem.
If you will let your daughters marry our young men, we will let our daughters marry your young men.
We will all live in this land together, we will trade with you, and you will acquire great wealth here."
Then Shechem said to Dinah's father and brothers, "If I find grace in your sight, I will give you whatever you ask.
No matter how much dowry or gifts you ask of me, I will give it to you, if you let her marry me."
Since Shechem had already had sex with their sister Dinah, Jacob's sons answered Shechem and Hamor deceitfully.
Jacob's sons spoke to them and said, "We cannot give you our sister, because you are uncircumcised which is unclean for us.
We can only allow this, if all of your men consent to be circumcised.
Then we will let you marry our daughters, and we will marry your daughters, and we can all live together as one people.
But if you do not consent to be circumcised, then we will take our daughters and go."
Hamor and his son Shechem were pleased when they heard this.
Prince Shechem immediately agreed to their terms, because he was delighted with Jacob's daughter, and he was the most honorable man in his father's house.
Hamor and prince Shechem returned and entered the gates of their city and spoke to the men in their city.

Hamor and Shechem spoke to the men in their city and said, "These men are peaceful with us, and that is why we want to let them live in our land, and trade with us because the land is large enough for them and us. So, we can marry their daughters, and they can marry our daughters.
Jacob's people will only consent to live with us as one people if every male among us is circumcised as they are.
Their cattle, their wealth, and all of their animals will be added to ours only if we consent to what they request, and then they will live with us."
They all listened to Hamor and Shechem, so all the men left the city gates and went to be circumcised.

On the third day, while they were still sore from the operation, two of Jacob's sons, Simeon and Levi, took their swords and went to the city and boldly killed all the males to avenge their sister Dinah.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with their swords, then they took Dinah from Shechem's house and left.
Jacob's other sons raided the city after they saw all the dead men that were killed because Shechem had defiled their sister.
They took their sheep, oxen, donkeys, and everything else that was in their city or their fields.
They took all their wealth, all their children, and they took their wives captive and destroyed everything else in their homes.

Then Jacob spoke to Simeon and Levi and said, "You have disgraced me, and made me stink to all the other inhabitants of the land. The Canaanites and the Perizzites have me greatly outnumbered, and when they join together against me, they will kill me and you, and they will destroy my entire household."
And they said, "Should we let him treat our sister like a prostitute?"
God spoke to Jacob and said, "Get up and go live in Bethel, and build an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau's face."
Then Jacob said to everyone in his household, "Put away your strange gods and be clean and change your clothes.
Arise because we are going to live in Bethel, where I will build an altar to God. The God who answered my prayers when I was in distress, and the same God who is with me wherever I go."
So they gave Jacob all the strange gods they had in their hands and all of their earrings. Then Jacob hid them under an oak tree near Shechem.
As they were traveling the terror of God fell on all the cities around them, so the people in the cities did not pursue Jacob and his sons.
So Jacob and his people arrived in Luz in the land of Canaan, which is also known as Bethel.
Jacob built an altar there and called the place El-Bethel because that's where God appeared to him when he fled from his brother's face.
Rebekah's nurse Deborah died, and she was buried under an oak tree below Bethel named Allon-Bachuth.
When Jacob left Padan-Aram, God appeared to him again and blessed him.
God spoke to Jacob and said, "Your name is Jacob, but you will no longer be known as Jacob, so from now on you will be named Israel," and God changed Jacob's name to Israel.
Then God said to Jacob, "I am God Almighty, be fruitful and multiply, many nations will come from your descendants, and you will father kings.
The land which I gave Abraham and Isaac, I will pass down to you and your descendants after you."
And God left him there.
Jacob set up a stone column where God had spoken to him, then he poured a drink offering and an oil offering on it.
Jacob named that place Bethel because God had spoken to him there.
They left Bethel and traveled a short distance to Ephrath, where Rachel began to give birth and she went into hard labor.
While Rachel was in labor, the midwife said to her, "Fear not, because this son will also be born."
That's why as Rachel's soul was departing her body, and she was dying Rachel named her son Benoni, but his father called him Benjamin.
Rachel died, and Jacob buried her on the way to Ephrath, which is also Bethlehem.
Jacob built a column over Rachael's grave, that still sits above her grave to this day.
Israel journeyed on, and he camped on the other side of the tower of Edar.
While Israel was living in that land, Reuben had sex with his father's concubine Bilhah, and Israel heard them. And Jacob had twelve sons.
Jacob's firstborn son came from Leah, and they named him Reuben. Then Leah gave birth to his other sons Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
Jacob's sons from Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.
Jacob's sons from Rachel's housemaid Bilhah were Dan and Naphtali.
Jacob's sons from Leah's housemaid Zilpah were Gad and Asher. These are the names of Jacob's sons who were born to him in Padan-Aram.
Jacob returned to his father Isaac in Mamre near the city of Arbah in Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac had stayed.
Isaac lived to be 180 years old.
Isaac was an old man when he gave up the ghost and died. All of his people gathered together for his funeral, and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him there.
Now, this is the history of the descendants of Esau who is Edom.
Esau's wives were from the daughters of Canaan. Esau was married to Elon the Hivite's daughter Adah, and Aholibamah the daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite.
Esau was also married to Bashemath who was Ishmael's daughter, and Nebajoth's sister.
Adah gave birth to Esau's son Eliphaz, and Bashemath gave birth to Reuel.
Aholibamah gave birth to Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah. These are Esau's sons who were born in Canaan.
Esau took his wives, his children, and everyone in his household, plus his cattle, beasts, and everything that he had acquired in Canaan, and moved away from his brother Jacob's face.
Esau and Jacob were too wealthy to live together because the land could not provide enough food and water for their livestock.
Esau who is Edom lived on Mount Seir.
Esau was the father of the Edomites who lived on Mount Seir, and this is the history of Esau's descendants.
These are the names of Esau's sons, Eliphaz who Esau's wife Adah gave birth to, and Reuel who Esau's wife Bashemath gave birth to.
Eliphaz had other sons named Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.
Esau's son Eliphaz had a concubine named Timna, and she gave birth to Amalek. Esau and Adah were Eliphaz's parents.
These are Esau and Bashemath's grandsons whom their son Reuel fathered Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.
Esau's wife Aholibamah gave birth to Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah. Aholibamah was Anah's daughter and Zibeon's granddaughter.
Some of Esau's descendants were dukes. Esau's firstborn son Eliphaz fathered Duke Teman, Duke Omar, Duke Zepho, and Duke Kenaz.
Duke Korah, Duke Gatam, and Duke Amalek. Eliphaz fathered all of these dukes in Edom. Esau and Adah were their grandparents and Eliphaz's parents.
These are the sons of Esau and Bashemath's son Reuel, who fathered Duke Nahath, Duke Zerah, Duke Shammah, and Duke Mizzah. All of these dukes were born to Reuel in the land of Edom.
Esau's wife Aholibamah gave birth to Duke Jeush, Duke Jaalam, and Duke Korah. Aholibamah was Anah's daughter and Esau's wife.
Esau who is Edom, had sons who were dukes.
Seir was a Horite, and these were the names of his sons who inhabited the land, Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, and Anah.
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan were also Seir's children and they were the dukes of the Horites, in the land of Edom.
Lotan's children were Hori and Hemam. Lotan's sister was Timna.
Shobal's children were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.
Zibeon's children were Ajah and Anah. Anah was the one that found the mules in the wilderness while he was feeding his father Zibeon's donkeys.
Anah's children were his son Dishon and his daughter Aholibamah.
Dishon's children were Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
Ezer's children were Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.
Dishan's children were Uz and Aran.
These were the dukes of the Horites, Duke Lotan, Duke Shobal, Duke Zibeon, and Duke Anah.
Hori's children were Duke Dishon, Duke Ezer, and Duke Dishan, and they lived in Seir.
Before there were kings that governed Israel, there were kings that governed Edom.
Beor's son Bela reigned in Edom from the city of Dinhabah.
Bela died, and Zerah's son Jobab reigned in his place. Zerah was from Bozrah.
Jobab died, and Husham reigned in his place. Husham was from Temani.
Husham died, and Bedad's son Hadad reigned in his place, and he governed from Avith where he lived. Bedad defeated Midian in the field of Moab.
Hadad died, and Samlah from Masrekah reigned in his place.
Samlah died, and Saul from Rehoboth reigned in his place. Rehoboth was near the river.
Saul died, and Achbor's son Baal-Hanan reigned in his place.
Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place and he lived in Pau. Hadar's wife's name was Mehetabel, and she was the daughter of Matred and Mezahab.
Esau had many descendants who were dukes and these are their names, sorted by their families, where they are from, and by their names, Duke Timnah, Duke Alvah, and Duke Jetheth.
Duke Aholibamah, Duke Elah, and Duke Pinon.
Duke Kenaz, Duke Teman, and Duke Mibzar.
Duke Magdiel, and Duke Iram. All of these dukes were from Edom. Esau was the father of the Edomites.
Jacob lived in Canaan, where his father had lived before as a stranger.

This is the history of Jacob's descendants. Joseph was seventeen years old when he was feeding the flock with his brothers, and Joseph's father's sons from his wives Bilhah and Zilpah. And Joseph brought his father an evil report about them.
Israel was an old man when Joseph was born, and he loved Joseph more than any of his other children, so he made Joseph a coat of many colors.
When Joseph's brothers saw that their father Israel loved Joseph more than the rest of them, they were jealous, they hated him, and they could not speak peacefully to him.
One night Joseph had a dream, but when he told his brothers about it, they hated him even more.
And Joseph said to them, "Let me tell you about the dream I had last night.
We were binding sheaves out in the field. My sheaf was tall and honest, and when I looked, your sheaves were paying homage to mine."
After Joseph's brothers heard what Joseph said about his dream, they hated him even more, and Joseph's brothers asked him, "Do you think you are going to govern and have power over us?"
Then Joseph had another dream, and he told his brothers about that one too. Joseph said, "I had another dream, and I saw the sun, the moon, and eleven stars bowing down to me."

When Joseph told his father and brothers about his dream, his father reprimanded him and said, "What kind of dream have you dreamed? Should your mother, brothers, and I have to come and bow down before you?"
Joseph's brothers envied him even more, but Joseph's father thought about what Joseph had said.
So Joseph's brothers went to feed their father's flock in Shechem.
And Israel said to Joseph, "Your brothers are feeding the flock in Shechem, I want you to go meet them there." And Joseph said, "OK, I will go."
Then Israel said, "Go see how your brothers and the flocks are doing, then come back and tell me how it is going." So, Joseph left the Hebron valley and went to Shechem.
A man found Joseph wandering around the field, and the man asked him, "What are you searching for?"
And Joseph said, "I am looking for my brothers, do you know where they went to feed their flocks?"
And the man said, "They left, but I heard them say they were going to Dothan." So, Joseph followed his brothers and found them in Dothan.
Joseph's brothers saw him coming from far away, but before he got near them, they conspired to kill him.
And Joseph's brothers said to one another, "Behold the dreamer is coming.
We should kill him and throw him into a pit, and we can say that an evil beast devoured him, then we shall see if his dream comes true."
When Reuben heard this, he stopped them and said, "Do not kill him."

And Reuben said to them, "Do not shed his blood, throw him into a pit in the wilderness, but do not hurt him." Reuben thought he could save Joseph from his brother's hands and return him to his father.
When Joseph arrived, they stripped his coat of many colors from him.
Then they threw him into an empty pit with no water.
They sat down to eat their bread, and they looked up and saw a company of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were loaded with spices, balm, and myrrh that they were hauling down to Egypt.
And Judah said to his brothers, "There is no profit in it for us if we kill our brother.
We can sell Joseph to the Ishmaelites, and then his blood will not be on our hands, because he is our own flesh and blood and he is our brother.
As the Midianite merchants were passing by, the brothers pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him for twenty pieces of silver, and the Ishmaelites took him to Egypt.
When Reuben returned, he noticed that Joseph was not in the pit and he was very distraught.
He went back to his brothers and said, "The child is not in the well, so where can I go now?"
So they killed a kid goat and dipped Joseph's coat of many colors in the blood.
They took his coat of many colors to their father Jacob and said, "We found this, and we think it is Joseph's coat of many colors."
When Jacob saw it, he knew it was Joseph's coat and he said, "This is my son's coat, an evil beast has torn him apart and eaten him."
Jacob tore his clothes and put on a sackcloth and mourned his son for many days.
All of Jacob's sons and daughters came to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. And Jacob said, "I will go down to my grave mourning my son," then he wept for him some more.
The Midianites went down to Egypt and sold Joseph to one of Pharaoh's officers, a man named Potiphar who was the captain of the guard.
After that, Judah left his brothers and went down to Adullam, where he stayed with a man named Hirah who was an Adullamite.
Judah saw Shuah the Canaanite's daughter, and they consummated their marriage after they were married.
She conceived and gave birth to a son who Judah named Er.
Shuah conceived again and gave birth to another son, and she named him Onan.
Then Shuah conceived again and gave birth to a son in Chezib, and she named him Shelah.
Judah found a woman named Tamar for his firstborn son Er to marry.
But Judah's firstborn son was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord killed him.
Then Judah said to Onan, "Go marry your brother Er's wife, and raise his children as your own."

Onan knew Tamar was pregnant with his brother's child, and that the baby would not be his. So, when he had relations with his brother Er's wife, he spilled his semen on the ground, because he did not want to be responsible for his brother's children.
This displeased the Lord, so he took his life too.

Then Judah said to his daughter-in-law Tamar, "Go live with your father, and I want you to remain a widow until my son Shelah grows up because I do not want him to die like his brothers." So, Tamar went to live in her father's house.

After some time had passed, Judah's wife died. When Judah finished grieving, Judah and his friend Hirah went to shear his sheep in Timnah. Judah's wife was Shuah's daughter, and Hirah was an Adullamite.
Someone told Tamar, "Your father-in-law is going to Timnah to shear his sheep."

So Tamar changed her widow's clothes and covered her face with a veil. Then she sat out in the open beside the road to Timnah because she knew that Judah's son Shelah was a grown man, and she had not been given to him as his wife.
When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute because her face was covered.

He did not know that she was his daughter-in-law, and when he saw her on the side of the road, he told her that he wanted to have relations with her. And Tamar said, "And what will you give me for this?"
And Judah said, "I will send you one of the kid goats from my herd." And Tamar said, "Will you give me something of value to hold until you send it to me?"
And Judah said, "What do you want?" And Tamar said, "Your signet, your bracelets, and that staff in your hand." So, Judah gave it to her and had relations with her, and she got pregnant.
When she got up and went home, she removed her veil and put her widow's clothes back on.
Then Judah sent Hirah his Adullamite friend, along with the young goat he had promised Tamar to retrieve his belongings, but Hirah could not find Tamar.
So Hirah asked the men there if they knew where the prostitute went, who was sitting by the side of the road and they said, "There are no prostitutes here."
When Hirah returned to Judah he said, "I could not find her and the men there said, that there were no prostitutes there."
And Judah said, "I sent the goat I promised her with you, but you did not find her, so let her keep everything or we will be humiliated."
About three months later, someone told Judah that his daughter-in-law Tamar was a prostitute and she was pregnant and Judah said, "Take her out and burn her."

When they went to get Tamar, she sent her father-in-law's signet, staff, and bracelets to him and she said, "I pray that the man who owns these things will recognize them because he is the father of this child."
Judah acknowledged that they were his things and he said, "She has been more righteous than me because I did not give her to be my son Shelah's wife," and Judah never had relations with Tamar again.
When Tamar went into labor, she gave birth to twins.
While Tamar was giving birth, the first baby put his hand out and the midwife tied a ribbon around his arm and said, "This one came out first."
Then the baby withdrew his hand, and his brother came out first and the midwife said, "How did you break out first?" So, he was named Pharez.
Then Pharez's brother who had the scarlet thread tied to his arm came out, and he was called Zarah.
Joseph was taken down to Egypt and an Egyptian named Potiphar, who was one of Pharaoh's officers and a captain of the guard bought Joseph from the Ishmaelites.
The Lord was with Joseph, and he became a prosperous man and lived in his Egyptian master's house.
Joseph's master Potiphar saw that the Lord was with Joseph, and the Lord made Joseph prosperous in everything that he did.
Potiphar saw Joseph in a favorable light, and he made Joseph his household manager and gave Joseph control over everything in his household.
From then on Joseph was the manager of Potiphar's entire household, the Lord blessed the Egyptian's house, along with everything he owned and everything in his field because of Joseph.
Potiphar gave Joseph control of everything, and he did not worry about anything that he owned except his food. Joseph was a good man, and everyone liked him.
After all this, Joseph's master Potiphar's wife tried to seduce Joseph and she said to him, "Let's go to bed and have relations."
But Joseph refused and he said, "My master does not worry about anything I do in this household, and he has committed everything he owns to me.
Nobody in this house is greater than me and he has not withheld anything from me except for you. You are his wife, so how can I betray him with this great wickedness and sin against God?"
Potiphar's wife talked to Joseph about it every day, but he would not listen to her, and he refused to go to bed with her.
About this same time, Joseph went to the house to do his business and there were no other men in the house.
Potiphar's wife grabbed Joseph's robe and said, "Go to bed with me!" So, Joseph ran out the door and fled, but she still had his robe in her hand.
When Potiphar's wife saw that Joseph had run away and she still had his robe.
She summoned the men of her household and told them, "Potiphar brought this Hebrew into this house to mock us. Joseph wanted to go to bed with me, so I screamed as loud as I could.
When Joseph heard me screaming and crying, he ran off without his robe."
Potiphar's wife laid Joseph's robe on the bed beside her, until Potiphar came home.
Potiphar's wife spoke to Potiphar and said, "This Hebrew servant, that you brought into this house came in here to mock me.
When I started screaming and crying, he fled without his robe.
After Potiphar heard what his wife said about his servant Joseph, he was very angry.
So Joseph's master put him in the king's prison, and he was kept there with all the other prisoners.
But the Lord was with Joseph and showed him mercy, and the prison warden saw him in a favorable light.
The warden put Joseph in charge of the other prisoners, and Joseph was responsible for everything that the other prisoners did.
The warden trusted everything he put under Joseph's control. For the Lord was with Joseph, and the Lord made everything that Joseph did very prosperous.
Sometime later, the Egyptian King's butler and his baker offended the Egyptian king.
Pharaoh was angry with both the chief butler and the chief baker.
He made them wards in Potiphar's house, Potiphar was Pharoah's captain of the guard, and he put them in the prison where Joseph was being held.
Potiphar made Joseph their servant, and they were kept in prison for a long time.
Both of them had a dream one night, and neither the butler nor the baker could interpret their dreams.
Joseph came in one morning, and he noticed that they were sad.
So he asked Pharaoh's officers, "Why are you so sad?"

And they replied to Joseph and said, "We have had dreams and there is no one who can interpret them for us." And Joseph said to them, "Do not dream interpretations belong to God? Tell me about your dream."
So the chief butler told Joseph about his dream and he said, "In my dream, I saw a vine in front of me.
The vine had three branches, it was budding and blossoming, and it was covered with clusters of ripe grapes.
Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I pressed the grapes into his cup, and I put the cup into his hand."
Then Joseph said to him, "This is how to interpret the dream, the three branches are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will take you out of this prison, and he will restore you to your former place as his chief butler, and you will place Pharoah's cup into his hand.
Do not forget me and remember to be kind to me when you are taken out of this place. I also pray that you will mention me to Pharaoh and ask him to bring me out of this house.
Because I was stolen from the land of the Hebrews, and I have done nothing to deserve being put into this dungeon."
When the chief baker saw that Joseph's interpretation of the butler's dream was good, he said to him, "In my dream, I had three white baskets on my head.
The top basket had all kinds of baked goods for Pharaoh, and the birds ate them out of the basket."
Joseph answered him and said, "This is how I interpret your dream; the three baskets are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will take you from this prison and hang you on a tree, then the birds will eat your flesh."
The third day was Pharaoh's birthday, and he brought the chief butler and chief baker out of prison to prepare a feast for his servants.
Pharaoh restored the chief butler to his position of prominence, and the butler put the cup into Pharaoh's hand.
But he hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had predicted.
But the chief butler did not remember Joseph and forgot all about him.
Two years later, Pharaoh had a dream that he was standing beside the river.
He saw seven fat cows come up out of the river, and they fed in a meadow.
Then seven poor, sick, and lean cows came up out of the river and stood beside the other cows on the riverbank.
The poor, sick, and lean cows ate the seven fat cows, then Pharaoh woke up.
Pharaoh went back to sleep and he had another dream, and he saw seven full, fat, and ripe wheat heads all on one stalk.
Then seven weathered and thin wheat heads sprung up, and they were blasted by an east wind.
The seven thin wheat stalks devoured the seven good wheat stalks, then Pharaoh woke up and realized it was a dream.
The next morning Pharoah's spirit was troubled, and he sent for all the sorcerers and wise men in Egypt. Pharaoh told the sorcerers and wise men his dream, but none of them could interpret it.
Then the chief butler told Pharaoh, "Today, I remember my transgressions.
When Pharaoh was angry with me and the chief baker, he made both of us wards in Potiphar's house and we were imprisoned.
Both of us had a dream one night, and neither one of us could interpret our dreams.
But there was a young Hebrew man in prison with us, who was a servant to the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he interpreted them for us.
When he interpreted our dreams everything, he said came true. He told me that I would be restored to my office, and he told the chief baker that he would be hanged."
Then Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and they immediately brought him out of the dungeon. He shaved, changed his clothes, and was brought to Pharaoh.
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I had a dream, and nobody knows how to interpret it. I have heard that you can understand and interpret dreams."
Joseph answered Pharaoh and said, "It is not me but God who will answer Pharaoh and give you peace of mind."
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "In my dream, I was standing on the bank of the river.
Seven fat cows came up out of the river and fed in a meadow.
Then seven poor, sick, and lean cows came up out of the river after them. I have never seen anything like that in Egypt before, it was bad.
The poor, sick, and lean cows ate the seven fat cows.
After they had eaten them, you could not even tell that they had eaten the healthy cows because they were still sick, poor, and lean, then I woke up.
I went back to sleep and I had another dream. In that dream, I saw seven full, fat, and good wheat heads on one stalk.
Then seven weathered and thin wheat stalks sprung up, and they were blasted by an east wind.
The thin wheat stalks devoured the seven good wheat stalks, I told the sorcerers about these dreams, but none of them could interpret them for me."
Then Joseph said to Pharaoh, "Both of Pharoah's dreams are the same dream, God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
The seven good cows and the seven good wheat stalks each represent seven years, and they are both parts of the same dream.
The seven lean and sick cows and the seven thin and weathered wheat stalks that were blasted with an east wind will be seven years of famine.
As I have told Pharaoh, God has revealed what he has planned for the future.
There will be seven years of great plenty throughout all of Egypt.
Then there will be seven years of famine, and the bounty throughout the land will be forgotten in Egypt, and a great famine will consume the land.
The abundance throughout the land will be forgotten because the famine that follows will be very grievous.
That's why Pharaoh's dream was doubled, because this thing that God has decided, will soon come to pass.
And that's why Pharaoh should find a wise and careful man and give him control over all of Egypt.
Pharaoh should appoint officers over the land and have them store up 20% of the land's harvest during the seven years of plenty.
The people should gather all the food during those good years, and store wheat in the cities under Pharaoh's control.
That food will be stored to protect the land against the seven years of famine so that the land of Egypt does not perish."
So both Pharaoh and all of his servants thought this was a good idea.
Then Pharaoh told his servants, "Where can we find a man who has the Spirit of God with him like this?"
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Because God has shown you all of this, nobody else is as wise and careful as you.
You will be over my house, and my people will be ruled by your word. The only place where I will be greater than you is in the throne room."
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I have given you control over the whole land of Egypt."
Pharaoh took the ring off his hand and put it on Joseph's hand. He clothed him in fine linen and put a gold chain around his neck.
He made Joseph his second in command and gave him a chariot and servants who ran out in front of him and shouted to the people to bow down, and he made Joseph the ruler over all the land of Egypt.
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh, but everyone in Egypt will follow your orders."
Pharaoh changed Joseph's name and called him Zaphnath-Paaneah. He gave Asenath to him for a wife, and she was the daughter of priest Potipherah from On, so Joseph ruled over all of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before the Egyptian Pharaoh, and when he left Pharaoh's presence, he traveled throughout Egypt.
During those seven years of plenty in Egypt, the earth produced crops very abundantly.
Joseph had all the food in Egypt gathered and stored in the cities during those seven years of bounty.
Joseph gathered wheat like it was the sand of the oceans, the harvest was too much to count.
Joseph's wife Asenath gave birth to two sons before the famine. Potipherah who was the priest of On, was Asenath's father.
Joseph named his firstborn son Manasseh because he said, "God has made me forget all my toil and my father's house."
He named his second son Ephraim because he said, "God has blessed me in the land where I have suffered."
Then the seven years of plenty ended.
Just as Joseph had said the seven years of famine began, and the shortage was everywhere but there was bread in Egypt.
When the famine came to Egypt, the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread and he said to them, "Go see Joseph, and do whatever he tells you to do."
The famine covered the entire earth, and Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold food to the Egyptians, and the famine grew worse.
All the other countries came to Egypt to buy wheat from Joseph because the famine throughout the world was so terrible.
When Jacob heard that there was wheat in Egypt, he said to his sons, "Why are you standing around staring at each other?
I just heard that there is wheat in Egypt, go down there and buy some wheat so we do not starve to death."
Ten of Joseph's brothers went to Egypt to buy wheat.
But Jacob did not send Joseph's brother Benjamin with them, because he was afraid something bad would happen to him.
Israel's sons were some of the many people who went to buy wheat in Egypt because there was famine throughout the land of Canaan.
Joseph was the governor of Egypt, and he sold wheat to people from every land, and his brothers came and bowed down to him.
When Joseph saw his brothers, he knew who they were but acted like they were strangers. He spoke forcefully and asked them, "Where do you come from?" And they said, "We came from Canaan to buy food."
Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
Then Joseph remembered the dreams he had told them about and he said, "You are spies, and you have come here to discover our weaknesses and vulnerabilities."
And they said, "No my Lord, we have come here to buy food.
We are the sons of a man, who taught us to be truthful men, we are your servants and we are not spies!"
And he said to them, "No, I believe you are spies, and I think you have come here to probe our weaknesses and vulnerabilities."

And they said, "We are not spies, we are your servants, we are ten of twelve brothers, and we are the sons of a man from Canaan. Our youngest brother is still with our father, and he is not here with us."
And Joseph said, "No, it is just as I said before, all of you are spies!"
Then Joseph said, "As long as Pharaoh lives, you will not be allowed leave here unless you bring your youngest brother here.

Send one of your brothers to fetch him, and I will keep the other brothers in prison until they return. If they return, it will prove that you are telling the truth, if they do not return it will prove that you are lying, but as surely as Pharaoh lives, I believe you are spies."
And Joseph put them all in prison for three days.
On the third day, Joseph said to them, "If you bring your youngest brother here, you will live because I fear God.
I want to see if you are honest men or not, so I will keep one of your brothers here in prison. The rest of you can go home and carry the wheat with you for your starving people.
But you must bring your youngest brother back to me, to prove that you are telling the truth and you will not die." So that's what they did.
And they said one to another, "We are being punished for what we did to Joseph, we saw his anguish when he begged for his life, and we refused to listen and that's why this distress come upon us."
Reuben answered them and said, "I told you not to harm the child, and you would not listen to me, and now we are being held responsible for the loss of his blood."
Joseph's brothers did not know that he could understand what they were saying, because he had used an interpreter to speak to them before.
Joseph turned away from them and wept, and when he turned back to them, he took Simeon from them and had him bound up in front of them.

Then Joseph commanded his servants to fill his brother's sacks with wheat and told them to put their money back in their sacks, and he also told his servants to give them enough provisions for their trip home.
They loaded their donkeys with wheat and left.
On the way home, one of the brothers opened his sack to feed his donkey, and he saw the money in his sack.
And he said to his brothers, "Look at this, I found my money in this sack." They were scared and afraid, and they said to each other, "What has God done to us?"
When they returned to Canaan, they told their father Jacob everything that had happened to them.
They said, "The Egyptian Lord, who was in charge there thought we were spies.
We told him that we were honest men and that we were not spies.
We told him that we were twelve brothers and that we all had the same father. We told him we were all there except for our youngest brother, who stayed in Canaan with our father.
And the Egyptian Lord said to us, "I will test you to see if you are honest men or not, leave one of your brothers here with me, and take food back to the starving people where you live.

Bring your youngest brother to me, then I will know that you are true and honest men and you are not spies. If you do this, I will return your brother to you, and you will be allowed to trade and barter here."
When we emptied our sacks, all of our money was in there. When they showed their father the bundles of money, they were all afraid.
And Jacob said, "You have taken my children from me. Joseph is not here, Simeon is not here, and now you want to take my youngest son Benjamin away from me, everything is against me."
And Reuben said to his father, "You can kill my two sons if I do not bring Simeon back to you, let me take Benjamin, and I will bring Simeon back to you."

And Jacob said, "Benjamin cannot go with you, because his brother is dead and he is the only one I have left. If something happened to Benjamin on the way, I would go to my grave in sorrow because of you."
The famine grew worse throughout the land.
After they had eaten all of the wheat they bought in Egypt, Jacob said to his sons, "Go back to Egypt and buy more food."
And Judah said to his father Jacob, "The man there was very serious when he said we would not be allowed to see him unless we brought our brother back with us.
If you send Benjamin with us, we will go back down there and buy more food.
If you do not let Benjamin go with us, we cannot go back there because the man said that we would not be allowed to see him if we did not bring our brother with us."
And Israel said, "If the man was so hostile towards you, why did you tell him you had another brother?"

And they said, "The man asked us straight out about our relatives, and he asked us if our father was still alive. Then he asked us if we had another brother, and we could tell by the tone of his voice that he did not trust us, so how could we have known that he would tell us to bring Benjamin down there?"

And Judah said to Israel, "Send the boy with me, and we will get up early in the morning and go down there, otherwise we are all going to starve to death including you and me, all of our children, and everybody else.
I will make sure he is safe, and I promise to bring him back to you safe and sound. If I do not, it will be my fault, and you can blame me forever.
If we had not lingered here, we could have already gone down there and back, twice."

And Israel said to them, "If we have to do this, take some of our best fruits from the land and carry a present to the man, a little balm, a little honey, some spices, some myrrh, some nuts, and almonds.
Take twice as much money with you, plus the money you brought back with you the last time you went there. Carry it all back down there, and maybe they just made a mistake.
Take your brother, get up early, go to Egypt and see the man again.

May God Almighty show mercy on you when you see that man again, and I will pray for him to send Simeon and Benjamin back home with you. But, if I must grieve for my children, then I have no choice but to grieve for my children."
They got up early the next morning and took the presents, all the money, and Benjamin with them down to Egypt, where they stood before Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin, he spoke to his house manager and said, "Bring these men to my home, and slaughter an animal and prepare a meal because these men will dine with me at noon."
Joseph's servant did what he was told and brought the men to his house.

They were afraid when they got to Joseph's house. So, they said to one another, "They are going to take our donkeys, and then they will take us as slaves, and it is all because of the money that we found in our sacks on the way home the last time we were here.
When they approached the door of Joseph's house, they said to his manager.
"Sir, the first time we came here, we only came to buy food.
When we arrived at the inn, we opened our sacks and our money was in the sacks, but we brought all of that money back to you.
We have also brought more money with us to buy food, and we do not know who put our money back in our sacks.
And he said, "Peace be with you, do not fear, your God and the God of your father has given you the treasure in your sacks, I had your money." Then he brought their brother Simeon to them.
The servant brought the men to Joseph's house and gave them water, they washed their feet and he fed their donkeys.
Joseph came home at noon, and they prepared the presents they had brought to him because they heard they were going to eat with him.
When Joseph came home, they brought him their presents and bowed down to him.
Joseph asked them if they were well and he said, "Is your father, the old man you told me about still alive?"
And they answered, "Our father is alive, and he is in good health." Then they bowed down and offered their gift to him.

When Joseph looked up, he saw his brother Benjamin, who was his mother Rachel's only other son. Joseph asked them, "Is this the younger brother you told me about?" Then Joseph spoke to the younger brother and said, "May God be gracious to you, my son."
Joseph had to hurry away because he was upset when he saw his brother Benjamin, so he went to his room to weep.
Joseph regained his composure, and after he washed his face, he returned to his brothers and said, "Serve the food."
They served Joseph by himself, and his brothers by themselves. The Egyptians also ate by themselves because they thought it was an abomination for Egyptians to eat with Hebrews.
Joseph's brothers sat before him, in order by their ages from the oldest to the youngest, and the men were absolutely amazed by the way they were being treated.
They were served from Joseph's table, but Benjamin's portion was five times more than any of the others. And they ate, drank, and made merry with him.
Joseph ordered his house manager to fill the men's sacks with as much food as they could carry, and he told him to put their money back in their sacks.
Joseph also told his house manager to put his personal silver cup and the youngest one's food money in his sack, and Joseph's servant did what he was told to do.
At morning's first light, the men left with their donkeys.

After Jacob's sons left the city, they had not gotten very far when Joseph spoke to his manager and said, "Follow them, and when you catch up with them, tell them, 'You have rewarded us evil for good?
This is my Lord's personal cup, that he also uses for prophecy? You have done an evil thing by stealing from him.'"
When Joseph's servant overtook them, he told them word for word what Joseph had told him to say.
And they said to him, "Why are you accusing us of stealing from your master? God forbid that we should sin against you.
We brought the money we found in our sacks back to you from Canaan, why would we steal gold or silver from your Lord?
If you find it in the possession of any of your servants, let him die and the rest of us will be my Lord's slaves."
And Joseph's man said, "It will be as you say, whoever is found to have it in their possession will be my slave, and the rest of you will be held blameless."
They quickly put their sacks on the ground and opened them.
He began his search with the oldest brother's sack and finished with the youngest, and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack.
Then they tore their clothes, loaded their donkeys and returned to the city.
Joseph was still at his house when Judah and his brothers returned, and they fell to the ground in front of him.
And Joseph said to them, "What have you done? Do you not know that a man like me can divinely discover things?"
And Judah said, "What can we say to clear ourselves my Lord? God has found the immorality of your servants, we are my Lord's servants, along with the one who was found with the cup."

And Joseph said, "God forbid that I should blame innocent men for the crimes of just one man. The man who had the cup in his possession will be my servant, and the rest of you can go in peace back to your father."
Then Judah moved closer to him and said, "Please my Lord, do not be angry with me and let me speak to you, because you are as powerful as Pharaoh.
You asked us if we had another brother or a father?
And we answered you and said, 'Our father is an old man. He had another son in his old age, but Benjamin's brother is dead. Benjamin is the only son left from his mother and his father loves him.'
You told us to bring him to you, because you wanted to see him.
And we said to you, 'The boy cannot leave his father, because his father will die if he leaves him.'
And you said to us, 'Unless you bring your youngest brother back with you, you will not be allowed to see me again.'
When we told our father what you said.
He told us to go and buy a little more food.
And we said, 'We cannot go there unless we bring our youngest brother with us, because the man said we will not be allowed to see him unless we bring our youngest brother with us.'
And our father said to us, 'You know that my wife bore two sons to me.
One of them left me and I said, "Joseph has been torn to pieces, and I will never see him again."
If you take this son from me and something happens to him; you will bring me down to my grave in sorrow and grief.'
My father's life is centered around that boy and if we return without him.
When our father sees that the boy has not returned with us, he will die of grief, and we will have to take him down to his grave in sorrow.
I guaranteed the boy's safety to my father and said, 'If I do not bring him back, then my father can blame me forever.'
That's why, I beg you to let me be your slave instead of the boy and let him go home with his brothers.
How can I return to my father without the boy because if I do, I will be forced to watch the evil that overcomes my father."
Joseph could not refrain himself any longer and he began to cry. He told all his men to leave and then he told his brothers who he was.
He began to weep out loud, and the Egyptians heard him crying and told everyone in Pharaoh's house.
Joseph said to his brothers, "I am your brother Joseph, is my father still alive?" But his brothers could not answer him because they were terrified of him.
And Joseph said to his brothers, "Please come over here." They approached him and he said, "I am your brother Joseph, the one you sold into slavery in Egypt.
