You should not be grieved or angry with yourselves for selling me into slavery, because God sent me here to save your life.
There has been a terrible famine in the land for the last two years, and it will last for another five years. There will be no crops to harvest.
God sent me here to save your lives and deliver you from starvation, and to protect your descendants.
So it was God who sent me here, not you. God made me a father to Pharaoh, Lord over his whole house and a ruler throughout Egypt.
I do not want you to waste any time, go back and tell father that God has made his son Joseph Lord over all of Egypt. Tell him I want all of you to come here and live with me.
Tell him I will give all of you a place to live in the land of Goshen. Bring your children, your children's children, your flocks, your herds, and everything that own.
I will provide for all of you because there are five more years of famine coming. If you do not come here, your entire household will become impoverished.
All of you including Benjamin can see for yourselves, that I am your brother Joseph.
So go and tell my father about the honor that has been bestowed upon me in Egypt. Tell him about everything you have seen, then bring him here as fast as you can."
Then Joseph hugged Benjamin's neck and wept, and Benjamin hugged him back and wept with him.
He kissed each one of his brothers, and they all wept with him. After that, he talked with them.
Everyone in Pharaoh's house heard that Joseph's brothers were there. Pharaoh and all of his servants were pleased to hear this news.
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Tell your brothers to load their pack animals and go back to Canaan.
Tell them to bring your father here, along with everyone else in his household. I will give them good lands in Egypt, and they will eat from the fat of the land."
Then Pharoah said to Joseph's brothers, "Take some wagons from Egypt to bring your wives, your children, and your father here.
Do not worry about your possessions, because you will be given everything you need when you get to Egypt."
Then Israel's sons did everything Pharoah told them to do. Joseph gave them wagons and enough provisions for their trip.
Joseph gave each man a change of clothing, but he gave Benjamin 300 silver shekels, and 5 changes of clothes.
Joseph also sent his father ten female donkeys loaded with wheat, bread, meat, and all the good things from Egypt.
So Joseph's brothers left, and he told them not to argue amongst themselves along the way.
They left Egypt and went back to Canaan, then straight to their father Jacob.
When they arrived, they said to their father, "Joseph is still alive, he is the governor over the whole land of Egypt," and Jacob's heart fainted because he did not believe them.
Then they told him everything that Joseph said, and when Jacob saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him there, his spirits were lifted.
And Israel said, "It is more than enough that my son Joseph is still alive, and I want to go see him before I die."
Israel left with everything he owned and went to Beersheba where he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
God spoke to Israel through visions that night and said, "Jacob, Jacob." And Israel said, "I am here."
And God said, "I am your father's God, and I do not want you to be afraid to go down to Egypt, because I will make you a great nation there.
I will go down to Egypt with you, and I will also bring you up again, and Joseph will be the one who closes your eyes with his hand when you die."
Jacob's sons carried him along with their wives and children when they left Beersheba and went to Egypt in the wagons that Pharaoh sent.
They took Jacob's offspring, their cattle, and everything else that they owned when they left Canaan and went down to Egypt.
Jacob took his sons, his grandsons, his daughters, his granddaughters, and all of his descendants down to Egypt with him.
These are the names of Israel's offspring that he took down to Egypt with him, beginning with his firstborn son Reuben.
Reuben's sons were named, Hanoch, Phallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
Simeon's sons were named, Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul who was the son of a Canaanite woman.
Levi's sons were named, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
Judah's sons were named, Er, Onan, Shelah, Pharez, and Zarah, but Er and Onan died in Canaan, and Pharez's sons were Hezron and Hamul.
Issachar's sons were named, Tola, Phuvah, Job, and Shimron.
Zebulun's sons were named, Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These are the names of all of Jacob and Leah's sons born in Padan-Aram. They also had a daughter named Dinah. So altogether Jacob and Leah's children totaled 33 souls.
Gad's sons were named, Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
Asher's sons were named, Jimnah, Ishuah, Isui, Beriah, and their sister's name was Serah. Beriah's sons' names were Heber and Malchiel.
Jacob and Zilpah's sons totaled 16 souls. Zilpah was a servant that Laban gave his daughter Leah when she married Jacob, and Leah gave Zilpah to Jacob as a wife because she wanted more children.
Jacob's wife Rachel had two sons, Joseph and Benjamin.
Joseph was married to Asenath the daughter of priest Potipherah of On in Egypt, who gave birth to two children named Manasseh and Ephraim.
Benjamin's sons were named Belah, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
Altogether Jacob and Rachel's sons totaled 14 souls.
Dan's son was named Hushim.
Naphtali's sons were named Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
When Jacob and Rachel were married, her father Laban gave his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel. Rachael gave Bilhah to Jacob for a wife, and Jacob and Bilhah had seven children.
Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt with him totaled 66 souls, not including his son's wives.
Joseph had two sons born in Egypt. And altogether Jacob had a total of 70 souls that went down to Egypt with him.
Jacob sent Judah to Joseph ahead of him, to get the directions to Goshen. When they arrived in Goshen,
Joseph took his chariot to meet his father Israel in Goshen. When Joseph arrived, he hugged his father and wept for a good while.
Then Israel said to Joseph, "Now I can die because now I know you are still alive!"
And Joseph said to his father and brothers, "I will go to Pharaoh and tell him, 'My brothers and father have come to see me from Canaan with their entire households.
They are shepherds and they have fed and herded cattle for their entire life. And they have brought their flocks, herds, and everything they own with them to Goshen.'
Someday Pharaoh will send for you, and he will ask you about your occupation.

Tell him that you are shepherds, and just like your fathers were before you, you have been herding cattle since you were children. Then he will allow you to live in the land of Goshen, because the Egyptians think that shepherds are an abomination."

Then Joseph went to tell Pharaoh that his family was in Goshen. Joseph said to Pharaoh, "My father and brothers have come here from Canaan. They brought their flocks, herds, and everything they own with them." Jacob was Joseph's father; Jacob was also known as Israel. God changed Jacob's name to Israel after Jacob stayed up all night wrestling with God's angel.
Then Joseph took five of his brothers to meet Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked them, "What is your occupation?" They answered Pharaoh and said, "We are your servants and we are shepherds, just like our fathers before us.
We have come here because the famine in Canaan is so severe that we have no pasture for our flocks. We have come to beg Pharaoh to let us live in the land of Goshen."
Pharaoh spoke to Joseph and said, "Your father and brothers have come to you for help.
The land of Egypt is yours to do with as you please, let your father and brothers live in the best land in Goshen, and if any of them have exceptional abilities, then let them manage my cattle."
Joseph brought his father to meet Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked Israel, "How old are you?"
Jacob answered Pharaoh and said, "I am 130 years old, I have lived a long, hard, and difficult life, but I still have not lived as long as my fathers did when they walked on the earth."
Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and left his presence.
Joseph did what Pharoah told him to do, and he gave his father and brothers possession of the best lands in the Rameses area of Egypt.
Joseph provided bread for his father, brothers, and everyone in each family based on the number of children in their household.
There was no bread anywhere because the famine was very severe, and the famine caused the entire lands of Egypt and Canaan to starve.
Joseph collected all the money in Egypt and Canaan for Pharoah for the wheat that all the people bought from him.
When the money in Egypt and Canaan failed, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, "Please give us some bread, or we will die in front of you because the money has failed."
Joseph said, "Since the money has failed if you bring your cattle here, I will give you bread for your cattle."
They brought their cattle to Joseph, and Joseph gave them bread in exchange for horses, flocks, herds of cattle, and donkeys. Then he fed them with bread that was paid for by their cattle that year.
When that year ended, they came to Joseph again and they said to him, "We have no money, my Lord has our herds of cattle, we have nothing left except for our bodies and our lands.

We are all going to die right in front of you, and so will our land without your help. We can only offer you our bondage and our lands, as payment for some bread. We will be Pharaoh's servants and give him our lands in exchange for seed so that we can survive, and the land is not left desolate."
So Joseph bought up all the land in Egypt for Pharaoh, because every man in Egyptian sold his field to him. Because the famine had left them no choice, so all the land became Pharaohs.
Joseph moved all the people to cities from one end of Egypt to the other.
The priests were the only ones who were not forced to sell their land to Pharaoh because he gave them enough food to survive.
Then Joseph said to the people, "Today I have bought you and your land for Pharaoh, in return you have received seed to sow the land.
When your crops are ready to harvest, you must give 20% of your harvest to Pharaoh. You may keep the remaining 80% to feed your children and yourselves.
And they said, "You have saved our lives, we hope to please my Lord, and we will be Pharaoh's servants."

Then Joseph passed a law in Egypt that is still in effect today, that says that Pharaoh will be paid 20% of the people's harvest, but Pharoah's priests were not forced to sell themselves to Pharaoh as slaves.
Israel lived and owned land in the Goshen area of Egypt, where they grew and multiplied abundantly.
Jacob lived in Egypt for 17 years, and he lived to be 147 years old.

Israel was old and near death when he asked to see his son Joseph. When Joseph arrived his father Israel spoke to him and said, "If you still love me, put your hand under my thigh, be kind to me and please do not bury me in Egypt.
Promise me that you will carry me out of Egypt and bury me where my fathers are buried. And Joseph said, "I promise I will do what you have asked me to do."
And Jacob said, "Swear it to me!" And Joseph swore to him, then Israel bowed to pray on the bed's headboard.
Sometime after that, someone told Joseph that his father was sick and he took his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim to visit him.
One of them said to Jacob, "Your son Joseph has come to visit you," and Israel sat up on the bed.
Then Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me."
And he said to me, 'I will make you fruitful, and I will multiply you and make your descendants a multitude of people, and I will give this land to your descendants as an everlasting possession.'
Now your two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh who were born in Egypt before I came here, are my descendants just as much as Reuben and Simeon.
Just like your sons' children will also be your descendants, and they will be named after their brothers, and they will be given their inheritance under their brothers' names.
As for me, when I came from Padan, Rachel died by my side in Canaan on the way to Ephrath, and I buried her there." Ephrath is also called Bethlehem.
Israel saw Joseph's sons and said, "Who are they?"
And Joseph said to his father, "They are my sons. God gave them to me when I came to Egypt." And Jacob said, "Please bring them here and I will bless them."
Israel was old and he was slowly losing his sight, so Joseph brought them over to their grandfather and he kissed and embraced them.
Then Israel said to Joseph, "I never thought I would see your face again, but God has brought me here, and I have seen you and your children."
Then Joseph picked his children up off of Israel's lap, and he bowed facedown toward him.
Joseph put Ephraim's right hand in Israel's left hand and Manasseh's left hand in Israel's right hand.
Then Israel put his right hand on Ephraim's head and his left hand on Manasseh's head. Manasseh was Joseph's firstborn son and Ephraim was his youngest son.
Israel blessed Joseph and said, "I ask my God, the same God that walked with my fathers Abraham and Isaac, the God that has fed me my whole entire life to this very day.
The angel who rescued me from all evil, I ask you to bless these boys and let them be named after me and my fathers Abraham and Isaac. Let them grow and multiply abundantly on the earth."
When Joseph saw his father laid his right hand on Ephraim's head he was displeased, and he tried to move his father's hand from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head.
And Joseph said to his father, "No father, put your right hand on Manasseh's head because he is my firstborn son."

Jacob refused and said, "I know that Joseph, I also know that he will grow to become a great people, but his younger brother will truly become greater than him, and his descendants will grow into a multitude of nations."
So Jacob blessed both of them that day and said, "You will be blessed in Israel's name, may God bless Ephraim and Manasseh," and he blessed Ephraim before he blessed Manasseh.
Then Israel said to Joseph, "I am dying, but God will be with you, and he will bring you back to the land of your fathers.
Besides that, I have given you a piece of land that overlooks your brothers' land. I took that land by force from the Amorites with my sword and bow."
Jacob gathered all his sons together and said, "I want to tell you what will happen to you in the last days.
Listen to me, I am your father Jacob, and I want you to listen to your father Israel.
Reuben, you are my firstborn, the source of my might and strength and you excel in dignity and power.
But, you are as unstable as water and you will not excel, because you defiled my bed with my concubine Bilhah.
Simeon and Levi are brothers, but they are both cruel to everyone in their homes.

I do not want to hear what they have to say. I do not want my honor or glory bestowed upon them because they killed men in anger. They knocked down a wall because they are cruel and stubborn, and they have no self-control.
Their anger is cursed because it was fierce, I will divide them among Jacob and scatter them in Israel.
Judah, your brothers will praise you and your hand will tighten around the neck of your enemies. Your father's children will bow down to you.
Judah, you are like a lion's cub and like a lion you take your prey. When you lay down with your prey like a lion, who will have the courage to awaken you?
The scepter and the lawgivers shall never leave Judah nor his descendants until Shiloh (the Messiah) comes and the people come to him.
He will bind his foal to a vine and his donkey's colt to the choicest vine. He will wash his clothes in wine, the life blood of grapevines.
His eyes will be red as wine and his teeth will be as white as milk.
Zebulun will live by the sea, and he will build a harbor for ships, and his border will extend to Sidon.
Issachar is a stubborn donkey that lays down between two burdens.
Issachar saw that his place to rest was good and pleasant land, so he bowed to forced labor and became a servant to pay taxes to others.
Dan will judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel.
Dan will be a serpent on the side of the road, an adder along the path that bites horses by the heel and causes the rider to fall backwards.
I have waited for your salvation, O Lord.
Gad will be overcome by foreign troops, but he will overcome in the end.
Asher's bread will be fat, and he will prepare rich foods for royalty.
Naphtali will produce beautiful words, and he will give good advice.
Joseph will be fertile and fruitful, like a well-watered tree planted beside a spring whose branches spread over the wall.
The archers have caused him great grief; they have shot at him and hated him.
But his bow remained strong, his arms and hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob. From there he is the shepherd and the stone of Israel.

Joseph, you will be blessed by the God of your father who will help you. The Almighty will bless you with blessings from heaven, and from the deep that lies below, and you will be blessed with many descendants.

The blessings of Joseph's father are greater than the blessings of my ancestors who stretched to the farthest borders of the everlasting hills. All this and more will rest on Joseph's head who was separated from his brothers.
Benjamin will be a ravenous wolf; he will devour his prey in the morning and at night he will divide what he takes."
These are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what Jacob said to his sons when he gave each one a suitable blessing.
Then Jacob said, "I want my people to bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite.
I want to be buried in the cave in Canaan that Abraham bought from Ephron to use for a cemetery. The cave in Machpelah's field near Mamre.
They buried Abraham and his wife Sarah there, in the same place they buried Isaac and his wife Rebekah, and the place where I buried Leah.
It is the cave and field that Abraham purchased from Heth's children."
When Jacob finished telling his children his wishes, he gave up the ghost and died, then his people gathered around him.
Joseph threw himself over his father's body and wept over him and kissed him.
Joseph ordered his physicians to embalm his father, so they embalmed Israel.
In those days, it took forty days to embalm someone, and the Egyptians mourned Jacob for seventy days after he was embalmed.
When the mourning period passed, Joseph spoke to Pharaoh's assistants and asked them to arrange a meeting for him to speak with Pharaoh, and he went there.
Then Joseph spoke to Pharaoh and said, "My father made me swear to bury him in his family cemetery in Canaan before he died. So, I have come to ask your permission to go there and bury my father."
And Pharaoh said, "You should keep the promise you made to your father, so go and bury him."
When Joseph left Egypt to go bury his father, he took many important people from Egypt with him. He took Pharaoh's servants, all of Pharaoh's elders, and all the elders in his own household.
Joseph took his brothers and everyone in their house, plus everyone in his father's house to the funeral. They left their children, their flocks, and their herds behind when they left Goshen.
He had chariots, horsemen, and a very large company to escort them to Canaan.
When they arrived at the Atad threshing floor, just beyond the Jordan River, they mourned his father for seven days.
When the Canaanites saw all the mourning in Atad they said, "The Egyptians are very grieved." So, they named the place Abel-Mizraim.
Then Israel's sons did what he had asked them to do.
They carried Jacob to Canaan and buried him in the cave in the Machpelah field, which was on the way to Mamre, where Abraham bought the cave and field from Ephron the Hittite to use as a cemetery.
After Joseph buried his father, he returned to Egypt with his brothers and everyone else who went with him to bury his father.
When Joseph's brothers realized that their father was dead, they were worried and said, "Joseph probably hates us and he may take revenge on us for all the evil that we have done to him."
So Joseph's brothers sent a messenger to him and said, "Before your father died, he told us to tell you something.

He told us to speak to you and say, 'Forgive your brothers for the sin and evil they committed against you.' So, we are begging you to forgive your brothers for what they have done because they also serve your father's God." And Joseph wept when he heard this.
Then Joseph's brothers went to him and bowed down and said, "We are your servants."
And Joseph said to them, "Please do not fear me because I am where I am because God put me here.
But as for you, you were evil to me, but God meant it for good, and it saved the lives of many people.
So you should not fear me, because I will provide for you and your children." And Joseph comforted his brothers and spoke kindly to them.
Joseph lived in Egypt with everyone in his father's house until he was 110 years old, then he died.
Joseph lived long enough to see his great-grandchildren from Ephraim and his grandchildren from Manasseh grow up. He loved them and when they were young, he often let them sit on his lap.
And Joseph said to his brothers, "I am dying, but God will visit you and bring you to the land that he promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."
Then Joseph asked Israel's children to make a promise to him and he said, "God will surely visit you, and you will carry my bones from Egypt back up to Canaan."
Then Joseph died in Egypt when he was 110 years old, and they embalmed him and put him in a coffin.
These are the names of Israel's children who went to Egypt with Jacob, including everyone in his household.
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah.
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin.
Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.
There was a total of seventy souls descended from Jacob who went with him to Egypt. Joseph was not one of them because he was already in Egypt.
So Joseph and his brothers died along with their entire generation.
Israel's children were fruitful and increased abundantly, they multiplied and filled the land and grew extremely powerful.
A new king who did not know Joseph, rose to power and took control of Egypt.
The new king said to his people, "The Israelis outnumber us and they are more powerful than us.
We must be wise and find a way to stop them because they will continue to multiply. What can we do if they leave the country and a war starts? They will join our enemies and fight against us."
So they put harsh taskmasters over them, and Pharaoh used their slave labor to build Pithom and Rameses where he kept his treasures.
But the more the Egyptians oppressed them, the more they multiplied. The Egyptians grew even more worried because the Israelis grew stronger and continued to increase in numbers.
The Egyptians continued to increase the burdens and hard labor they placed on the Israelis.

The Israelis grew increasingly bitter because of their bondage in Egypt. The Egyptians continued to increase the Israelis hardships and heavy workloads, and they were forced to labor out in the fields and haul bricks and mortar.
The Egyptian king spoke to Shiphrah and Puah the Hebrew midwives.
And he said, "When you help the Hebrew women give birth, I want you to kill the boys but save the girls."
But the midwives feared God, and they did not want to do what Pharoah had ordered them to do, so they saved the boys' lives.
The king of Egypt sent for the Hebrew midwives and he asked them, "Why did you ignore my orders and save these boys' lives?"
And the midwives said to Pharaoh, "Hebrew women are different than Egyptian women because they deliver their babies before we get there."
So God treated the midwives well and Israel's people multiplied and grew to be very powerful.
God built houses for the midwives because they feared him.
Then Pharaoh ordered his people to throw the newborn boys into the river.
At about that time, a man and a woman from Levi's house got married.
The woman conceived and gave birth to a son, she saw that he was a good baby, so she hid him for three months.

When she could no longer keep him hidden, she wove a basket out of bulrush stalks. She plastered it and covered it with pitch, then she put the child in the basket, and she put the basket in the reeds beside the riverbank.
The baby's sister stood off at a distance to see what would to her brother.
Then Pharaoh's daughter came down to the river to take a bath, and her young maids walked along the riverbank with her. When Pharaoh's daughter saw the basket, she sent her maid to fetch it.
When Pharaoh's daughter opened the basket, she saw the child and the baby started crying. She had compassion for him and she said, "This is one of the Hebrew children."
Then the baby's sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, "Do you want me to go find a Hebrew woman to nurse him for you?"
And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Yes, go find a nurse for the baby." So, the boy's sister went and told the child's mother about Pharoah's daughter.
Pharaoh's daughter spoke to the boy's mother and said, "II will pay you a fair wage to nurse this child for me." And the woman took the child and nursed him.

When the child grew, she brought him back to Pharaoh's daughter and he became her son. She named him Moses which means 'taken out' or 'saved from the water' and she said, "I named him Moses because I pulled him out of the river."
When Moses was grown, he went out to see his Hebrew brothers and he saw their hardships. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave who was one of his brothers.
He looked around and did not see anybody there, so he killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
The next day, he saw two Hebrew men fighting with each other, and he asked one of them, "Why are you fighting with a fellow Hebrew?"

And the man answered him and said, "Who made you a prince to judge over us? Are you planning to kill me the same way you killed the Egyptian." When Moses heard this, he was afraid and he said to himself, "People know that I killed that man."
When Pharaoh heard that Moses had killed an Egyptian, he was planning to execute him. But Moses fled Egypt and went to Midian. Moses stayed there and one day as he was sitting beside a well.
Some women who were the daughters of Reuel the priest of Midian, came to draw water from the well to fill the water troughs for their father's herds.
While they were there, some shepherds came and pushed the women out of the way, but Moses stood up to them and helped the women water their animals.
When they returned to their father Reuel he asked them, "Why have you returned home so early?"
And they said, "An Egyptian man saved us from a bunch of shepherds, he helped us draw water and he watered the herd too."
And Reuel said to his daughters, "So where is he? Why have you left him out there all alone? Go and ask him to come and eat some bread with us."
Reuel invited Moses to move in with them, and Moses accepted the offer and he was happy living there. At some point Moses and Reuel's daughter Zipporah, got married.
Zipporah gave birth to a son, and Moses named him Gershom which means 'expelled one', 'exiled', or 'alien'. And Moses said, "I named him Gershom because I was a stranger living in a strange land."
Eventually, the king of Egypt died, and the Israelis were still suffering from the bondage of slavery. So, they cried out to God, and God heard the cries caused by their suffering.
God heard their cries, and he remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
And God had respect for the Israelis.

Jethro was Moses' father-in-law and Moses took care of his herd, Jethro was also known as Reuel and he was Midian's priest. Moses led the herd to God's mountain near Horeb on the other side of the desert.
Where the Lord's angel appeared to him in the flames from a fire in the middle of a burning bush. He saw that the bush was on fire, but the bush was not consumed.
And Moses said, "This is amazing, I cannot believe what I am seeing, this bush is on fire, but it is not burning."
When the Lord saw Moses' astonishment, God called out to him from the middle of the bush and said, "Moses, Moses." And Moses answered him and said, "I am here."
And God said, "Do not come any closer and take off your shoes because the ground you are standing on is holy ground."
And the Good Lord said, "I am your father's God, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." Then Moses hid his face because he was afraid to look at God.
Then God said, "I have seen the hardships afflicted on my people by the Egyptians, and I have heard the cries caused by the sorrows their overlords have inflicted on them.

So I have come down to set them free from the Egyptians. I am going to take them to a good place where the land flows with milk and honey. I am going to take them to the land where the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites live.
That's why the cries of the Israelis have come to me, and I have seen the Egyptians' oppressions.
And that's why I am sending you to Pharaoh, and you are going to lead my people the Israelis out of Egypt."
Then Moses asked God, "Who am I to stand up to Pharaoh and lead the Israelis out of Egypt?"
And God said, "I will be with you, and you will know that I have sent you when you bring the people out of Egypt, and you will worship God on this mountain."
Then Moses said to God, "When I tell the Israelis that the God of their fathers has sent me to set them free, they will ask me your name? What am I supposed to tell them?"
And God said to Moses, "Tell them, I AM THAT I AM, and the Great I AM has sent me here."

Then God said to Moses, "Tell them the Lord God of their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob has sent you. Tell them this will be my name forever, and it is the name that their descendants will call me.

Go to the Israeli elders and tell them, the Lord God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, appeared to me and said that he visited me because he has seen what has been done to you in Egypt.

And the Great I AM will free you from the afflictions caused to you by the Egyptians. He will lead you from Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, into a land flowing with milk and honey.

They will listen to you, then you will go to Pharoah with the Israeli elders and tell the Egyptian king, that the Lord God of the Hebrews has met with you and wants you to beg Pharoah to let God's people go. Tell him you must travel out into the wilderness for three days to make a sacrifice to your Lord God.
I am sure the king of Egypt will not let you go unless he is forced to by a mighty hand.
So I will reach out with a powerful hand and project great power into Egypt and defeat Pharoah, then he will let you go.
I will make the Egyptian people respect you, and they will not go empty-handed when they leave.
Every Israeli woman will borrow clothes, gold, and silver jewelry from their Egyptian neighbors, and they will put them on their children, and you will take the Egyptian wealth with you when you go."
And Moses answered God and said, "But they will not believe me, they will not listen to me, and they will say I have not seen the Lord."
And the Lord spoke to Moses and asked, "What do you have in your hand?" And Moses said, "It is my staff."
And the Lord said, "Throw it on the ground." When Moses threw it on the ground it became a serpent, and he fled to get away from it.
And the Lord said to Moses, "Grab it by the tail with your hand." So, Moses caught it by the tail, and it turned back into his staff.
And God said, "This will prove to them that the Lord God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob has appeared to you."
And the Lord also said, "Put your hand in your robe." So, Moses put his hand in his robe, but when he pulled it out, his hand was covered with leprosy and it had turned white as snow.
And God said, "Put your hand back into your robe." And Moses put his hand back into his robe, and when he pulled it out again his hand had turned back into healthy flesh.
Then the Lord said, "If they do not believe you, or they do not believe the first miracle, they will believe the second miracle.
If they do not believe these two miracles and they refuse to listen to you, pour some river water out on dry ground. The water you pour on the ground will turn into blood."
And Moses said to the Lord, "Please Lord do not send me to that place, I am not an eloquent speaker. I have never been a good speaker because I stutter and my speech is slow."
And the Lord said to Moses, "Who made man's mouth? Who created the deaf, dumb, blind, and the people who can see? Was it not me the Lord?
That's why I want you to go, I will teach you what to say and give you the words to say it."
And he said, "O my Lord, I beg you to send someone else."
Moses made the Lord very angry and he said, "Is Aaron the Levite your brother? He is a good speaker, and he is coming to meet you, and his heart will be happy to see you.
When you talk to him tell him what to say, I will be with you, and I will teach both of you what to say and do.
Aaron will be your spokesman, and he will listen to you as if you were God.
You will take this staff and perform miracles for the people to see."

Then Moses returned to his father-in-law Jethro and said, "I beg you to let me go so I can return to my brothers in Egypt, I want to see if they are still alive." And Jethro said to Moses, "Go in peace."
Then the Lord appeared to Moses in Midian and said, "Go back to Egypt, the men who wanted to kill you are all dead."
Moses took his wife and his sons to Egypt, and he carried God's staff in his hand.
And the Lord said to Moses, "When you return to Egypt, make sure you perform the miracles with your staff for Pharaoh to see, but I will harden Pharaoh's heart and he will not let the people go.
Then speak to Pharaoh and say, 'The Lord says, "Israel is my firstborn son.
And I am telling you to let my son go, so that he may serve me and if you refuse to let him go, I will kill your firstborn son."'"
Along the way at a roadside inn, the Lord confronted Moses and was planning to kill him for not having his son circumcised
Then Zipporah took a sharp stone, cut off her son's foreskin and threw it at the feet of Moses and said, "You are just a bloody husband to me."
And Zipporah said to God, "Let him go because this circumcision has made him my bloody husband."
And the Lord spoke to Aaron and said, "Go out and meet with Moses in the wilderness." Then Aaron went to God's mountain where he met Moses and kissed him.
Moses told Aaron that the Lord had sent him, then he told him what the Lord told him to do. He also told him about all the signs that God had told him to perform.
Moses and Aaron assembled Israel's elders together.
Then Aaron told them what the Lord had said to Moses, and Moses performed the miracles in front of them.
The people believed Moses and Aaron, and when they heard that the Lord had visited the Israelis and seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshipped God.
Afterward, Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, "The Lord God of Israel said, 'Let my people go, so they can hold a feast for me in the wilderness.'"
And Pharaoh said, "Who is this Lord, why should I obey him and let Israel go? I do not know this Lord and I will not let them go."

And Moses and Aaron said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us, and we beg you to let us go. We must travel into the desert for three days and make sacrifices to our Lord God, or he will bring a pestilence or the sword against us."
And the king of Egypt said, "Moses and Aaron have distracted the people from their work, and they must go back to work."
And Pharaoh said, "There are too many people living here and they have to work, but because of you they have stopped working."
That day Pharaoh said to the Israeli officers and his overlords.
"Until now you have been supplying the people with straw to make bricks, do not give them any more straw, let them gather their own straw.

It is your job to make sure that they continue to make the same number of bricks every day that they have been making. Do not let them make any less because they have too much free time on their hands. Too much free time is why they have been crying and begging me to let them go and sacrifice to their God.
Give the men more work and do not listen to anything they say."
Pharaoh's overlords and the Israeli officers left, and they went to the people and said, "Pharaoh says, we are not allowed to give you any more straw.
From now on you will have to gather your own straw, but you will still have to make the same number of bricks that you have been making."
So the people scattered all over Egypt to gather straw.
Pharaoh's overlords did what he told them to do and forced the people to make the same number of bricks per day that they made when they were being given straw.
Pharaoh's overlords beat the Israeli officers because they could not meet their daily brick quota for two days in a row.
Then the Israeli officers appealed to Pharaoh and said, "We are your servants, so why do you beat us because we cannot meet your quotas?
You do not provide us with straw, and your overlords tell us to make more bricks, when we cannot keep up, they beat us, but it is your people who are to blame."
But Pharaoh said, "You have too much time on your hands, your people are idle and then you say to me, 'Let us go so we can make sacrifices to the Lord.'
Go back to work, there will be no more straw, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks."
After hearing that, the Israeli officers knew that they were in a lot of trouble because they knew they could not make that many bricks.
When the Israeli officers left Pharaoh, they met Moses and Aaron who were standing outside waiting for them.
They said to Moses and Aaron, "The Lord will judge you because you have made Pharaoh hate us, and he has put a sword in the hands of the overlords to kill us."
Moses returned to the Lord and said, "Lord, why have you sent me to these people? Why have you afflicted them with so much trouble?
Ever since I spoke to Pharaoh in your name, he has treated your people horribly and you still have not set them free."
Then the Lord said to Moses, "Now you will see how I deal with Pharaoh because when I show him the strength of my hand, he will let my people go and drive them out of Egypt."
God continued speaking to Moses and said, "I am the Lord.
I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob by the name of God Almighty, but they did not know me by my name Jehovah.
I established my covenant with them and promised to give them the land of Canaan, where they were strangers traveling through a foreign land.
I remembered my covenant with the Israelis when I heard their groaning because they are in bondage to the Egyptians.
That's why I want you to tell the Israelis that I am the Lord, and I will set them free. I am going to rescue them from the Egyptians with an outstretched arm and mighty judgments.
They will be my people, and I will be their God, and they will know that I am the Lord their God when I free them from the Egyptians' burdens.
I will bring them into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give them this inheritance because I am the Lord."
Moses spoke to the Israelis and told them what God said, but they would not listen because their spirit was so tormented over the cruel bondage they had suffered under the Egyptians.
And the Lord spoke to Moses again.
And the Lord said, "Go and speak to Pharaoh the king of Egypt and tell him to let the Israelis go.
And Moses replied to the Lord and said, "The Israelis do not listen to me, because I stutter when I speak. So why would Pharaoh believe anything I say?"
Then God spoke to Moses and Aaron about Pharaoh again, and he told them to bring the Israelis out of Egypt.
These are the heads of Israel's household, his firstborn son Reuben had sons named Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
Simeon had sons named Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul who was the son of a Canaanite woman.
According to the records Levi's sons were named Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi was 137 years old when he died.
Gershon's sons were Libni and Shimi.
Kohath had three sons named Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, and Kohath was 133 years old when he died.
According to the records Merari's sons were Mahali and Mushi.
Amram was Jochebed's son and he married his father's sister. She gave birth to his sons Aaron and Moses. Amram was 137 years old when he died.
Izhar's sons were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
Uzziel's sons were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Zithri.
Elisheba was Amminadab's daughter and Naashon's sister, she married Aaron and gave birth to his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
Korah's sons were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph, they were the families of the Korhites.
Aaron's son Eleazar married one of Putiel's daughters and she gave birth to his son Phinehas, and according to the records these are the fathers of the Levites.
These are the Israelis that the Lord told Aaron and Moses to bring out of Egypt like an army.
Moses and Aaron were the ones who spoke to Pharaoh about bringing the Israelis out of Egypt.
On that day the Lord spoke to Moses in Egypt.
And the Lord said to Moses, "I am the Lord, speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt and tell him everything say to you."
And Moses said to the Lord, "But I am a poor speaker, so why should Pharaoh listen to me?"
And the Lord said to Moses, "I have made you like a god to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet.
Tell Aaron to speak to Pharaoh and tell him to send the Israelis out of his land.
But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and my signs and wonders will be multiplied throughout the land of Egypt.
But Pharaoh will not listen to you, and I will lay my hand with great judgements on Egypt and bring the Israelis and my armies out of Egypt.
Then the Egyptians will know when I stretch out my hand against them and bring the Israelis out of their land, that I am the Lord."
So Moses and Aaron did what the Lord told them to do.
Moses was 80 years old, and Aaron was 83 years old when they spoke to Pharaoh.
Then the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron again.
And the Lord said, "When Pharaoh asks you to show him your miracles, tell Aaron to throw your staff on the ground in front of him and it will become a serpent."

So Moses and Aaron went to see Pharaoh, and they did what the Lord told them to do. Aaron threw his staff on the ground in front of Pharaoh, and it became a serpent. Pharaoh's servants were there and they saw it too.
Then Pharaoh called for all of the wise men and sorcerers in Egypt, and they performed similar magic tricks.
They threw their staffs down, and the staffs became serpents, but Aaron's staff swallowed their snakes.
Then God hardened Pharaoh's heart, and just as the Lord had said and Pharaoh refused to listen to them.
And the Lord spoke to Moses and said, "Pharaoh's heart is hardened and he refuses to let the people go.
Go to Pharaoh when he goes down to the river in the morning. Stand on the riverbank and meet him face to face, then take the staff that was turned into a serpent in your hand.
And say to him, 'The Lord God of the Hebrews has sent me to tell you that you refused to listen to me until now. So now, I am telling you to let my people go, so they can serve me in the wilderness.
So that you know that I am the Lord, I am going to put my staff in the river and turn the water into blood.
All the fish in the river will die, the river will stink and the Egyptians will hate having to drink the river water.'"

And the Lord spoke to Moses and said, "Tell Aaron to take your staff and stretch it out over all the streams, rivers, ponds, pools, and water reservoirs in Egypt, and they will turn to blood. There will be blood throughout Egypt, even in the Egyptians' stone and wooden bowls.
Moses and Aaron did what the Lord told them to do, and Aaron lifted the staff before Pharaoh and his servants and put it into the water, and all the water in all the rivers turned into blood.
All the fish died, the river stank, the Egyptians could not drink the river water, and all the water throughout Egypt was turned into blood.
The Egyptian sorcerers did the same thing with their magic spells. Pharaoh's heart was hardened again, and he refused to listen to them just as the Lord said.
Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he was not worried about the river being turned into blood.
All the Egyptians had to dig wells around the river because they could not drink the river water.
And seven days passed after the Lord struck the river.
And the Lord spoke to Moses and said, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him that the Lord says, 'Let my people go so they can serve me.
If you refuse to let my people go, I will send frogs to invade your land.
Frogs will come out of the river and invade your houses, your bedrooms, your beds, your servants' house, your people, your ovens, and your kneading troughs.
The frogs will cover you, your people and all of your servants.'"
And the Lord spoke to Moses and said, "Tell Aaron to wave your staff over the streams, rivers, and ponds. Then the frogs will come up out of the water and cover the land throughout Egypt."
So Aaron waved his staff over the Egyptian waters, and the frogs came up out of the water and covered the land.
Pharaoh's sorcerers did the same thing with their magic spells and frogs crawled out of the water and covered the land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, "Please beg the Lord to take the frogs away from me and my people and I will let the people go so they can sacrifice to the Lord."
And Moses said to Pharaoh, "So that you may have the glory over me. When would you like for me to ask the Lord to destroy your invading frogs, except for the ones in the rivers?"
And Pharaoh said, "Ask him tomorrow." And Moses said, "I will go and plead with the Lord for you tomorrow, then you will know that there is no one like our Lord God.
The frogs will leave you, your houses, your servants, and your people, and they will only be in the river where they belong."
Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to the Lord about the frogs he had brought against Pharaoh.
The Lord did as Moses asked and the frogs died everywhere except in the rivers.
The Egyptians piled them up into heaps and the land stunk.
But just as the Lord had said, when Pharaoh saw that the frogs were gone, his heart was hardened and he did not listen to them.
And the Lord said to Moses, "Tell Aaron to wave your staff over the land and turn the Egyptian dust into lice throughout the land."
And they did what the Lord told them to do, Aaron waved his staff over the earth's dust throughout Egypt, and it became lice. Men and beasts were infested with lice throughout the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh's sorcerers tried to use their magic spells to create lice, but they could not, so man and beast were infested with lice.
Then the sorcerers said to Pharaoh, "This is God's work." But just as the Lord had said, Pharaoh's heart was hardened and he refused to listen to them.
And the Lord said to Moses, "Get up early in the morning, and go see Pharaoh when he comes out to the water and say to him, 'The Lord says, "Let my people go, so they can go and serve me.

If you do not let my people go, I will send swarms of flies to infest you, your servants, your people, and your houses. The Egyptians' houses will be full of flies, and even the ground they stand on will be infested with flies.
But in Goshen where my people live there will be no swarms of flies and in the end, you will know that I am the Lord of the earth.
And tomorrow, I am going to separate my people from your people as a sign."'"
The Lord did what he said he was going to do, and a horrible swarm of flies infested Pharaoh's house, his servants' houses, and the entire land of Egypt was corrupted by the flies.
Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and he said to them, "Go! Sacrifice to your God but you must stay in Egypt!"
And Moses said, "We cannot do that, because the Egyptians think our sacrifice to our Lord God is an abomination, if we make our sacrifice in front of them, they will stone us?
We must travel three days into the wilderness and sacrifice to our Lord God, as he has told us."
And Pharaoh said, "I will let you go sacrifice to your Lord God in the wilderness, but do not go very far away and plead with your God for me."

And Moses said, "I will leave tomorrow, and I will plead with the Lord for you. I will ask him to remove the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people, but you must not lie to us again about letting the people go to sacrifice to the Lord."
Then Moses left Pharaoh and pleaded with the Lord.
And the Lord did as Moses asked, and removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people until none remained.
But Pharaoh hardened his heart again and he would not let the people go.
Then the Lord said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him that the Hebrew's Lord God says, 'Let my people go so they can serve me.
If you continue to hold my people and refuse to let them go.
There will be a horrible plague out in the field, and the Lord will cause all of your cattle, horses, donkeys, camels, oxen, and sheep to suffer greatly.
The Lord will separate Israel's cattle from Egypt's cattle, and none of the Israeli cattle will die.
And the Lord has set a time for this to happen, and he said that he is going to do this thing tomorrow.'"
The next day the Lord did what he said he was going to do and all the cattle in Egyptian died except for Israel's cattle.
Pharaoh saw that none of Israel's cattle died, but once again his heart was hardened, and he would not let the people go.
And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron and said, "Moses, take several handfuls of ashes from the furnace and throw them into the air in front of Pharaoh.
A cloud of fine dust will settle all over Egypt, and both man and beast will be covered with boils."
So they took the ashes and stood before Pharaoh, Moses threw the ashes up toward heaven and boils broke out all over man and beast.
The Egyptians and their sorcerers were unable to stand in front of Moses because they were covered with boils.
And just as the Lord had said, Pharaoh's heart was hardened once again, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron.
Then the Lord said to Moses, "Get up early tomorrow morning, and go tell Pharaoh that the Hebrew's Lord God says, 'Let my people go so they can serve me.
Because this time I am going to send my plagues against you, your heart, your servants, and your people. And after I do that, you will know that there is no one else like me on earth.
I could have raised my hand and sent a plague to wipe you and your people from the face of the earth.
But I have allowed you to stay in order to show you my power, so that my name can be proclaimed everywhere on earth.
But you still glorify yourself over my people and refuse to let them go.
So pay attention and watch closely because at about this time tomorrow I am going to send a terrible rain and hailstorm against Egypt, the likes of which has never seen before.

That's why I am telling you to bring your cattle and everything else you have in from the field because every man and beast found out in the field tomorrow will not come home, and the hail will kill them all.'"
Some of Pharaoh's servants feared the Lord's word and they brought their servants and cattle into their houses.
The people who did not believe the Lord's word left their servants and cattle out in the field.
And the Lord said to Moses, "Raise your staff toward heaven and the hail will destroy everything in the field, including every man, beast, and herb in Egypt."
When Moses raised his staff toward heaven, the Lord sent thunder and lightning, and the hail rained down on Egypt.
Since the beginning of the Egyptian nation, the Egyptians had never seen such a terrible storm or as much rain, hail, and lightening come from heaven.
The hail came down and destroyed everything in the Egyptian's fields, including man, beast, and herbs and the storm tore down all the trees in the field.
But there was no hail where the Israelis lived in Goshen.
Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron again and said to them, "This time I have sinned against the righteous Lord. For I am wicked and so are my people.
Please ask the Lord to end this storm because there has been enough thunder, lightning, and hail and I will let you go because I no longer want any of you here."
And Moses said to Pharaoh, "As soon as I have left the city, I will ask the Lord to end the thunder, lightning, and hail. Then you will know that the earth belongs to the Lord.
But as for you and your servants, I know that you still do not fear the Lord God.
The blooming flax and the mature barley were destroyed.
But the wheat and rye were not destroyed because they had not yet sprouted."
Moses left Pharaoh's city and went to pray to the Lord for the thunder, lightning, and hail to stop. Then the storm ended and it stopped raining on the earth.
But Pharaoh continued to sin even after he saw that the rain, thunder, lightning, and hail had stopped because his heart and his servants' hearts were hardened.
The Lord told Moses that Pharaoh's heart had been hardened again, and just as the Lord had said it would happen, Pharaoh refused to let the Israelis go.
And the Lord said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh because I have hardened his heart and his servants' hearts so that he will see the miracles I am going to perform.
And you can tell your son, and your son's son about the miracles which I have performed in Egypt so that all of you will know that I am the Lord."
Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, "The Lord God of the Hebrews says, 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go so that they can go serve me.
If you refuse to let my people go, tomorrow I will bring locusts to your coast.
They will cover the face of the earth so that no one will be able to see the ground. The locusts will eat all the trees and anything else that was not destroyed by the hail.

They will fill your houses, your servants' houses, and every Egyptians' house. There will be swarms of locusts the likes of which your fathers nor your fathers' fathers have ever seen!" And Moses left Pharaoh's presence.

Pharaoh's servants asked him, "How long will you let this man continue to bring God's judgment against us? Let them go so they can go serve their Lord God, have you not noticed that God has already destroyed Egypt?"
Then they brought Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and he said to them, "Go, serve your God! Who are you planning to take into the wilderness with you?"
And Moses said, "We are going to take our young, our old, our sons and daughters, our flocks, and our herds because we must hold a feast for the Lord."
And Pharaoh said, "May the Lord be with you if I let you go with your children, because it is clear that you have evil intentions.
That will not happen, so you may only take your men to go serve the Lord, because that's what you have been asking for." Then Pharaoh sent them away.
And the Lord said to Moses, "Wave your staff over Egypt and locusts will cover the land, they will eat every plant that the hail did not destroy."
Then Moses waved his staff over all of Egypt, and the Lord blew an east wind over the land all day and all night, and the east wind brought the locusts the next morning.
The locusts covered Egypt but stopped at the Egyptian coasts. It was the worst locust swarm the world had ever seen or would ever see again.
They covered the whole earth and darkened the land. They ate every plant, every fruit tree, and everything the hail had not destroyed. No plants or anything else green survived in Egypt.
Pharaoh hastily sent for Moses and Aaron and he said, "I have sinned against you and your Lord.
Please forgive me just this once and plead with your God to take this death away from me."
They left Pharaoh's presence and pleaded with the Lord.
The Lord sent a powerful west wind, which blew the locusts out into the Red Sea and not one locust remained in Egypt.
But the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart again and he would not let the Israelis go.
And the Lord spoke to Moses and said, "Wave your staff toward heaven and severe darkness will cover Egypt."
So Moses waved his staff toward heaven and thick darkness covered Egypt for three days.
The Egyptians could not see each other, nobody left their place for three days, but the Israeli homes were all lit up.
Pharaoh sent for Moses again and said, "Go away! Go and serve your Lord! Take your children with you but leave your flocks and herds."
And Moses said, "You must give us our sacrifices and burnt offerings, we need them to sacrifice to our Lord God.
Our cattle must go with us; we will not leave them behind because we do not know what we are going to need to serve our Lord God until we arrive there."
But the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart again and he would not let them go.
And Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me, and do not come back here because when you see my face again you will die."
And Moses said, "You have spoken the truth, I will never see your face again."

And the Lord spoke to Moses and said, "I am going to bring one more plague against Egypt and the Pharaoh, and when I am finished with him, not only will he let you go, but he will drive you out of there.
So speak to the Israelis people, and tell them to borrow as much gold, silver, and jewels from their Egyptian neighbors as they can."
And the Lord caused the Egyptian people to see the Israelis in a favorable light, and Moses was thought of as a very great man among Pharaoh's servants and the Egyptian people.
And Moses said to the people, "The Lord says that he is going to move throughout Egypt at about midnight tonight.
All of Egypt's firstborn will die, including Pharaoh's firstborn, his servants' firstborn, and all the firstborn animals.
A great cry will be heard throughout the land of Egypt, the likes of which the world has never heard before and never will again.

But none of the Israelis will die, and among the Israelis not even a dog will bark at man nor beast. After that you will know that your Lord God recognizes the difference between the Egyptians and the Israelis.
After this, your officials will come and bow down to me and say, 'Get out and take your people with you!' Then I will leave!" And Pharaoh was very angry when Moses left.
And the Lord said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you and he will see my miracles multiplied throughout the land of Egypt."
Moses and Aaron performed all of these miracles in front of Pharaoh, but the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he refused to let the Israelis leave Egypt.
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron in Egypt again and said,
"This will be the first month of the year for you.
Speak to the Israeli congregation and say, 'On the tenth day of this month every household will prepare a lamb.
If the household is too small to eat the entire lamb, they can share it with their neighbor's. If it is not enough to feed everyone, they can take more lambs.
Take an unblemished firstborn male lamb from the sheep or goats.
On the fourteenth day of the first month of the year, the whole Israeli community must kill their lambs in the evening.
Then spread the lamb's blood on their door's lintels and side posts of each house where they will be eating.
They must eat the roasted lamb with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
Do not boil the meat or eat it raw, but roast it in the fire including the head, legs, and inner organs.
Do not leave any leftovers until the next morning, if anything remains it must be burned in the fire.
Eat it hastily while fully clothed, with shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand. It will be the Lord's Passover.
Because on this night I will pass through and destroy all the firstborn in Egypt, including the firstborn of man and beast. I will execute judgment against all of Egypt's gods, for I am the Lord.
The blood on the door of each house will be a reminder to me of where you are. When I see the blood, I will pass over your house, and the plague will not destroy you when I destroy Egypt.
From now on and forever, you must prepare a feast for the Lord, and this day will be legally recognized as a memorial for you.
Starting with the first day, you must eat unleavened bread for seven days, during that time, anyone who eats leavened bread will be cut off from the rest of Israel.
On the first and seventh days, the people must gather for a holy assembly. During that time, you must not do any work of any kind except for preparing food.
You and your descendants will be legally required to observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread forever because this day will be remembered as the day that I brought your armies out of Egypt.
From the fourteenth to the twenty-first day of the first month, you must eat unleavened bread every evening.

Do not keep any leavened bread in your homes for seven days. Anyone who eats bread leavened with yeast, whether they were born in Israel or they are immigrants, will be cut off from the Israeli congregation.
You must not eat anything leavened, and everyone in your home must eat unleavened bread."
Then Moses assembled all the Israeli elders together and said to them, "Slaughter a Passover lamb for each of your families.
Dip a bunch of hyssop branches in the sink with the lamb's blood, then paint the lintel and side posts of your house with the blood. Do not leave your house until the next morning!

Because the Lord will pass through the land tonight and destroy the Egyptians. When he sees the blood on your lintel and side posts, the destroyer will pass over your house, and your homes will not be destroyed.
The Passover will be established as a legal memorial for you and your sons forever.
Someday, when you arrive in the land that the Lord promised you, you must continue to observe this memorial.
When your children ask you, what is this service all about.

Tell them, 'It is the Passover sacrifice to the Lord, to commemorate the night he passed over the houses of the Israelis and destroyed the Egyptians, and the Israelis bowed their heads to worship God.'"
The Israelis did everything the Lord told Moses and Aaron to do.
At about midnight the Lord destroyed all the firstborn children in Egypt, from Pharaoh's firstborn to the firstborn of the people in prison to all the firstborn cattle.
Pharaoh, all his servants, and all the Egyptians got up in the middle of the night, and there was a great outcry in Egypt because someone died in every house.
Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron that night and told them to leave, he told them to take the Israelis with them, and to go serve the Lord.
He told them to take their flocks and herds and go, and he asked them to bless him too.
The Egyptians sent them out of the land in great haste. They said it was because they would all be dead if they did not leave.
The people were already dressed and ready to go, and they hoisted the unleavened dough and their kneading bowls up on their shoulders.
The Israelis had done everything that Moses told them to do, they borrowed gold, silver jewelry, and clothes from the Egyptians.
Because the Lord made the Egyptians look favorably upon the Israeli people, and they lent them everything they asked for. So, the Israelis took all of the Egyptians' wealth with them.
About 600,000 Israeli men, plus their women and children traveled from Rameses to Succoth.
A mixed multitude went with them, including their flocks, herds, and lots of cattle.
They baked unleavened bread from the dough they brought with them. Because they were forced to leave Egypt in the middle of the night and they did not have time to prepare food for themselves.
The Israelis had lived in Egypt for 430 years.
After living there that long, the Lord's hosts left Egypt.
It was a night that the Israelis and their descendants will remember forever, when they celebrate and worship the Lord for bringing them out of Egypt.
And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the Passover law, no strangers are allowed to eat the Passover meal.
But any circumcised servant that you bought for money will be allowed to eat the Passover meal.
A foreign hired servant will not be allowed to eat the Passover meal.
The Passover meal must be eaten inside the house, do not carry any of it out of the house and do not break any bones.
The entire Israeli congregation must keep this decree.

When a stranger lives with you and wants to keep the Passover and worship the Lord, then all the males in his household must be circumcised. If they are circumcised, they will be allowed to take part in the Lord's Passover, but any uncircumcised men will not be allowed to eat the Passover meal.
Everyone will be subject to the same law including the strangers who live among you.
And the Israelis did everything that the Lord told Moses and Aaron to do.
That was the day that the Lord brought the Israelis and their armies out of Egypt.
Then the Lord spoke to Moses again and said,
"Sanctify the firstborn male of every man and beast to me."
And Moses said to the people, "Remember this day because this is the day that the Lord's strong hand brought you out of Egyptian bondage. Do not eat any leavened bread on this day.
This day must be remembered in Abib, which is the first month of the year.

You will remember the day the Lord brought you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites. This is the day that the Lord brought you into the land flowing with milk and honey that he promised to give your fathers. You must remember this day during this month.
You must eat unleavened bread for seven days and you will hold a feast to the Lord on the seventh day.
You must only eat unleavened bread during those seven days, and no leavened bread will be allowed in your house or in your possession.
Tell your children the reason you remember those days is because of what the Lord did when he brought you out of Egypt.

These days will be like a sign on your hand and an ornament on your forehead. This is so you will remember to teach the Lord's law, because the Lord brought you out of Egypt with a strong and powerful hand.
That's why you must keep this decree at the same time every year.
After God keeps his promise to you and your fathers and brings you to Canaan, he will give you the promised land.
You must give to the Lord every firstborn male that comes from the womb, whether it is human or animal.
You can redeem the firstborn donkey with a lamb, if you do not redeem it, you must break its neck. You must redeem and rescue all your firstborn male children.
In the future when your children ask you, 'What's this about?' You will tell them, 'The Lord brought us out of the Egyptian house of bondage with a strong and powerful hand.

When Pharaoh refused to let us go, the Lord killed all the firstborn males, both man and beast in Egypt. That's why I sacrifice all the males that open the matrix to the Lord, but I will rescue all my firstborn children.
It will be like a sign on your hand and an ornament on your forehead to remind us of the Lord's powerful hand that brought us out of Egypt.'"

When Pharaoh finally let the people go, God did not lead his people through the Philistines land even though it would have been shorter. And God said, "I did this because if the people were to see war, they might have changed their minds and returned to Egypt."
God led the people through the wilderness to the Red Sea, and the Israelis left Egypt fully armored.
Moses took Joseph's bones with him because Joseph had made the Israelis swear to carry his bones with them when they left Egypt.
They left Succoth and traveled to Etham where they set up camp on the edge of the wilderness.
During the day the Lord appeared as a pillar of cloud to show them the way, and by night a pillar of fire gave them light, so they could travel both day and night.
God left the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night with the people, and it led the way for them.
Then the Lord spoke to Moses again.
And the Lord said, "Speak to the Israelis and tell them to go toward Pi-Hahiroth near Baal-Zephon, between Migdol and the sea, and set up their camp by the ocean.
Because Pharaoh will say 'The Israelis are cornered and the wilderness has them trapped.'
I will harden Pharaoh's heart again and he will pursue them, I will be glorified by Pharaoh and his armies, and the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord."
When the Egyptian king was told that the Israelis had fled, Pharaoh and his servants' hearts were hardened and they said, "Why did we let the Israelis leave and stop serving us?"
So Pharaoh harnessed his horses and took his chariot and armies with him.
He took his captains, 600 of his best chariots, plus every other chariot in Egypt.
The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart as he left Egypt to pursue Israel's children who defiantly left.
But Pharaoh pursued them and he took his horses, chariots, horsemen, and the Egyptian army and they overtook them by the sea where they were camped near Pi-Hahiroth before you get to Baal-Zephon.
As Pharaoh and his armies approached, the Israelis looked up and saw the Egyptians marching towards them. Then they were extremely frightened and they all cried out to the Lord.
And they said to Moses, "There were plenty of graves in Egypt, why did you bring us out here to die in the wilderness? Why did you do this to us, and why did you bring us out of Egypt?
Did we not tell you to leave us alone so we could serve the Egyptians? We were better off serving the Egyptians than dying out in the wilderness."
And Moses said to the people, "Do not fear, stand still and watch as the Lord saves you. After today you will never see the Egyptians again.
The Lord will fight for you and all you have to do is remain quiet."
And the Lord said to Moses, "Because you have cried out to me, tell Israelis to move forward.
Lift up your staff, and stretch it out over the sea, the Red Sea will be parted, and the Israelis can move forward.
I will harden the Egyptians' hearts, and they will follow them, Pharaoh and his armies, chariots, and horsemen will all see my glory.
The Egyptians will know that I am the Lord when Pharaoh and his chariots and horsemen see my glory."
God's angel and the pillar of cloud which had been leading the Israelis moved behind them.
Then God's angel stood between the Egyptians and the Israelis. The Egyptians faced a dark cloud, but it gave light to the Israelis all night long, and neither side came close to the other.
Moses stretched his staff out over the sea and the Lord made a strong east wind blow all night long, it parted the Red Sea and dry land appeared between the divided waters.
The Israelis walked on the dry land in the middle of the sea, and there was a wall of water on both sides.
Pharaoh and the Egyptians including all of their horses, chariots, and horsemen pursued them into the middle of the ocean.
That morning the Lord looked out through the cloud and the pillar of fire and saw that the Egyptians were disoriented and confused.
The Egyptians drove their chariots so furiously that the wheels came off and they said, "Let us flee from the Israelis because the Lord fights for them and against us."
And the Lord said to Moses, "Stretch your staff over the ocean and the divided waters will come crashing down on the Egyptians, and their chariots and horsemen.
The next morning Moses waved his staff over the ocean, and the sea came crashing down. The Egyptians tried to flee but the Lord caught them in the middle of the ocean.
And the waters came crashing down on Pharaoh's armies, chariots, and horsemen. None of them survived.
But the Israelis walked through the middle of the ocean on dry land with a wall of water on both sides.
That day the Lord saved the Israelis from the Egyptians and brought them to safety, and they saw the dead Egyptians all over the beaches.
The Israelis saw what the Lord had done to the Egyptians, after that they believed Moses and feared the Lord.
Then Moses and the Israelis sang this song to the Lord, "I will sing to the Lord because he has gloriously triumphed and thrown the horses and riders into the sea.
The Lord is my strength and song, he is my salvation, he is my father's God and he is my God, I will prepare a home for him and I will glorify him.
The Lord is a man of war, and the Lord is his name.
He has thrown Pharaoh's chariots, captains, and armies into the Red Sea where they drowned.
The ocean covered them and they sank like a stone to the bottom of the sea.
O Lord, the glorious power of your right hand has dashed the enemy to pieces.
Your great power has overthrown those who rose up against you. You sent your anger against them, and it consumed them as if they were straw.
The waters were parted by a blast from your nostrils, and the depths of the heart of the sea was piled up on each side, and you made a path through the Red Sea.
And the enemy said, 'I will pursue, I will overtake, and I will divide their wealth. My lust for them will be satisfied, for I will draw my sword, and my hand will destroy them.'
O Lord, you made the winds blow and the sea covered them, they sank in the mighty waters like they were made of lead.
O Lord, who among the gods is like you? Who else is gloriously holy, who else offers heartfelt praises and does the wonders that you do?
You stretched out your right hand, and the earth swallowed them all.
You have rescued the Israeli people with your mercy and strength, and you have led them to your holy home.
The Palestinian people will hear about it and they will fear you, and then they will be filled with great sorrow.
The dukes of Edom will be amazed, the mighty men of Moab will tremble with fear, and the inhabitants of Canaan will disappear.
O Lord, the Canaanite people will fear and dread you, your great arm will make them as still as a stone until your people have passed through.
O Lord, you will bring the people to the mountain you gave them. They will settle there with you in a sanctuary that you built with your own hands.
The Lord will reign forever and ever.
Because Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen went into the sea and the Lord brought the waters of the sea crashing down on them. But the children of Israel walked on dry land in the middle of the ocean."
Aaron's sister Miriam the prophetess, and all the other women took their tambourines and started dancing.
Miriam sang to them and said, "Sing to the Lord because he has gloriously triumphed, and he has thrown the horses and riders into the sea."
So Moses and the Israelis left the Red Sea and for three days they traveled in the wilderness of Shur, but they could not find water.
When they arrived in Marah, they could not drink the bitter water there and they named the place Marah because Marah means 'bitterness.'
The people started whispering behind Moses' back and they said, "What are we going to drink?"
Moses cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed Moses a tree which he threw into the bitter waters which made the waters sweet. That's where God made a law to test them.

And God said, "If you diligently listen to your Lord God, do what is right in his sight, listen to what he says and keep his laws, I will not put any of the diseases on you which I brought on the Egyptians, because I am the Lord who heals you."
Then they went to Elim where there were twelve water wells and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the water.

On the fifteenth day of the second month after they left Egypt, the Israelis restarted their journey and left Elim. The entire Israeli congregation traveled to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai.
The whole Israeli congregation started complaining about Moses and Aaron out in the wilderness.

The Israelis said to Moses and Aaron, "It would have been better for us if the Lord had killed us in Egypt. We had all the bread and meat we wanted to eat there, but you brought all of us out here into this wilderness to starve us to death."

Then the Lord said to Moses, "Behold I will rain down bread from heaven for you, and the people must gather enough for a one day's supply every day. That is how I will test whether or not they will abide by my laws.
On the sixth day of the week they must gather and prepare twice as much bread than they gathered on the other days of the week."
Then Moses and Aaron said to the entire Israelis congregation, "In the evening you will know that the Lord has brought you out of Egypt.
In the morning, you will see the Lord's glory because he hears you speaking against him and against us."

And Moses said, "In the morning the Lord will give you bread to eat, and meat in the evening because he hears your complaints about him. So, who are we? For you are complaining about the Lord, not us."
And Moses spoke to Aaron and said, "Speak to the Israeli congregation and say, 'Come before the Lord because he has heard your complaints.'"
While Aaron was speaking to the congregation they looked toward the wilderness and the Lord's glory appeared in the cloud.
Then the Lord spoke to Moses again.

And the Lord said, "I have heard the Israelis complaining, and I want you to speak to them and say, 'In the morning you will be filled with bread, in the evening you will eat meat and you will know that I am your Lord God.'"
That evening quail came and covered the entire camp, and in the morning the dew covered the ground around the camp.
After the dew evaporated, the ground was covered with small round grayish-white flakes.
When the Israelis saw it, they said, "It is manna!" They did not know what it was, so Moses spoke to them and said, "This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat.
The Lord has said that you must gather an omer of manna for each person in your tent to eat."
The Israelis did what the Lord told them to do, some gathered more and some gathered less.
When they measured an omer, those who gathered much had nothing left over, and those who gathered little lacked nothing, and everyone had plenty to eat.
And Moses said, "Do not save any leftovers until the next morning."
Some of them did not listen to Moses and they saved some leftovers until the next morning, but it stank and was full of maggots, and Moses was angry with them.
So the people gathered enough every morning for each person to eat, and when the sun grew hot, it all melted.
On the sixth day, the congregation rulers went to Moses and told him that they had gathered twice as much manna, enough for two omers of bread per person.
And he said to them, "This is what the Lord said to me, 'Tomorrow is the Lord's Holy Sabbath, bake and boil everything you will need to eat, and keep any leftovers until tomorrow morning.'"
So they did what Moses told them to do and stored it until the next morning, and it did not stink or have maggots in it.
And Moses said, "Eat your leftovers today, because today is the Lord's Holy Sabbath and you will not find any manna out in the field.
You must gather manna for six days, but there will not be any to gather on the seventh day because it is the Sabbath day."
On the seventh day, some of the people went to gather manna and they could find nothing.
And the Lord said to Moses, "How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and laws?
Look, the Lord has given you the Sabbath, so he gives you enough manna on the sixth day to last for two days, and all of you are supposed to stay home on the seventh day."
