So the Philistines were defeated and they no longer came to the borders of Israel, and the Lord's hand was against the Philistines the entire time that Samuel lived.

The cities that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to them, from Ekron all the way to Gath. All the lands within Israel's borders were delivered from the hands of the Philistines, and there was peace between them and the Amorites.
And Samuel judged Israel for his entire life.
Samuel traveled a circuit annually from Bethel to Gilgal then to Mizpah, and he judged Israel in all of those places.
Then Samuel returned to his home in Ramah, where he judged Israel and built an altar to the Lord.
One day after Samuel had grown old, he made his sons judges over Israel.
His firstborn son was named Joel, and his second son was named Abiah, they were judges in Beersheba.
His sons did not walk in his ways, but they turned away from God and chased after money. They took bribes and their judgments were perverted.
Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and went to Samuel in Ramah.
And the elders of Israel spoke to Samuel and said, "Behold you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways, so appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations!"
But Samuel was very displeased when they said, "Appoint a king to judge us!" So, Samuel prayed to the Lord.
And the Lord said to Samuel, "Listen to everything your people say, because they have not rejected you, they have rejected me, for they do not want me to reign over them.
Just as they have since the day that I brought them out of Egypt until this day. They have forsaken me and served other gods, which they are also doing to you.
So listen to them, but you must solemnly protest to them and warn them of the type of king that they will have reigning over them."
Then Samuel spoke to the people who were asking for a king, and he told them what the Lord had said.

And Samuel said, "This is the kind of king that will reign over you. He will take your sons for himself, they will care for his chariots, they will be his horsemen, and some will be appointed to run before his chariots.
He will appoint captains over fifties and thousands, they will plant his fields and reap his harvests, and they will make instruments of war and weapons for his chariots!
He will take your daughters as his confectioners, cooks, and bakers.
He will take the best of your fields, vineyards, and olive groves to give to his servants.
He will take 1/10h of your seed and your vineyards and give them to his officers and servants.
He will take your male and female servants, your best young men, and your donkeys, and put them to work for himself.
He will take 1/10th of your sheep, and you will be his servants.
Then you will cry out in those days because of the king you chose for yourselves, and the Lord will not hear you."
Nevertheless, the people refused to listen to or obey Samuel and they said, "No! We want a king for ourselves!
We want to be like all the other nations with a king to judge us, lead us, and fight our battles."
Samuel heard everything the people said, and he repeated their words to the Lord.
Then the Lord said to Samuel, "Listen to what they said and appoint a king for them." Then Samuel spoke to the Israelis men and said, "Every one of you must go back to your own city."

There was a man from Benjamin named Kish, who was the son of Abiel, who was the son of Zeror, who was the son of Bechorath, who was the son of a Benjamite named Aphiah, who was a mighty and powerful man.
He had a son named Saul, who was a good handsome young man, and no one was a better person than him in all of Israel, and he was taller than everyone else.
One day the donkeys of Saul's father Kish were lost, and Kish spoke to his son and said, "Saul, take one of the servants with you and go find the donkeys."

They searched through Mount Ephraim and the land of Shalisha, but they could not find them. Then they passed through the land of Shalim, and they could not find them there either. And they passed through the land of the Benjamites but they still could not find them.
When they entered the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant, "Come on, let us return home or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys, and he will start worrying about us."

Then the servant said, "Behold, there is a man of God in this city, and he is an honorable man, everything that he says surely comes to pass. So let us go there and perhaps he can show us which way to go."
Then Saul said to his servant, "But, if we go there what can we bring to the man of God? We have eaten all of our bread, and we do not have a present to bring to him. So, what do we have?"
And the servant answered Saul again and said, "Look, I have 1/4th of a silver shekel that I can give the man of God, to tell us which way to go."
In the past in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God he would say, "Let us go to the seer," because back then a prophet was called the seer.
Then Saul answered his servant and said, "Well said, come on let us go." So, they went to the city where the man of God lived.
As they were climbing the hill up to the city, they met some young women coming out to draw water and they spoke to them and asked, "Is there a seer here?"
The women answered them and said, "There is, if you hurry you can see him, because he came to the city today to offer a sacrifice from the people in the high place.

As soon as you enter the city, you will see him before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people will not eat until he comes, but they will eat after he blesses the sacrifice. So go now, because it is just about the right time to find him."
And they went into the city, and they saw Samuel coming towards them on his way up to the high place.
Now the Lord had whispered in Samuel's ear the day before Saul came and said,

"At about this time tomorrow I will send a man from the land of Benjamin to you, and you must anoint him as the leader over my people Israel. He will rescue my people from the hands of the Philistines, for I have seen them and I have heard their cries.
When Samuel saw Saul, the Lord said to him, "Behold this is the man that I told you was coming! He will be the one to reign over my people.
Then Saul moved closer to Samuel as he stood in the gate and asked, "Where can I find the seer's house?"

Samuel answered Saul and said, "I am the seer, walk before me up to the high place, for you will eat with me today. Then tomorrow I will tell you everything that is in your heart and send you on your way.

As for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not worry about them, because they have been found. But what you do not know, is that all of Israel desires to put their hope in you and your father's house?"

Saul answered Samuel and asked, "Am I not a Benjamite, one of the smallest tribes of Israel? And is not my family the least of all the families from the tribe of Benjamin? So why are you telling me this?"
Then Samuel brought Saul and his servant into the parlor, where about 30 other people were seated and made them sit at the head of the table.
And Samuel said to the cook, "Bring the portion I gave you to set aside."

So, the cook brought the shoulder with everything that was attached to it and set it in front of Saul. Then Samuel said, "This is what we have set aside for you to eat, because we kept it for just this occasion ever since I said, 'I have invited these people.'"So, Saul and Samuel ate together that day.
After they came down from the high place into the city, Samuel spoke to Saul on the rooftop of his house.
They got up early in the morning that spring day, and Samuel called out to Saul on the rooftop and said, "Get up, so I can send you on your way." So, Saul got up and they both left together.
As they were headed toward the city border, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell your servant to go on without us, but I want you to stay a while, so I can reveal the word of God to you." And the servant left.
Then Samuel took a vial of oil and poured it on Saul's head and kissed him and said, "Has not the Lord anointed you ruler over his inheritance?

When you leave today, you will find two men beside Rachel's tomb on the border of Benjamin in Zelzah. They will say to you, 'The donkeys you were looking for have been found. Your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and he has started worrying about you. And your father Kish said, "What should I do about my son?"'

Then you will go on from there to the Plain of Tabor, and you will meet three men there going up to God in Bethel. One will be carrying three kid goats, another will be carrying three loaves of bread, and the third will be carrying a bottle of wine.
They will salute you and give you two loaves of bread, which you will accept from their hands.

After that you will come to the Hill of God, where the Philistines have a garrison stationed. When you arrive in that city, you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with a harp, tambourines, flutes, and lyres and they will prophesy.
And the spirit of the Lord will come upon you and you will prophesy with them, and you will be transformed into another man.
When these signs come to you, do whatever the occasion requires of you; for God is with you.

You must go down to Gilgal before me, and I will come down to you to offer burnt offerings and make sacrificial peace offerings. Wait there for me for seven days until I come to meet you, and I will show you what to do."
When Saul turned to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart, and all of those signs came to pass that same day.
When they arrived at the place on the hill, Saul was met by a company of prophets, and the spirit of God came upon Saul and he prophesied with them.
When everyone who had known Saul before saw him prophesying with the prophets, they said to one another, "What happened to Kish's son? Is Saul also a prophet?"
But a man who lived there spoke to them and asked, "Who is their father?" So this saying became a proverb that people ask: "Is Saul also one of the prophets?"
When Saul finished prophesying, he came to the high place.
And Saul's uncle questioned him and his servant and asked, "Where did you go?" And Saul answered his uncle and said, "To look for the donkeys, and when we could not find them, we went to see Samuel."
Then Saul's uncle said, "I pray that you will tell me what Samuel said to you."
Saul replied to his uncle and said, "He told us that the donkeys had been found." But he did not tell his uncle about the kingdom that Samuel had spoken of.
Samuel summoned the people together before the Lord at Mizpah.

And Samuel said to all of the Israelis, "This is what the Lord God of Israel says, 'I brought all of Israel out of Egypt, and delivered you from the hands of the Egyptians and the other kingdoms that oppressed you.

Today you have rejected your Lord God, who saved you from your adversities and your tribulations. But you said to him, 'No, we want you to appoint a king to reign over us.' So, present yourselves before the Lord by your tribes and families."
When Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel together, the tribe of Benjamin was chosen.
When Samuel had the tribe of Benjamin come forward by their families, Saul and the Matri family was chosen, but when they looked for Saul, they could not find him.
So the people inquired of the Lord again and asked, "Has the chosen man shown up yet?" and the Lord answered, "Behold, he has hidden himself among the stuff.
They ran and brought Saul back, and when he stood among the people, he was head and shoulders taller than any of the other people.
Then Samuel spoke to all the people and said, "Do you see the one whom the Lord has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people." And all the people shouted and said, "God save the king!"
Then Samuel explained how the kingdom would work to all of the people, and he wrote it down in a book and laid it before the Lord. After that Samuel sent the people back to their homes.
Saul also went home in Gibeah, and a band of men whose hearts had been touched by God also went with him.
But the sons of Belial said, "How can this man save us?" So they despised him, and brought him no presents, but Saul said nothing and remained silent.
Then Nahash the Ammonite came and camped near the Jabesh-Gilead border, and the men of Jabesh came to Nahash and said, "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you."
Nahash answered them and said, "I will make a treaty with you on this one condition, I am going to gouge out everyone's right eye, and lay them down to bring shame and disgrace upon all of Israel."
The Jabesh elders responded to him and said, "Give us seven days to send messengers throughout Israel to see if anyone will come to save us, if not we will come out and surrender to you."
Then the messengers reached Saul in Gibeah, and when they told the people there what was happening in Jabesh-Gilead, they all cried out and wept.
As Saul returned from plowing the field he said, "What is wrong with the people, what is causing them to weep?" And they told him about the men from Jabesh.
The Spirit of God came upon Saul when he heard what they had to say, and he became very angry.

So Saul carved a pair of oxen into pieces and sent them with his messengers throughout all of Israel with this message, "Anyone who does not follow Saul and Samuel, will have this done to their own oxen." This caused the fear of the Lord to fall upon the people, and they all rallied as one people.
When Saul counted all the soldiers in Bezek there were 300,000 Israelis, and 30,000 men from Judah.

Then they sent the messengers back with this message and said, "Speak to the men of Jabesh-Gilead and say, 'Tomorrow by the time the sun is hot, you will have help!'"When the messengers went back and told the men of Jabesh, they were very happy.
So the men of Jabesh went to Nahash and said, "Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you can do with us whatever seems good to you."

So the next day Saul organized his army into three companies. Then they attacked and killed the Ammonites until the heat of the day, and those that survived were scattered. Not even two of them were left together.
And the people asked Samuel, "Who said that we should not have Saul reign over us as our king? Bring them out so we can put them to death."
And Saul said, "Nobody will be put to death today, because the Lord has brought salvation to Israel this day."
Then Samuel said to the people, "Come with me to Gilgal, and we can renew the kingdom there."

So everyone went to Gilgal, where they made Saul the king before the Lord in Gilgal. Then they made sacrificial peace offerings before the Lord. Then Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced and celebrated.
Samuel spoke before all of Israel and said, "Behold I have listened to everything that you said to me, and I have appointed a king to rule over you.
And now you have a king that walks before you. I am old and gray headed and my sons are with you, and I have been your leader since my childhood until now.

So, here I am for you to bear witness against me before the Lord and his anointed. Whose ox or donkey have I taken, and who have I defrauded or oppressed, and from whom have I received a bribe to look away? Tell me, and I will return it to you."
And they said, "You have not defrauded or oppressed us, and you have not taken bribes from anyone's hand."
Samuel answered them and said, "The Lord and his anointed are witnesses against you today, that you have not found any bribes in my hand." Then they answered and said, "He is a witness."
And Samuel said to the people, "The Lord is the one who appointed Moses and Aaron, and he also brought your fathers up from the land of Egypt.
Therefore stand still, so that I may reason with you before the Lord about all of the righteous acts he has done for you and your fathers.
When Jacob entered into Egypt and your fathers cried out to the Lord. The Lord sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and led them to this place.
When they forgot their Lord God, he sold them into the hands of Sisera, who was the leader of the army of Hazor, and into the hands of the Philistines and the king of Moab, who fought against them.

Then the people cried out to the Lord and said, 'We have sinned, because we have forsaken the Lord and served Baal and Ashtaroth, but if you now deliver us from the hands of our enemies, we will serve you.'
And the Lord sent Jerub-Baal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel who delivered you from the hands of your enemies on every side, and you lived in safety.
When you realized that King Nahash of Ammon had come out against you and you said to me, 'No, we want a king to reign over us,' but you already knew that your Lord God was your king.
Therefore, the Lord has appointed a king to rule over you, and you have the king that you desired and the king you have chosen!

If you fear, obey, and serve the Lord, and you do not rebel against the Lord's commandments, and both you and the king who reigns over you continues to follow your Lord God, then all will go well for you.
But if you do not obey the Lord and you rebel against his commands, then his hand will be against you, as it was against your fathers.
Therefore, stand and see what a great thing the Lord will do right before your eyes.

Today is the wheat harvest day, is it not? So, I will call out to the Lord, and he will send rain and thunder, and you will see how great your wickedness is. Then you will see what you have done in the Lord's sight by asking for a king."
So Samuel called out to the Lord, and he sent rain and thunder, and all the people were greatly afraid of Samuel and the Lord.
All of the people pleaded with Samuel and said, "Pray to your Lord God for your servants, so that we do not die, because we have added the evil of asking for a king to all of our other sins."
Samuel responded to the people and said, "Do not be afraid, even though you have done all of these wicked things, do not turn away from following the Lord, but serve the Lord with all your heart.
Do not turn away, and do not chase after vain things which cannot profit nor deliver you, because they are vain.
Because the Lord will not forsake his people for his great name's sake, because it pleases him to make you his people.
As for me, God forbid that I should sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you, but I will continue to teach you the good and the right way.
Only fear the Lord, serve him in truth with all your heart, and consider the great things he has done for you.
But if you decide you still want to do wicked things, both you and your king will be consumed."
Saul reigned for one year, and after he had reigned over Israel for two years.

Saul chose 3,000 Israeli men for his army, 2,000 were with him in Michmash and on Mount Bethel, and the other 1,000 were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin, and he sent the rest of the men back to their homes.
Jonathan defeated the garrison of Philistines stationed in Geba, and when the Philistines heard about it, Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land and said, "Let the Hebrews hear."
All of Israel heard that Saul had defeated a garrison of Philistines, and that Israel had defeated and disgraced the Philistines, and the people were called to come to Gilgal and join Saul.
The Philistines gathered 30,000 chariots, 6,000 horsemen, and people as numerous as sand on the beach to fight Israel. They came and camped in Michmash, just east of Bethaven.
When the Israelis saw that they were in danger, the people became very distressed and they hid in caves, thickets, rocks, and in high places and pits.
Some of the Hebrews crossed over the Jordan River into Gad and Gilead. Saul stayed in Gilgal, and the people who followed him trembled with fear.
Saul waited there for seven days until Samuel's appointed time, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and Saul's people began to desert him.
And Saul said, "Bring me a burnt offering and some peace offerings." And Saul offered up the burnt offering.
As soon as Saul finished making his burnt offering Samuel arrived, and Saul went out to greet him.
And Samuel asked, "What have you done?" And Saul said, "I could see that the people were deserting me, and you had not come at the appointed time, and the Philistines were assembled in Michmash.
So I said, 'The Philistines will come down and attack me in Gilgal, and I have not made a plea to the Lord, so I forced myself to offer a burnt offering.'"
Then Samuel said to Saul, "You have been very foolish, you have not kept the commandment your Lord God has given you; if you had, the Lord would have established your kingdom over Israel forever.
But now your kingdom will not continue, the Lord has sought a man after his own heart and appointed him to rule over his people, because you have not kept the Lord's commandment."
Samuel got up and left Gilgal and went to Gibeah of Benjamin, and Saul counted about 600 men that were there with him.
Saul and his son Jonathan, and the people with them lived in Gibeah of Benjamin, but the Philistines camped in Michmash.
The raiders came from the Philistine camp in three companies, and one company turned toward Ophrah in the land of Shual.
Another company turned toward Beth-Horon, and another company turned toward the border that overlooks the valley of Zeboim near the wilderness.
No blacksmiths could be found throughout the land of Israel because the Philistines had said, "The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears!"
So the Israelis would go down to the Philistines to sharpen their plowshares, mattocks, axes, and sickles.
But they had to pay two-thirds of a shekel for plowshares and pickaxes, and a third of a shekel for sharpening the axes and cattle prods.
On the day of the battle, none of the people with Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear, only Saul and his son Jonathan had such weapons.
And the Philistine garrison headed toward the passage of Michmash.
One day Saul's son Jonathan said to his young armor-bearer, "Come with me to the Philistine garrison over on the other side." But he did not tell his father.
One day Saul was living in Migron near the far side of Gibeah and he had about 600 men with him under a pomegranate tree.

This included Ahiah who was wearing an ephod. Ahiah was Ahitub's son, who was Ichabod's brother, who was the son of Phinehas, who was Eli's son, who was the Lord's priest in Shiloh. But the people did not know that Jonathan had left.
There were large sharp rocks on either side of the river fjords where Jonathan intended to cross to reach the Philistine garrison. One was named Bozez and the other Seneh.
One stood northward near Michmash, and the other stood southward near Gibeah.

Jonathan said to his young armor-bearer, "Come with me over to the garrison of these uncircumcised men. Maybe the Lord will work for us, because nothing can restrain the Lord from saving, whether it is by many or by few."
And his armor-bearer said to him, "Do whatever is in your heart, because I am with you in heart, soul, mind, and body."
Then Jonathan said, "Behold we will cross the river and reveal ourselves to these men.
If they say wait for us until we come to you, then we will wait there, and we will not approach them.
But if they say, 'Come on up," then we will go, because this will be a sign that the Lord has delivered them into our hands.
So they presented themselves to the Philistine garrison and the Philistines said, "Behold the Hebrews have come out of their hiding holes."

The men of the garrison answered Jonathan and his armor-bearer and said, "Come on up, and we will show you a thing or two!" And Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Follow me, because the Lord has delivered them into Israel's hands."
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, and the Philistines fell before him, and his armor-bearer followed him and finished them off.
After their first attack Jonathan and his armor-bearer killed about 20 men, who were spread out over a half an acre of land.
The Philistine soldiers in their camps and fields, their people in the garrison, and their raiders all panicked. Then the earth quaked and began to tremble.
Saul's watchmen stationed in Gibeah of Benjamin looked out and saw the Philistine army melting away, and they were trampling one another trying to escape.
Then Saul said to the soldiers with him, "Count and see how many men we have with us!" After they counted the men, they found that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were the only ones not there.
Then Saul said to Ahiah, "Bring God's Ark of the Covenant here." Because at that time the Ark was with the Israelis.
As Saul spoke to the priest, the Philistines noise and commotion increased and their cries grew louder and louder, and Saul said to the priest, "Withdraw your hand."
So Saul assembled his troops and marched into the battle, and they found the Philistines in total disarray, they embarrassed themselves and turned their swords against one another.
Then the Hebrews who had allied themselves and fought with the Philistines before that time, turned and joined the other Israelis with Saul and Jonathan.
When the Israelis men who were hiding on Mount Ephraim heard that the Philistines had fled, they chased hard after them in battle.
So the Lord saved Israel that day, and the battle spread all the way to Bethaven.

The Israelis men were weary and distressed that day, because Saul had formally ordered the soldiers not to eat anything until the evening and said, "Any man that eats anything before evening is cursed, so that I may take vengeance on my enemies." So nobody ate anything.
When they marched through the land and came to the forest, they found honey laying on the ground.
The soldiers marched into the woods, and they saw the honey dripping on the ground, but no one tasted it, because they feared the oath they were forced to take.
But Jonathan had not heard his father order the men to take the oath, so he stretched out his staff and dipped it in a honeycomb and put it in his mouth and his eyes were enlightened.
Then one of the soldiers and said, "Your father ordered the people to take an oath that said, 'Cursed be the man that eats anything today,' and the men are exhausted."
Then Jonathan said, "My father has caused a lot of trouble for our land, see how refreshed my eyes have become, because I tasted a little honey.
How much better would it have been, if the men had been allowed to eat freely from their enemies' spoils? How many more Philistines would we have been able slaughter today?"
So they defeated the Philistines that day from Michmash all the way to Aijalon, but the soldiers were exhausted.
Then they took the spoils of war from their enemy including the sheep, oxen, and calves. They killed them on the ground, but they ate the meat with the blood still in it.

Then someone spoke to Saul and said, "Behold the soldiers are sinning against the Lord, and they are eating the spoils with the blood." So Saul said, "You have transgressed, roll a stone over here now!"

And Saul said, "Spread out among the people and say to the men, "Bring all of your sheep here, then slaughter them here and eat the meat here. But do not sin against the Lord by eating meat with the blood'"So all the soldiers brought their spoils and slaughtered them there that night.
Then Saul built an altar to the Lord, which was the first altar he had ever built to the Lord.

And Saul said, "Let us chase and slaughter the Philistines all night tonight and leave no survivors." And the people said, "Do whatever you think is good." Then the priest said, "Let us draw near to God."
Saul asked for God's counsel and said, "Should I go down and attack the Philistines? Will you deliver them into Israel's hands?" But God did not answer him that day.
And Saul said, "Summon all the chiefs of the people here, so we may discover what sin caused this today.
Because as the Lord that saves Israel lives, whoever commits these sins will surely die, even if it is my son Jonathan." But none of his men in the whole army would answer him.
Then Saul spoke to all of Israel and said, "You stand to one side, and my son Jonathan and I will stand on the other side." So the army replied to him and said, "Do whatever seems good to you."
So Saul prayed to the Lord God of Israel and said, "Cast lots with the Thummim and Urim to decide," and Saul and Jonathan were chosen, but the people's guilt was cleared.
And Saul said, "Cast lots between me and my son Jonathan," and Jonathan was chosen.
Then Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done!" So Jonathan told him and said, "I used my staff to taste a little honey, and now I must die."
Saul answered and said, "May God punish me even more so, if you Jonathan do not surely die."

But the people said to Saul, "Why must Jonathan die? For Jonathan has worked this great salvation for Israel, and he has worked with the Lord today and as the Lord lives, God forbid that one hair should fall from his head to the ground." So the people rescued Jonathan and he did not die.
Then Saul stopped chasing the Philistines, and the Philistines went back to their own place.

So Saul took over the kingdom Israel and fought his enemies on all sides. He fought against Moab, Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. And every direction he turned, he defeated them.
He assembled a vast army and defeated the Amalekites and delivered Israel from the hands of those that plundered them.
Saul sons were named Jonathan, Ishui, and Melchi-Shua. He had two daughters; his firstborn was named Merab and the younger one was named Michal.
Saul's wife was named Ahinoam, who was the daughter of Ahimaaz. The top commander of his army was Abner, who was the son of Saul's uncle Ner.
Saul's father Kish and Abner's father Ner were Abiel's sons.
There was a severe ongoing war against the Philistines during Saul's entire life, and when he noticed an extra strong or courageous man, he recruited them into his service.
Samuel also spoke to Saul and said, "The Lord sent me to anoint you as king over his people in Israel, so listen to the words of the Lord's voice.
This is what the Lord of Hosts says, 'I remember what Amalek did to Israel, how he laid in wait for him along the road when he came up from Egypt.
Go and defeat Amalek and completely destroy everything that they have. Do not spare anyone or anything, but kill all the men, women, infants, oxen, sheep, camels, donkeys, and unweaned livestock.'"
Saul assembled the army and counted them in Telaim, and there were 200,000 footmen, plus 10,000 men from Judah.
Saul marched to one of Amalek's cities and laid in wait in the valley.

Saul warned the Kenites and said, "Because you showed kindness to the Israelis when they left Egypt, leave and get away from the Amalekites, otherwise I will destroy you along with them!" So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites.
And Saul defeated the Amalekites from Havilah all the way to Shur, which is near Egypt.
Saul captured King Agag of Amalek alive but completely destroyed all the people there with the sword.

So Saul and his army spared Agag and saved the best of the Amalekites fat calves, sheep, oxen, and lambs. But they did completely destroy everything else that was worthless, useless, and vile! And they did not destroy anything that was good.
Then the Lord's word came to Samuel and said,

"I regret that I have made Saul the king, because he has turned away from me and he does not follow me, and he has not done what I told him to do." When Samuel heard this, he was overcome with grief, and he cried out to the Lord all night.
Early the next morning Samuel got up to go meet Saul, but he was told, "Saul went to Carmel to set up a place for himself, then he went down to Gilgal."
When Samuel finally saw him, Saul said, "May the Lord bless you; I have done what the Lord commanded."
So Samuel asked, "So why do my ears hear all of these sheep bleating and oxen mooing?"
And Saul said, "They came from the Amalekites, because the people spared the best of the sheep and oxen, to sacrifice to your Lord God, but we completely destroyed the rest."
Then Samuel said to Saul, "Be quiet, and I will tell you what the Lord said to me last night," and Saul said, "Please tell me what he has said."
And Samuel said, "There was a time when you did not think so much of yourself. And did you not become the head of all the tribes of Israel? And did not the Lord anoint you the king of Israel?
The Lord sent you on a journey and said, "Go and completely destroy the Amalekite sinners, and attack them until they have been consumed.
So did you obey the Lord's voice, or did you take the spoils and do evil in the Lord's sight?"
Then Saul said to Samuel, "Yes, I have obeyed the Lord's voice, and I went wherever the Lord sent me. I captured King Agag of Amalek and completely destroyed the Amalekites.
But the people took the spoils including the sheep, oxen, and the best things which should have been completely destroyed, to sacrifice to your Lord God in Gilgal."

And Samuel said, "Does the Lord take as great a delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as he does in obeying his voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice and to listen is better than the fat of rams.
Because rebellion is like the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is the same as immorality and idolatry. And because you have rejected the Lord's word, he has rejected you as king."
Then Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned, because I have transgressed against the Lord's commandment and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.
So I pray that you will pardon my sin, and return with me, so that I may worship the Lord.
And Samuel said to Saul, "I will not return with you, because you have rejected the Lord's word, and the Lord has rejected you as king of Israel."
As Samuel turned to leave, Saul grabbed the hem of his robe, and it tore.
And Samuel said to him, "The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand this day and he has given it to your neighbor who is better than you.
Israel's strength or glory does not lie or repent, because God is not a man who should repent.
Then Saul said, "Yes I have sinned, but please honor me now before the elders of my people and all of Israel, and return with me, so that I may worship your Lord God."
So Samuel returned with Saul and Saul worshipped the Lord.
Then Samuel said, "Bring King Agag the Amalekite to me." So Agag cautiously came to Samuel and said to himself, "Surely the bitterness of death has passed."
And Samuel said, "As the sword has made women childless, your mother will also be childless among women." And Samuel carved Agag into pieces before the Lord in Gilgal.
Then Samuel left for Ramah, and Saul went home in Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel never visited Saul again not even to the day of his death, nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul, but the Lord regretted that he had ever made Saul the king of Israel.

And the Lord spoke to Samuel and said, "How long are you going to mourn for Saul, for I have rejected his reign over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go see Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have chosen a king for myself from among his sons."
And Samuel said, "How can I go? If Saul hears about it, he will kill me." And the Lord said, "Take a heifer with you and say, "I have come to sacrifice to the Lord.
Then call Jesse to the sacrifice and I will show you what to do, and you must anoint the one that I name for you."
So Samuel went to Bethlehem as the Lord had told him. The town elders trembled when he arrived and they said, "Do you come in peace?"
And Samuel said, "I come in peace to sacrifice to the Lord, so sanctify yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice." Then Samuel sanctified Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they arrived, Samuel looked at Eliab and thought, "Surely this is Lord's anointed one."

But the Lord said to Samuel, "Do not look at his appearance or the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the Lord does not see as man sees, man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks within the heart."
Then Jesse called Abinadab to pass before Samuel and he said, "The Lord has not chosen this one either."
Then Jesse made Shammah pass before Samuel, who said, "And the Lord has not chosen this one either."
Once again, Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel, but Samuel said to Jesse, "The Lord has not chosen any of these."

And Samuel spoke to Jesse and asked, "Are all of your children here?" And Jesse said, "The youngest one who keeps the sheep is not here." And Samuel said to Jesse, "Send for him, because we will not sit down for dinner until he comes."
So Jesse sent for him and brought him in, and he appeared ruddy but was handsome to look at. And the Lord said, "Get up and anoint him because he is the one."
Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him amongst his brothers, and the Lord's spirit was on David from that day forward. So Samuel got up and went to Ramah.
But the Lord's spirit left Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.
And Saul's servants said to him, "Behold, you are troubled by an evil spirit from God.
So command your servants to find a man who is a skillful harp player, and when the evil spirit from God is upon you, he will play his harp, and you will be well."
And Saul said to his servants, "Find someone who can play the harp well and bring him to me."

Then one of the servants answered him and said, "Behold I have seen one of Jesse's sons from Bethlehem skillfully playing the harp. He is an attractive, mighty, and courageous man of war, who is prudent in many matters, and the Lord is with him."
So Saul sent messengers to Jesse who said, "Send your son David the shepherd to me."
Jesse sent a donkey loaded with bread, a bottle of wine, and a kid goat to Saul along with his son David.
David went and stood before Saul, and Saul greatly loved him and David became his armor-bearer.
Then Saul sent word to Jesse and said, "I pray you will let David stay with me because he has found favor in my sight."
After that, whenever the evil spirit from God came upon Saul, David would pick up his harp and play, then the evil spirit would leave him, and Saul would be well and refreshed.
The Philistines assembled their armies and prepared for battle at Shochoh which belongs to Judah. They camped between Shochoh and Azekah in Ephes-Dammim.
Saul summoned the men of Israel and camped by the Valley of Elah and prepared their battle array against the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on one side of a mountain, and Israel stood on the other side of the mountain, with a valley between them.
A champion named Goliath who was from Gath, came out from the Philistine camp. He was six cubits and one span in height.
Goliath had a brass helmet on his head, and he wore a brass chainmail coat that weighed about 5,000 shekels.
Goliath had brass shin armor on his legs, and a brass javelin slung between his shoulders.
The staff of Goliath's spear was as thick as a weaver's beam, with an iron blade that weighed 600 shekels, and his armor-bearer carried his shield before him.

Goliath stood out front and taunted the Israelis army and said, "Why have you come out arrayed for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not Saul's servants? Choose a man from among you and let him come out and fight me.
If he fights me and kills me, then we will be your servants, but if I prevail and kill him, then you will serve us and be our servants."
And Goliath the Philistine said, "Today, I defy the armies of Israel, so send someone out to fight me."
When Saul and the Israelis heard what Goliath the Philistine said, they were dismayed and terribly afraid.
In the days of Saul, David was the son of the Ephrathite named Jesse from Bethlehem-Judah. At that time Jesse had eight sons, and he was a very old man.
Jesse's three oldest sons followed Saul into battle, and his firstborn son that followed Saul into battle was Eliab, the next was Abinadab, and the third was Shammah.
David who was the youngest, and the three oldest sons followed Saul.
But David returned from Saul to feed his father's sheep in Bethlehem.
Goliath the Philistine moved closer and showed himself every morning and every evening for forty days.
Jesse spoke to his son David and said, "Run to your brothers camp and take them an ephah of dried wheat and ten loaves of bread.
Take these ten cheeses to your brothers' commanding officer, and see how your brothers are doing, and bring a report back to me."
Saul, David's brothers, and the Israelis army were fighting the Philistines in the valley of Elah.

So David got up early in the morning and left the sheep with another shepherd and took the food and did as Jesse had commanded him. David came to the trench, as the army was moving out to the battlefield, and they shouted a great war cry as they went.
Because Israel and the Philistines had arrayed army against army on the battlefield.
David left his carriage with the carriage keeper and ran out amongst the army, where he found and saluted his brothers.
As David was talking with them, Goliath the Philistine from the army of Gath came out to challenge the Israelis again, and David heard what he said.
When the Israel men saw Goliath, they fled from him and they were extremely frightened.

The Israelis men said, "Have you seen this man who keeps coming out to challenge Israel? The king will reward whoever kills him with great riches, and he will give his daughter in marriage to him and set his father's house free in Israel."

David spoke to the men standing near him and said, "What will the king do for the man who kills this Philistine, and removes this disgrace from Israel? Who is this uncircumcised Philistine who thinks he can defy the armies of the living God?"
The men answered him and told him what the king was offering and they said, "This is what the king will do for the man who kills Goliath."

David's oldest brother Eliab heard what he had been saying to the men, and his anger was kindled against David. And he said, "Why have you come down here? Who did you leave those sheep with out in the wilderness? I know the pride and naughtiness of your heart, because you have come down to see the battle!"
And David said, "What have I done now? Is it not just a question?"
Then David turned toward another soldier and asked him the same question, and the men gave him the same answer as before.
When they heard what David said, someone reported it to Saul and Saul sent for him.
David spoke to Saul and said, "Let no man's heart fail because of this Philistine, your servant will go and fight him."
And Saul replied to David and said, "You cannot fight this Philistine, because you are just a youth, and he has been a warrior from his youth."
David answered Saul and said, "Your servant has kept his father's sheep, and when a lion or bear took a lamb from the flock.
I would track it down, kill it, and pull the lamb out of its mouth. And if it attacked me, I would grab its fur, strike it down, and kill it.
Your servant has killed both lions and bears, and this uncircumcised Philistine will be just like one of them, because he has defied the armies of the living God."
David also said, "The Lord who delivered me from the lion and bear's paw, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." And Saul said to David, "Go, and may the Lord be with you."
So Saul dressed David with his armor and a chainmail coat and put a brass helmet on his head.

David strapped his sword to his armor and he tried to go, but he was not used to wearing armor. David said to Saul, "I cannot go wearing this armor, because I am not used to it," so David took them off.
And David took his staff in his hand and chose five smooth stones from the brook and put them in his shepherd's bag. With his sling in his hand, he moved closer to the Philistine.
And Goliath the Philistine moved closer to David, and his armor-bearer carried his shield before him.
When Goliath saw David, he disrespected him because he was just a ruddy youth of fair appearance.
And the Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come to me with your staff?" Then the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said to David, "Come to me, and I will feed your flesh to the birds and the beasts of the field."

Then said David to Goliath the Philistine, "You come to me with a sword, a spear, and a shield, but I come to you in the name of the Lord of Hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

Today the Lord will deliver you into my hands and I will defeat you. I will take your head and feed the Philistine army carcasses to the birds of the air and beasts of the field, so that the whole earth knows that there is a God in Israel.
Today this entire assembly will know that the Lord does not save with sword and spear, because the battle belongs to him, and he will deliver you into our hands."
When Goliath the Philistine got up and marched to meet David, that hastened David and he ran toward the army to meet him.

Then David put his hand into his bag and put a stone in his sling and slung it. It hit Goliath the Philistine in his forehead, and the stone sunk into his forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground.
So David prevailed over the Philistine with his sling and a stone. Goliath was defeated and killed, but David had no sword in his hand.

Then David ran and stood over Goliath the Philistine and drew his sword from its sheath and killed him. Then David cut Goliath's head off, and the Philistines fled when they saw that their champion was dead.

The Israelis men and the men of Judah jumped up and shouted and pursued the Philistines into the valley and to the gates of Ekron, and the wounded Philistines fell by the wayside to Shaaraim, and all the way to Gath and Ekron.
When the Israelis army returned from chasing the Philistines, they took the spoils of war from their tents.
David took the Philistine's head and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put Goliath's armor in his own tent.

When Saul saw David fight the Philistine, he spoke to his military commander Abner and said, "Abner, whose son is this young man?" And Abner said, "O king, as surely as your soul lives I do not know."
And the king said, "Find out whose son this young man is."
As David returned from the Philistine slaughter, Abner brought him before Saul with the Philistine's head in his hand.
And Saul spoke to him and asked, "Young man, who is your father?" David answered him and said, "I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem."
After David finished speaking to Saul, Saul's son Jonathan and David's souls were knit together, and Jonathan loved David as much as he loved his own soul.
From that day forward Saul kept David by his side and would not let him go home to his father.
Then Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as much as he loved his own soul.
Jonathan stripped off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David along with his other garments including his sword, bow, and belt.
David went wherever Saul sent him and he behaved very wisely. Saul made him his military commander over all his warriors, and he was accepted by all the people, including Saul's servants.

As the army returned from the battlefield after David killed Goliath the Philistine, the joy filled women from the Israelis cities came out singing and dancing to meet King Saul. And they brought all of their musical instruments including their tambourines.
The women sang together as they played their instruments and they said, "Saul has killed thousands, and David has killed tens of thousands."

Saul was very angry and displeased when he heard this saying and he said, "They have given David credit for tens of thousands, and they give me credit for just thousands. What more can he have but the kingdom?"
From that day forward Saul kept a jealous eye on David.
The next day the evil spirit from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied in the house as David played his harp as before, but Saul had a javelin in his hand.
And Saul threw the javelin, because he said, "I will pin David to the wall." But David avoided his presence twice.
Saul was afraid of David because the Lord had left him, but he was with David.
So Saul removed David from his top position and made him the commander of a thousand men, and David led them to the battlefield and back.
David behaved very wisely in everything that he did, because the Lord was with him.
When Saul saw David's wisdom, he was afraid of him.
But everyone in Israel and Judah loved David, because he led them into battle and back.

One day Saul said to David, "Behold, I will give you my oldest daughter Merab to be your wife, but I need you to be courageous for me and fight the Lord's battles." But Saul was thinking to himself, "I do not need to raise my hand against David, because the hand of the Philistines will be against him."
And David said to Saul, "Who am I, and what is my life or my father's family in Israel, that I should be the king's son-in-law?"
So when Saul's daughter Merab should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite instead.
But Saul's daughter Michal loved David and when Saul heard this, he was very pleased.

So Saul thought, "I will give her to him, so that she may be a snare to him and the Philistines hand may also be against him." So Saul said to David, "Today, for the second time you will be my son-in-law."
Then Saul commanded his servants and said, "Speak to David secretly and say, 'Behold the king is delighted with you, all his servants love you, so you should be the king's son-in-law.'"

When Saul's servants gave this message to David, he replied to them and said, "Does it seem to you that being a king's son-in-law is an insignificant thing, especially since I am a poor man and lightly esteemed?"
Saul's servants returned to him and told him what David said.

Saul further instructed his servants and said, "This is what I want you to say to David, 'The king wants no dowry except for a hundred Philistine foreskins to avenge his enemies.'"But Saul thought David would fall by the hand of the Philistines.
When his servants told David this, he was well pleased to become the king's son-in-law. Before the wedding day arrived,

David and his men went and killed 200 Philistine men, and David brought their foreskins and gave them as full payment to the king to be the king's son-in-law. King Saul gave his daughter Michal to become his wife.
Saul could see and he knew that the Lord was with David, and that his daughter Michal loved David.
Because of this, Saul was even more afraid of David, and he became David's constant enemy.
Then the Philistine leaders left and after they left, David behaved even more wisely than all of Saul's servants, so his name became highly esteemed.
Saul spoke to his son Jonathan and all of his servants and said that they should kill David.

But Saul's son Jonathan loved David very much and he spoke to him and said, "My father Saul wants to kill you, so I pray that you will be very careful and find a secret place to hide until the morning.
I will go stand beside my father in the field where you are and ask him about you, then I will tell you what I find out.
Jonathan said good things about David to his father Saul and said, "Do not let the king sin against his servant David, because his works have been very good for you and he has not sinned against you.

Because he put his own life on the line and killed Goliath the Philistine, and the Lord worked a great salvation for all of Israel. You saw what happened and rejoiced, so why do you want to sin against innocent blood and kill David without cause?"
And Saul listened to Jonathan, and he swore an oath and said, "As surely as the Lord lives, David will not be killed."
So Jonathan summoned David and told him all these things. Then Jonathan brought David to Saul, to serve him as he had before.
But once again there was war and David went to fight the Philistines, and there was a great slaughter, and they fled from David.
The Lord's evil spirit came upon Saul once again as he sat in his house with his spear, as David played his harp.
Saul thought he would pin David to the wall with the spear, but that night when Saul threw the spear it hit the wall, but David escaped.

Saul also sent messengers to David's house to find him and kill him in the morning. But David's wife Michal warned him and said, "If you do not run for your life tonight, you will be dead by tomorrow."
So Michal lowered David down through a window, and he escaped and fled.
Michal laid an idol on the bed and put some goat's hair on its head and covered it with a blanket.
When Saul sent messengers to attack David, she told them that he was sick.
Saul sent his messengers to see David again and he gave them his orders and said, "Bring him to me in his bed so I can kill him."
When the messengers went into David's room, they saw an idol with goat's hair laying in his bed.
Saul confronted Michal and said, "Why did you deceive me, and help my enemy escape? And Michal answered Saul and said, "Because he told me that he would kill me, if I did not let him go."
So David escaped and fled from Saul. He went to see Samuel in Ramah and told him what Saul had done to him, and he and Samuel moved to Naioth to live.
Saul was told about it and said, "David is living in Naioth in Ramah."
Saul sent messengers to take David, but when they saw the prophets prophesying, and that Samuel had been appointed over them, the Spirit of God came on Saul's messengers, and they also prophesied.
When Saul was told about this, he sent more messengers and they also prophesied, then he sent messengers a third time, and they too prophesied.
Then Saul went to Ramah himself, and he came to the great well in Sechu and he asked, "Where are Samuel and David?" And someone said, "Behold they are in Naioth of Ramah."
Saul went to the place in Naioth of Ramah, and the Spirit of God also came upon him, and Saul prophesied as he traveled until he arrived in Naioth in Ramah.
So Saul stripped off his clothes and prophesied before Samuel as the others, and he lay there naked all day and night. That's why they ask, "Is Saul also one of the prophets?"
David fled Naioth in Ramah and went to Jonathan and asked, "What have I done? What is my immorality, and what is my sin before your father, that makes him want to kill me?"
Jonathan replied to David and said, "God forbid, you will not die! Behold my father does nothing great or small that he does not tell me about. Why should he hide this from me? It is not so."

David swore and said, 'Your father certainly knows that I have found grace in your sight. And he says, 'Do not tell Jonathan about this, or he will be grieved.' But as surely as the Lord and your soul lives, there is just one step between me and death."
Then Jonathan spoke to David and said, "I will do whatever your soul desires."
And David said to Jonathan, "Behold, there is a new moon tomorrow, and I am supposed to have dinner with King Saul. But I will go and hide in the field until the evening of the third day."
If your father Saul misses me at all then you can say, 'David asked me to let him go, so he could go to his hometown of Bethlehem, because he and his whole family make an annual sacrifice there.'
If your father Saul says, 'That's good.' Then your servant will have peace, but if he is very angry, then you will surely know that he has evil intentions.

Therefore deal kindly with your servant, for you have brought me into the Lord's covenant with you. But, if there is any immorality in me then kill me yourself, why should you have to bring me to your father?"
And Jonathan said, "I would never do that, if I knew for certain that my father had evil intentions toward you, would I not tell you?"
Then David said to Jonathan, "Who will let me know if your father answers harshly?"
And Jonathan said to David, "Come, and let us go out into the field," and they both went out into the field.

Then Jonathan said to David, "By the Lord God of Israel, I will find out from my father by this time tomorrow or the next day. If the news toward you is favorable, then I will send for you and tell you.
But if my father intends to do you evil, then I will tell you and send you away, so that you may go in peace. May the Lord be with you, as he has been with my father.
And you will show me the Lord's kindness while I yet live, so that I do not die.
But also so you do not cut off your kindness from my house forever, not even after the Lord has cut off David's enemies from everyone on the face of the earth."
So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David and said, "Let the Lord require accountability of David's enemies by his hand."
Jonathan made David swear again because he loved David as he loved his own soul.
Then Jonathan said to David, "There is a new moon tomorrow, your seat will be empty, and you will be missed.
After you have stayed three days, go down to the place you hid when this trouble began, and wait by the stone of Ezel.
I will shoot three arrows into its side, as if I were shooting at a target.
And I will send a boy to find the arrows. If I tell the boy that the arrows are on this side of you, take them and come to me because as the Lord lives there is no danger and you will be safe.
But if I tell the boy that the arrows are beyond you, leave because the Lord has sent you away.
As for what you and I have spoken of the Lord will be a witness between us forever."
So David hid in the field and when the new moon came, the king sat down to eat his meat.
King Saul sat on his seat by the wall as before and Jonathan got up, and Abner sat beside Saul, but David's place was empty.
Nevertheless, Saul said nothing that day because he thought, "Something must have happened to make him unclean, surely he must be unclean."
The next day which was the second day of the month, David's place was empty, and Saul spoke to his son Jonathan and asked, "Why did Jesse's son not come to eat yesterday or today?"
Jonathan answered Saul, "David asked me if he could leave to go to Bethlehem.

And David said, 'Please let me go, because our family has to make a sacrifice in the city. And my brother has commanded me to be there. Therefore, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me go and see my brothers.' And that's why he has not come to the king's table.

Then Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan and he said, "You are the son of a perverse rebellious woman. Do you think that I do not know that you have chosen Jesse's son to your own confusion, and the disgrace of your own mother's nakedness?
Because as long as Jesse's son lives on the earth neither you nor your kingdom will be established. So you will send him to me, because he must surely die."
Jonathan answered his father Saul and said, "Why must he be killed? What has he done?"
Then Saul threw a spear at Jonathan, and he knew that his father was determined to kill David.
So Jonathan got up from the table in fierce anger, and he ate no meat on the second day of the month, because his father had shamed him and he was grieved for David.
The next morning, Jonathan went out to the field at the time that he and David had agreed upon and he took a little boy with him.
And Jonathan said to the boy, "Run and find the arrows that I shoot into the field." And the boy ran, but he shot the arrow beyond him.
When the boy reached the place where Jonathan had shot the arrow, Jonathan cried out to the boy and said, "Is the arrow not beyond you?"
Then Jonathan cried out to the boy, "Do not stop, make haste and speedily return." So Jonathan's young boy collected the arrows and returned to his master.
But the boy did not know anything about Jonathan's arrangement with David.
Jonathan gave his artillery to the boy and said, "Go and carry them into the city."

As soon as the boy was gone, David got up from his place on the south side of the stone and fell facedown to the ground and bowed three times. Then he and Jonathan kissed each another and they both wept until David could weep no more.

And Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace, because we have both sworn in the name of the Lord when we said, 'May the Lord be a witness between us, and between our descendants forever.'"Then David got up and left, and Jonathan went into the city.
Then David went to Ahimelech the priest in Nob, but Ahimelech was afraid to meet with David and he asked, "Why are you alone, and why is nobody with you?"

David replied to the priest and said, "The king has ordered me on his official business, and he told me not to tell anyone anything about the business he has sent me to take care of, which I also command you. And I have also asked my servants to meet me at a secret place.
So, do you have five loaves of bread? If you do, I need them, and if not, I will take whatever you have on hand."
The priest answered David and said, "I have no common bread on hand, but there is holy bread you can have, if the young men have kept themselves from women."

Then David answered the priest and said, "The truth is since we left, we have been separated from women for at least the last three days. The young men's equipment is always kept holy, even on our common missions, as if it had been sanctified in a vessel today."

So the priest gave David the holy bread, because there was no other bread there except for that which was taken from the offerings laid before the Lord. For the priests had replaced what was taken away with the hot bread.
One of Saul's servants was there that day, detained before the Lord. He was an Edomite named Doeg, and he was one of Saul's chief herdsmen.

David spoke to Ahimelech and asked, "Is there a spear or sword here? Because I left in such a hurry that I forgot to bring my sword or any other weapons, because the king's business required such haste.

And the priest said, "The Philistine whom you killed in the valley of Elah Goliath's sword is here wrapped in a cloth behind the robe. If you want it, take it, but there are no other weapons here." And David said, "There are no others like it, give it to me."
That day David got up and fled for fear of Saul and went to King Achish of Gath.

Achish's servants said to him, "Is not David the king of the land? Did they not sing to one another about him while they danced when they said, "Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands?"
David took these words to heart, and he was extremely frightened of King Achish of Gath.
He immediately changed his behavior and pretended to be crazy as they took him into custody, and David scribbled on the city gates, and let spit drool down his beard.
Then Achish spoke to his servants and said, "Look, you can see that this man is a madman, why have you brought him to me?
Do I need a madman, for you have brought this fellow to play the madman in my presence? Must this fellow come into my house?"
So David escaped and went to the Adullam cave, and when his brothers and the people in his father's house and heard about it, they went to see him.
So did everyone else who was in distress, in debt, or discontent, they all came to him, and he became the leader of about 400 men.
David went to Mizpah in Moab, and he spoke to the Moab king and said, "I pray that you will let my father and mother stay with you, until I know what God has planned for me."
And David brought them to the king of Moab, where they lived the entire time that David was in the stronghold.
One day the prophet Gad said to David, "Do not stay in the stronghold, leave and go to the land of Judah." So David left and went to the forest of Hareth.
Saul heard that David and his men had been discovered. At that time Saul lived in Gibeah under a tree in Ramah. One day Saul had a spear in his hand, and his servants were all standing around him.
Then Saul said to them, "Listen to me you Benjamites! Is the son of Jesse going to give all of you fields and vineyards, and make you all captains of thousands and hundreds?

All of you have conspired against me and not one of you told me that my son made a treaty with Jesse's son. And not one of you feels sorry for me or even told me that my son has stirred up my own servant against me today!"
Then Doeg the Edomite who was standing there with Saul's officer answered him and said, "I saw Jesse's son going to see Ahitub's son Ahimelech in Nob.
Ahimelech asked the Lord for his advice for David, and he gave him some prepared food and Goliath the Philistine's sword."
Then the king sent for priest Ahimelech and everyone in his father's house, and all the priests in Nob, and they all went to see the king.
And Saul said, "Listen to me you son of Ahitub!" And Ahimelech answered the king and said, "Here I am my Lord."

And Saul said, "Why have you and Jesse's son conspired against me?" Why did you give him bread and a sword, and why have you asked God to help him? Is it so that he could lie in wait and rise up against me, as he does today?
Then Ahimelech answered the king and said, "Who among all of the servants in your house is as faithful and honorable as your son-in-law David, who goes and does your bidding?
Was that the first time I asked God's help for him? Far be it from me and my father's house, for the king impute any disloyalty to us, because we more or less knew nothing about all of this."
And the king said, "Ahimelech, you and your father's house will all surely die."

Then the king said to the footmen standing around him, "Kill the Lord's priests, because they are loyal to David, and they knew when he fled that he did not represent me. But the king's servants would not turn against the Lord's priests.
So the king turned to the Edomite Doeg and said, "Attack the priests!" And Doeg turned against the priests and killed 85 men wearing linen ephods that day.
Doeg attacked Nob the city of priests with the edge of the sword. He killed the men, women, children, oxen, donkeys, sheep, and the unweaned.
But one of Ahimelech's sons named Abiathar, escaped and fled to David. Ahimelech was Ahitub's son.
Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the Lord's priests.
And David said to Abiathar, "I knew the day that I saw the Edomite Doeg, that he would surely tell Saul, and it is my fault that your entire family was killed.
But you can stay with me in safety, and do not be afraid because the man who wants to kill you seeks to take my life as well. But you will be safe with me."
Then they told David and said, "The Philistines are attacking Keilah, and they are stealing grain from the threshing room floors."
So David prayed to the Lord and said, "Should I go defeat the Philistines?" And the Lord said to David, "Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah."
David's men spoke to him and asked, "We are afraid here in Judah, we will be even more terrified if we have to go to Keilah and attack the Philistine armies?"
Then David asked the Lord again, and the Lord answered him and said, "Get up and go down to Keilah, for I will deliver the Philistines into your hands."
So David and his men went to Keilah where they fought and slaughtered the Philistines. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah and brought the Philistines cattle back with them.
When Ahimelech's son Abiathar fled to David in Keilah, he arrived with an ephod in his hand.
When Saul was told that David had gone to Keilah he said, "God has delivered David into my hands, for he has trapped himself in a town behind gates and bars."
So Saul assembled his armies for war, to go to Keilah to lay siege against David and his men.
David knew that Saul was secretly planning to attack him, and he spoke to Abiathar the priest and said, "Bring the ephod here."
Then David said, "O Lord God of Israel, your servant has certainly heard that Saul intends to come to Keilah and destroy the city because of me.
Will the men of Keilah deliver me up into his hands? Will Saul come as I have heard and attack me? O Lord God of Israel, I beg that you answer your servant." And the Lord said, "He will come."
Then David said, "Will the men of Keilah deliver me and my men into Saul's hands?" And the Lord said, "Yes, they will deliver you up!"
So David and about 600 of his men got up and left Keilah, and they traveled around from one place to another. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he did not bother to go there.
David lived in the wilderness strongholds and remained on a mountain in the Ziph wilderness. Saul searched for David every day, but God did not deliver David into his hand.
David knew that Saul still wanted to take his life, and he was living in the woods in the wilderness of Ziph.
One day Saul's son Jonathan went to meet David in the woods, and he strengthened David's hand in God.
And Jonathan spoke to David and said, "Fear not, for my father Saul will not find you, and you will be the king of Israel. I will be next to you, and my father Saul also knows this."
Then the two of them made a covenant before the Lord. So, David lived in the woods, and Jonathan went home.
After that the Ziphites came to Saul in Gibeah and said, "Does not David hide among us in his strongholds in the woods, on the hill of Hachilah, which is on the south side of Jeshimon?"
So now O king, come down whenever your soul desires, and we will do our part and deliver David into your hands."
And Saul said, "May you be blessed by the Lord, for you have compassion for me.
I pray you will go and make preparations. Find David's hiding place and the places that he haunts. And find out who has seen him there, because I have been told that he deals very subtlety.

Find all of the hiding places where he lurks, and when you know for certain where he is, return to me and I will go with you. If he is anywhere in the land, I will find him wherever he is among all the thousands of Judah."
So they got up and went to Ziph ahead of Saul, but David and his men were hiding in the wilderness of Maon, in the plains on the south side of Jeshimon.

But Saul and his men also went to find him and David was told they were looking for him. So he went down to the rock and lived in the wilderness of Maon. But when Saul heard this, he pursued David into the wilderness of Maon.

Saul was traveling along one side of the mountain and David, and his men were on the other side of the mountain. Out of fear, David quickly left to get away from Saul, because Saul and his men had surrounded David and his men.
But a messenger came to Saul and said, "You must come quickly, because the Philistines have invaded the land."
So Saul stopped pursuing David, and went to attack the Philistines, and they called that place Sela-Hammahlekoth.
Then David left and went to live in the strongholds of En-Gedi.
When Saul returned from chasing the Philistines he was told, "Behold David is hiding in the wilderness of En-Gedi."
Then Saul chose 3,000 men from all of Israel and went looking for David and his men on Rocks of the Wild Goats.
As Saul passed the sheep pens along the road there was a cave nearby, and Saul went into the cave to relieve himself. But David and his men were hiding inside the cave.

David's men said to him, "Behold the day has come in which the Lord said to you, 'I will deliver your enemy into your hands, so that you may do to him whatever seems good to you.'"Then David got up and secretly cut off the skirt of Saul's robe.
Afterward, David suffered a broken heart because he had cut the skirt from Saul's robe.
And David said to his men, "Lord forbid that I should attack my master, whom the Lord has anointed. I cannot stretch out my hand against him, since he is the Lord's anointed one."
So David stopped his servants with these words and would not let them rise up against Saul. So Saul left the cave and went on his way.
Soon David also left the cave and cried out to Saul and said, "My Lord the king!" When Saul turned around and looked, David stooped and bowed facedown to the ground.
And David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to these men when they say, 'Behold, David wants to hurt you'?

Behold, you can see with your own eyes that the Lord delivered you into my hands in the cave today, and I was told to kill you. But I spared your life and I said, 'I will not raise my hand against my Lord, because he is the Lord's anointed one.'

Besides that my father, do you see this piece of robe in my hand? Because I cut it from the skirt of your robe, and I did not kill you. You must see and know that I have no evil intentions against you, and I have not sinned against you, yet you hunt me down to take my life.
May the Lord judge between us, and may the Lord take vengeance on you, but my hand will never be against you.
As the ancient proverbs say, 'Wickedness proceeds from the wicked.' But my hand will never be against you.
Who has the king of Israel come out to attack? Who do you pursue? Do you pursue a dead dog or a flea.
So let the Lord be judge and judge between us, and he will see and plead my case and deliver me from your hand."
When David finished speaking Saul said, "Is that you David my son?" And Saul began to weep loudly.
And Saul said to David, "You are more righteous than I am, because you have treated me good, even after I have rewarded you with evil.
And you have treated me well today, because when the Lord delivered me into your hands, you did not kill me.
For if a man finds his enemy, does he let him get away? So the Lord will reward you with good for what you have done for me today.
And now I know that you will surely be the king, and that the kingdom of Israel will be established by your hand.
So swear to me by the Lord, that you will not cut off my descendants, and that you will not destroy my name from my father's house."
So David swore an oath to Saul and Saul went home, but David and his men went back to their stronghold.
One day Samuel died, and all the Israelis gathered together to mourn him. They buried him in his home at Ramah, and David got up and went down to the wilderness of Paran.
There was a very wealthy man in Maon who kept his possessions in Carmel. He had 3,000 sheep and 1,000 goats that he was shearing in Carmel.
His name was Nabal, his wife's name was Abigail, and he was from the house of Caleb. She was a wise, good, and beautiful woman, but Nabal was mean spirited, rude, and did evil things.
David was out in the wilderness, and he heard that Nabal was shearing his sheep.
David sent ten young men to speak to Nabal in Carmel, and he told them to say, "Go greet him in my name.
And say to the prosperous man who lives there, 'Peace be to both of you, to your home, and to everything that you own.
Now I hear that you have shearers in Carmel, and the whole time your shepherds were with us, we did not hurt them and nor was anything taken from them.

Ask your young men, and they will tell you this is true. So let my young men find favor in your eyes, because we have come to you on a good day. So I pray you will give whatever you can afford to your servants and your son David.'"
When David's young men arrived, they spoke to Nabal on David's behalf, and they told him everything they were told to say, and they waited for his answer.
Nabal answered David's servants and said, "Who is David, and who is this son of Jesse? There are many servants these days that break away from their masters.
Must I give my bread, my water, and the meat that I have prepared for my shearers, and give it to men that I do not know?"
So David's young men left and went back and told David everything that was said.
Then David said to his men, "Pick up your swords." So David and about 400 of his men strapped on their swords and left, but about 200 men stayed behind with their stuff.
But one of Nabal's young men told Nabal's wife Abigail what was happening and he said, "Behold David sent messengers from the wilderness to salute our master, and he screamed at them.
But these men were very good to us, we were not hurt, and nothing was stolen from us when we were out in the fields, the entire time we lived among them as long as we talked to them.
They were around us night and day, the whole time we were with them keeping our sheep.
So consider what needs to be done, because evil is determined against our master and his entire household. For he is such a son of Belial, that nobody can talk to him."
Then Abigail hurriedly loaded 200 loaves of bread, two bottles of wine, five dressed sheep, five measures of dried wheat, 100 raisin clusters, and 200 fig cakes on some donkeys.
And she said to her servants, "Go on ahead of me, and I will follow you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
She rode her donkey until she arrived near the shelter on the hill, where she saw David and his men coming down against her, and she met with them.
Now David had said, "Surely I have protected everything this fellow owns out in the wilderness in vain. Nothing he owns has gone missing and he has repaid me evil for good.
May God also do more to the enemies of David, if I let any male of anything in this man's household that pisses against the wall survive until morning."
When Abigail saw David, she hurriedly jumped off her donkey, bowed and fell facedown toward the ground before David.
She fell at his feet and said, "Let this immorality be on me my Lord. I pray you will let your housemaid speak to you, so that you may hear my words.

My Lord, I pray you do not listen to what this man Nabal of Belial says, because his name means 'fool', and he is a foolish man, but I am your housemaid and I did not meet with the young men that you sent.

So my Lord, as the Lord and your soul lives, the Lord has prevented you from coming to shed blood and avenge yourself by your own hand. Let your enemies who seek to do evil against my lord, be as cursed as Nabal.
And now your housemaid has brought this blessing to my Lord, so give it to the young men who follow you.
I pray you will forgive my trespass, and may the Lord make my Lord's house a steadfast house, because you fight the Lord's battles, and no evil has been found in you since you were born.

But if a man rises to pursue you and seeks to take your soul, he will not prevail. But your soul will be bound in the bundle of life with your Lord God. And God will sling your enemies' souls out, as if they were shot from a sling.
When the Lord has done all the good things for you that he has promised, and he appoints you ruler over Israel.

After all this happens, there will be no grief to you because you have shed blood or avenged yourself against Nabal's household for no reason. But after the Lord has dealt well with my lord, please remember your housemaid."
Then David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today.
And blessed are you and your advice, for you have kept me from shedding blood and avenging myself by my own hand today.

For it is indeed the very living Lord God of Israel himself, who has kept me from hurting you. For if you had not come this quickly to meet me, there would not have been any of Nabal's men left by morning."
So David accepted what she brought him and he said to her, "Go home in peace, and behold I have listened to you and accepted your people."
When Abigail returned to Nabal, he was having a feast like a king's feast in his house, and his heart was merry because he was very drunk, so more or less she told him nothing until the next morning.
But in the morning, when the wine was gone and Nabal sobered up his wife told him these things, and his heart turned to stone and died he inside.
About ten days later the Lord defeated Nabal and he died.
