When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the Lord, who has pleaded my cause of disgrace from Nabal, and has kept his servant from evil. Because the Lord has returned Nabal's wickedness on his own head." So David sent messengers to Abigail with his marriage proposal to her.
When David's servants went to see Abigail in Carmel, they spoke to her and said, "David sent us with a message for you, he wants you to be his wife."
She got up and bowed facedown to the ground and said, "Behold let me be your housemaid and I am your servant and I am ready to wash the feet of my Lord's servants."
Abigail hurriedly got up and followed David's messengers on her donkey as five of her girls followed them, and she became his wife.
David also married Ahinoam of Jezreel and both of them were his wives.
But Saul had given his daughter Michal, who was David's wife to Phalti the son of Laish of Gallim.
The Ziphites came to Saul in Gibeah and said, "David is hiding on the Hill of Hachilah near Jeshimon."
Then Saul went down to the wilderness of Ziph with 3,000 men he chose from Israel, to find David in the Ziph wilderness.
Saul camped on the Hill of Hachilah before Jeshimon, but David lived in the wilderness, and he realized that Saul had followed him into the wilderness.
So David sent spies to find out for certain if Saul had arrived.

David got up and went to the place where Saul had camped. David could see where Saul and Ner's son Abner, who was the commander of his forces had camped. Saul lay in the trench, and his army was camped all around him.
Then David said to Ahimelech the Hittite and Joab's brother Zeruiah's son Abishai and said, "Who will go down to Saul's camp with me?" Abishai answered him and said, "I will go down there with you."

So David and Abishai entered the camp at night and behold, they saw Saul sleeping in the trench, and his spear was stuck in the ground beside his pillow, but Abner and the soldiers were asleep all around him.

Then Abishai said to David, "God has delivered your enemy into your hands tonight. So I pray that you will please let me kill him. I will thrust the spear all the way through him, and it will only take one thrust to shove it into the ground, and I will not have to spear him a second time."
David answered Abishai and said, "Do not attack him, because who can stretch out their hand against the Lord's anointed one without guilt?"
Furthermore David said, "As surely as the Lord lives, the Lord himself will defeat Saul, or his day to die will come, or he will descend into battle and perish.
God forbid that I should stretch out my hand against God's anointed one but let us take the spear beside his pillow and his small cup of water and go."

So David took the spear and the small cup of water from Saul's pillow and they left. Nobody saw them or knew they had been there, because a deep sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them, and they were all sound asleep.
Then David went over to the other side and stood on top of a hill far away with a considerable distance between them.
David cried out to Ner's son Abner and the soldiers with him and said, "Why do you not answer Abner? Then Abner answered and said, "Who cries out to the king?"
David said to Abner, "Are you a courageous man, and who else is like to you in Israel? So why then, did you not protect your king, when someone came to kill him?

This is not good thing that you have done. As the Lord lives, you are worthy of death, because you have not protected your master, the Lord's anointed. So where is the king's spear, and the small cup of water that was beside his pillow?"
Then Saul recognized David's voice and said, "Is that you my son David?" And David said, "Yes, it is my Lord, O king."
And David said, "Why does my Lord pursue his servant again? What evil have I done to you?"

So I pray that my Lord the king will hear the words of his servant. If the Lord has stirred you up against me, let him accept an offering. But if men have caused this, then let them be cursed before the Lord. Because today they have driven me out to prevent me from sharing in the Lord's inheritance and they said, 'Go and serve other gods.'
So, do not let my blood fall on the ground before the Lord, for the king of Israel has come out looking for a flea, as when one hunts a quail in the mountains.

Then Saul said, "David my son, I have sinned against you, please come back because I will never again try to harm you. My soul was precious in your eyes and behold I have played the fool and made a terrible mistake today."
And David answered Saul and said, "Behold the king's spear! Send one of your young men to come fetch it.
May the Lord repay every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness, because the Lord delivered you into my hands today, but I would not stretch out my hand against the Lord's anointed one.
And behold, as surely as I have valued your life today, let my life be worth as much in the eyes of the Lord, and let him deliver me from all this tribulation."
Then Saul said to David, "Blessed are you my son David, you will do great things, and you will also prevail." So David went on his way, and Saul returned home.

And David said to himself in his heart, "One day I am going to perish at Saul's hand, the best thing for me would be to escape into the land of the Philistines. And someday Saul will tire of looking for me all over Israel, and I will escape from his hand."
David got up and took the 600 men with him to Maoch's son Achish the king of Gath.
David and his men lived with Achish in Gath, and each man had their own household, and David had two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelite, and Nabal's widow Abigail the Carmelite.
And Saul was told that David had fled to Gath, so he stopped looking for him again.
And David said to Achish, "If I have found grace in your eyes, please give me a place to live in some town out in the country. Why should your servant live with you in the royal city?"
That day Achish gave him Ziklag, and to this day Ziklag belongs to the kings of Judah.
And David lived in the Philistine country for one year and four months.
David and his men invaded the Geshurites, the Gezrites, and the Amalekites, because from ancient times those nations inhabited Shur all the way to the land of Egypt.
When David defeated the land, he left no men or women alive, but he took their sheep, oxen, donkeys, camels, and apparel and returned to Achish.
And Achish asked David, "Where did you raid today?" And David answered him and said, "I raided the south of Judah, the south of the Jerahmeelites, and the south of the Kenites."

And David let no men or women survive, to be brought to Gath because he said, "If they survive, they will report us and say, 'So this is what David did.'"This was the way David lived the entire time he stayed in the Philistine country.
Achish believed in David and he said, "David has made his people in Israel completely abhor him, so he will be my servant forever."
In those days the Philistines assembled their armies for warfare to fight with Israel. And Achish said to David, "You must know that you and your men must go to battle with me."
And David said to Achish, "I can assure you that you will know what your servant can do." And Achish said to David, "And that's why I will make you my bodyguard forever."
By that time Samuel had died and all of Israel mourned him, and they buried him in his own city Ramah. And Saul had removed the wizards and those who used familiar from the land.
The Philistine army moved and camped in Shunem, and Saul assembled the Israelis army together, and they camped in Gilboa.
When Saul saw the size of the Philistine armies, he was afraid, and his heart trembled.
When Saul asked the Lord what to do, the Lord did not answer him, not through his dreams, not through the prophets, and not through the Urim.
Then Saul said to his servants, "Find me a woman with a familiar spirit, so that I may go and ask her." And his servants said to him, "Behold there is a woman with a familiar spirit in Endor."

So Saul disguised himself with different clothes and went to the women with two of his men. They went at night and Saul spoke to her and said, "I pray that you can divine a familiar spirit for me whose name I will give you."

And the woman said to him, "Look you know what Saul has done, he has cut off the people who use familiar spirits and wizards from the land. So you only want to lay a snare for my life and cause my death?"
And Saul swore to her by the Lord and said, "As surely as the Lord lives, there will be no punishment if you do this thing."
Then the woman said, "Who do you want me to bring up for you? And he said, "Bring up Samuel."
When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice and she spoke to Saul and said, "Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul."
And King Saul said to her, "Do not be afraid! What have you seen?" And the woman said to Saul, "I saw the gods ascending from the earth."
And Saul said to her, "What does he look like?" And she said, "An old man came up, and he is wearing a robe." And Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he stooped and bowed facedown to the ground.

Samuel spoke to Saul and asked, "Why have you disturbed me and brought me up here?" Saul answered him and said, "I am extremely distressed, because the Philistines are making war against me and God has left me. He no longer answers me through the prophets or dreams. So I have summoned you to tell me what to do."
Then Samuel replied to Saul and said, "So since the Lord has left you and become your enemy, you have come to ask me for advice?
The Lord has done exactly what he said he would do when he spoke through me. He has torn the kingdom from your hands and given it to your neighbor David.
Because you did not obey the Lord's voice and execute his fierce anger against Amalek, the Lord done this thing to you today.

Furthermore, the Lord will also deliver Israel along with you into the hands of the Philistines. Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me, and the Lord will deliver the Israelis army into the hands of the Philistines."
Then Saul immediately fell on the ground, and he was extremely frightened, because of what Samuel said. And he had no strength left, because he had eaten no bread that whole day or night.

And the woman came to Saul and saw that he was terribly upset and she said to him, "Behold your housemaid has obeyed your voice. I have taken my life into my own hands, and I have listened to what you said to me.
So I pray that you will listen to me and let me serve you some bread, so you can eat and have the strength to be on your way."
But he refused and said, "I will not eat." But the woman and his servants together compelled him to listen to them. So he got up off the ground and sat on the bed.
The woman had a fat calf that she quickly killed, and she kneaded some flour and baked some unleavened bread.
She brought it to Saul and his servants and they ate, and that night they got up and left.
The Philistines assembled all their armies together in Aphek, and the Israelis camped near a fountain in Jezreel.
And the Philistine lords marched out their hundreds and thousands, but David, his men, and Achish marched around behind them.

Then the Philistine commanders said, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" And Achish replied to the Philistine commanders and said, "Is this not David the servant of King Saul of Israel? He has been with me for years, and since the day he came to me until today, I have found no fault in him."

But the Philistine commanders were angry with Achish and they said, "Send this fellow back to the place that you appointed him. Do not let him go into battle with us, he could turn on us and become our adversary. What better way for him to reconcile himself to his master than with the heads of our own men?
Is this not the David about whom they sing and dance and say, "Saul killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands?"

Then Achish called for David and said to him, "As surely as the Lord lives, you have been honest with me in your comings and goings, and your army is good in my sight. And since the day that you came to me until today, I have no found evil in you, nevertheless the commanders do not trust you.
Therefore go in peace, so that you do not displease the Philistine commanders."
And David said to Achish, "But what have I done? You have trusted your servant since I first came to you until today, so what would make you not trust me to go fight the enemies of my Lord the king?
And Achish answered David and said, "I know that you are as good as an angel of God in my sight, but the Philistine commanders have said, 'He must not go into battle with us.'
So get up early in the morning, take your master's servants that came here with you, and leave at first light.
So David and his men got up early in the morning and returned to the land of Philistine, and the Philistines went to Jezreel.
On the third day David and his men arrived in Ziklag, and they discovered that the Amalekites had invaded the south and attacked Ziklag and burned it down.
They had captured all the women there both young and old. They did not kill any of them, but they left and carried them away.
When David and his men returned to the city, they saw that it had been burned, and their wives, sons, and daughters had been taken captive.
So David and the men with him cried out and wept, until they could no longer weep.
David's two wives Ahinoam the Jezreelite, and Nabal's widow Abigail the Carmelite had also been taken captive.
And David was greatly distressed, because the people spoke of stoning him. The men's souls grieved for their sons and daughters, but David encouraged himself through his Lord God.
So David said to Ahimelech's son Abiathar the priest, "I pray that you will bring me the ephod," and Abiathar brought the ephod to David.

David spoke to the Lord and asked, "Should I pursue these troops, and will I overtake them?" Then the Lord answered him and said, "Pursue them, because you will surely overtake them, and you will recover everything."
So David and the 600 men with him went to the Brook of Besor, where some stayed behind.
But David continued to pursue them with the 400 men he had left, because 200 men who were too weak to cross the Brook of Besor were left behind.
The men found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. They gave him some bread and water and he ate and drank.
And they gave him a piece of fig cake and two clusters of raisins, after he had eaten his spirit returned to him, because he had eaten no bread nor drank any water for three days and three nights.

And David spoke to him and asked, "Who do you belong to, and where are you from?" And the man said, "I am an Egyptian, an Amalekite's servant, and my master left me because I got sick three days ago."
We invaded the land south of the Cherethites along the borders of Judah, and the land south of Caleb where we burned Ziklag."
And David said to him, "Can you lead me to this company?" And the man said, "Swear to me by God, that you will not kill me or deliver me into my master's hands, and I will lead you to them."

When the man led them down, the Amalekites were spread out all over the land, eating, drinking, and dancing. They were celebrating all the great spoils that they had stolen from the land of the Philistines and Judah.
David attacked them from the evening twilight until the evening of the next day. None of them escaped except for 4,000 young men who fled on camels.
So David recovered everything that the Amalekites had carried away, and he rescued his two wives.
They had lost no one neither young or old or sons or daughters. They lost no spoils or anything else that had been taken, David had recovered it all.
David recovered all of the flocks and herds, which his men had driven before the other cattle and they said, "This is David's plunder!"
So David returned to the 200 men who had been too weak to follow him and stayed behind at the Brook of Besor. The men went out to meet David and his people, and David greeted them as he approached.

Then all the wicked men and men of Belial with those who went with David said, "Because they did not go with us, we will not share the plunder we have recovered with them, except each man can have his wife and children. So, they can take them and leave.
Then David said, "No my brothers, do not do this with what the Lord has given us. God has protected us and delivered the raiders who attacked us into our hands.
Who will listen to your suggestions? Everyone will share equally from the spoils, whether they went into battle or not, their shares will all be the same."
So from that day forward, David made it a law and a legal decree for Israel that lasts until today.
When David returned to Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to his friends the elders of Judah and said, "Behold this is a present for you from the plunder of the Lord's enemies."
He sent gifts to those who were in Bethel, Ramoth, and Jattir.
And to those in Aroer, Siphmoth, and Eshtemoa;
And to those in Rachal, and in the Jerahmeelite and the Kenite cities.
And to those in Hormah, Corashan, and Athach.
And to those in Hebron, and to all the other places that David and his men haunted.
Now Israel fought and fled from the Philistines, and they were killed on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines chased Saul and his sons in pitched battle, and they killed Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Melchi-Shua.
The battle went badly for Saul, and he was hit by the archers and critically wounded.

Then said Saul to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and thrust it through me, do not let these uncircumcised men thrust their swords through me, and abuse me." But his armor-bearer would not do it, because he was extremely frightened, so Saul took a sword and fell on it.
When the armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell on his sword and died with him.
So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that same day.

When the Israelis men on the other side of the valley and the Jordan River realized that the Israelis had fled, and they saw that Saul, his men, and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled. And the Philistines moved in and lived there.
The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found that Saul and his three sons had fallen on Mount Gilboa.
So they cut off his head and stripped off his armor and sent it throughout the Philistine land. They put it on display in the house of their idols, and among the people.
They put his armor in the house of Ashtaroth and nailed his body to the wall of Beth-Shan.
When the inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul.
All their courageous men got up and traveled all night and took Saul and his sons' bodies from the wall of Beth-Shan. They carried them to Jabesh and burned their bodies.
Then they took their bones and buried them under a tree in Jabesh and fasted for seven days.
After Saul died, and David returned from the Amalekite slaughter, he lived in Ziklag for two days.
On the third day, a man came from Saul's camp with torn clothes and dirt on his head, and when he came to David, he bowed down to honor him.
David spoke to him and asked, "Where did you come from?" And he replied, "I escaped from the Israelis camp."

Then David asked him, "I pray you will tell me how it went there?" He answered and said, "Saul and his son Jonathan are dead, most of the people that fled the battle have fallen and they are also dead."
And David asked the young man, "How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?"
The young man answered him and said, "I happened upon Mount Gilboa by chance, and I saw Saul leaning on his spear, and the chariots and horsemen had caught up with him."
When he turned around, he saw me and called out to me and I answered, "Here I am."
Then he asked me, "Who are you?" And I answered him, "I am an Amalekite."
He spoke to me again and said, "I pray that you will stand over me and kill me, because anguish has overcome me, but I am still alive.

So I stood over him and killed him, because I was convinced that he could not live with the wounds he had suffered. I took the crown from his head and the bracelet from his arm, and I brought them here to my Lord."
Then David tore his clothes, and so did all the men who were with him.
They mourned, wept, and fasted until the evening for Saul and for his son Jonathan, the Lord's people, and the House of Israel because they had fallen by the sword.
David spoke to the young man who had told him what had happened and asked, "Where are you from?" And he answered, "I am the son of a foreigner, I am an Amalekite."
And David asked to him, "Why were you not afraid to raise your hand to destroy the Lord's anointed one?"
Then David summoned one of his young men and said, "Go and kill him!" So he struck him down and he died.
And David said, "Your blood is on your own head, because you testified against yourself and said, 'I killed the Lord's anointed one.'"
So David mourned and sang this lamentation over Saul and his son Jonathan.
David ordered that the children of Judah be taught the Song of the Bow, as it is written in the Book of Jasher.
"The beauty of Israel was killed on your heights, O how the mighty have fallen!
Do not tell it in Gath, and do not publish it on the streets of Askelon, otherwise the Philistine daughters will rejoice, and the daughters of the uncircumcised will triumph.
Let there be no dew or rain on the mountains of Gilboa and no fields of offerings, because the mighty Saul has been shamed. His shield was thrown away, as if he had not had it anointed with holy oil.
From the blood of the slain and from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan did not retreat, and the sword of Saul did not return empty.
Saul and Jonathan lived lovely and pleasant lives, they were not divided in death. They were swifter than eagles and stronger than lions.
O Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul who clothed you in scarlet and luxury and put gold ornaments on your apparel.
O how the mighty have fallen in the middle of the battle! O Jonathan, you were killed in high places.
I grieve for my brother Jonathan, you were very pleasant to me, your love to me was wonderful, surpassing the love of women.
O how the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!"

After this, David spoke to the Lord and asked, "Should I go to one of these cities in Judah?" And the Lord answered him and said, "Yes go there." And David asked, "Where should I go?" And the Lord said, "Go to Hebron."
So David went to Hebron with his two wives Ahinoam the Jezreelite, and Nabal the Carmelite's widow Abigail.
David also brought his men and their households with him, and they lived in the Hebron cities.
Then the men from Judah went to Hebron where they anointed David as king over the house of Judah. They spoke to David and said, "The men of Jabesh-Gilead were the ones who buried Saul."
So David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-Gilead with this message, "May the Lord bless you, for showing such kindness to Saul when you buried him.
Now may the Lord show kindness and truth to you, and I will also show you favor for the kindness you have shown.
Therefore, be strong and courageous, for even though your master Saul is dead, the house of Judah has anointed me as their king."
But Ner's son Abner, who was the commander of Saul's army took Saul's son Ish-Bosheth over to Mahanaim.
And made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and over all of Israel.
Saul's son Ish-Bosheth was 40 years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for two years. But the house of Judah followed David.
And King David had reigned over the house of Judah in Hebron for seven years and six months.
One day Ner's son Abner and the servants of Saul's son Ish-Bosheth left Mahanaim and marched to Gibeon.
Zeruiah's son Joab and David's servants marched out to meet them near the pool of Gibeon. David camped on one side of the pool, and his opponents camped on the other side of the pool.
And Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men get up and play for us." And Joab replied, "Let them get up and play."
So twelve Benjamite men from Saul's son Ish-Bosheth's side got up, and twelve servants from David's side got up.
Then each man grabbed the other fellow by the head, and thrust his sword through their sides, so they all fell together, so they now call that place in Gibeon, Helkath-Hazzurim.
They fought a pitched battle, and Abner and the men of Israel were beaten by David's servants of that day.
Three of Zeruiah's sons were there that day Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel was as fleet of foot as a wild deer.
Asahel pursued Abner, and he did not turn to the right or left as he followed Abner.
Then Abner looked behind him and said, "Are you Asahel?" And he answered, "I am."
And Abner said to him, "Turn to the left or right and grab one of those young men, and take their armor." But Asahel would not stop chasing him.
Again Abner said to Asahel, "Stop following me, why should I have to strike you down to the ground? How could I face your brother Joab?"

But he refused to stop, so Abner thrust the end of the spear under his fifth rib, and it came out behind him. And he fell there and died. Suddenly everyone there stopped and stood still where Asahel had fallen and died.
So Joab and Abishai also pursued Abner, and just the sun went down when they came to the Hill of Ammah, that lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjamite soldiers regrouped and rallied around Abner, and they formed one troop, and took their stand on top of a hill.

Then Abner called out to Joab and said, "Must the sword devour forever? Do you not know that fighting will only cause bitterness in the end? How long will it be before people decide to stop chasing their brothers?"
And Joab said, "As surely as God lives, if you had not spoken up, the troops would have continued chasing their brothers until tomorrow morning."
So Joab blew a trumpet, and the troops stopped fighting and chasing the Israelis.
Abner and his men marched through the plains all that night. They crossed the Jordan and passed through all of Bithron until they arrived in Mahanaim.
After Joab returned from chasing Abner, he gathered all of his troops together, but Asahel and nineteen of David's servants were missing.
But David's servants had killed 360 Benjaminite men who were with Abner.
So they buried Asahel in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. Then Joab and his men traveled all night until they arrived in Hebron at daybreak.
Saul and David had been at war with each other for a long time, but David grew stronger and stronger, and Saul grew weaker and weaker.
David's sons were born in Hebron, and his firstborn was named Amnon whose mother was Ahinoam the Jezreelite.
His second son was named Chileab whose mother was Abigail the widow of Nabal the Carmelite, and his third son was named Absalom whose mother was King Talmai's daughter Maacah of Geshur.
His fourth son was named Adonijah whose mother was Haggith, and his fifth son was named Shephatiah whose mother was Abital.
His sixth son was named Ithream whose mother was David's wife Eglah. These were the sons of David who were born in Hebron.
Abner strengthened his hand in Saul's household the entire time that Saul and David were at war with each other.
Saul had a concubine named Rizpah who was Aiah's daughter. One day Ish-Bosheth questioned Abner and said, "Why have you slept with my father's concubine?"

Then Abner became very angry with Ish-Bosheth and said, "Am I a dog's head that belongs to Judah? Have I not shown kindness to your father Saul's house and to his brothers and friends? I have protected you from King David, but today you charge me with inappropriate conduct with this woman.
So may God punish Abner much more severely, unless I do for David what the Lord has sworn to do for him.
Which is to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and establish the throne of David over Israel and Judah, from Dan all the way to Beersheba.
After that Ish-Bosheth feared Abner so much, that he could not say another word to him.
Then Abner sent messengers to speak to David on his behalf who said, "Whose land is this? If you make an alliance with me, I will help bring all of Israel under your control."
And David said, "Well said, I will make an alliance with you but you will not be allowed to see me, unless you first bring Saul's daughter Michal to me when you come."
So David sent messengers to Saul's son Ish-Bosheth and said, "Bring my wife Michal back to me, who was promised to me in marriage for one hundred Philistine foreskins."
And Ish-Bosheth sent some men and took her from Laish's son Phaltiel who was her husband.
Her husband followed her weeping all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go, and return home!" So he returned.
One day Abner met with the Israelis elders and said, "In times past you sought to make David your king.
Now is the time to do it, because the Lord has spoken to David and said, "Through my servant David I will save my people of Israel from the Philistines and all of their enemies."
Abner also spoke to the elders of Benjamin, then he spoke to David in Hebron and reported that everything seemed good to the Israelis and the whole house of Benjamin.
So Abner and twenty men went to see David in Hebron, and David prepared a feast for them.

Then Abner said to David, "I will go and assemble all of Israel before my Lord the king. So that they may make an alliance with you, and you can reign over everything your heart desires." And David sent Abner away in peace.
Then David's servants and Joab returned from a raid, and they brought great plunder back with them. But Abner was not with David in Hebron, because David had sent him away in peace.
When Joab and his army returned, he was told, "Ner's son Abner came to see the king, who sent him away in peace."
Then Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Abner came to see you, and you sent him away. Why did you let him get away?"
You know that Ner's son Abner came to deceive and spy on you. He wants to find out everything he can about you, including your comings and goings."
When Joab left David, he sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the Well of Sirah, but David knew nothing about it.

When Abner was brought back to Hebron, Joab took him away at the city gates and secretly stabbed Abner under his fifth rib and he died quietly. Abner died because the blood of Joab's dead brother Asahel was on his hands.
David heard about it afterward and he said, "My kingdom and I are forever guiltless before the Lord, for the shedding of Ner's son Abner's blood.
Let it rest on Joab's head and his father's house! Let Joab's house always have someone who is sick, leprous, crippled, killed by the sword, or starves for a lack of bread."
So Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner, because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle of Gibeon.
Then David spoke to Joab and everyone with him and said, "Tear your clothes and wear sackcloth to mourn Abner," and King David himself followed the body as it was carried to the grave.
They buried Abner in Hebron where the king spoke, then he and all the people wept at Abner's grave.
And the king lamented over Abner, and said, "Did Abner die as a fool dies?
Your hands were not bound, your feet chained. As a man falls before wicked men, so you have also fallen." And all the people wept over him again.

Then all the people tried to make David eat something while it was still daylight. But David swore an oath and said, "Let God punish me even more severely, if I taste any bread before the sun goes down."
All the people took notice and they were pleased, because whatever the king did pleased everyone.
So that day, everyone in Israel understood that it was not the king who had killed Ner's son Abner.
And the king said to his servants, "Do you not realize that a prince and a great man has fallen in Israel on this day?
Today I am weak, even though I have been anointed king, these men the sons of Zeruiah are too powerful for me. But may the Lord repay the evildoer for the wickedness he has done."
When Saul's son Ish-Bosheth heard that Abner had died in Hebron, he was weak and feeble, and all the Israelis were troubled.

Saul's son had two men that were commanders of his raiding parties, one of them was named Baanah, and the other was named Rechab. They were the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, from the tribe of Benjamin, because the town of Beeroth was considered to be part of the territory of Benjamin.
The Beerothites fled to Gittaim where they are foreigners until this very day.

Saul's son Jonathan had a son named Mephibosheth who was lame. He was five years old when the news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and fled, and as she ran to get away, he fell and became lame.
Now the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite Rechab and Baanah, traveled in the heat of the day to Ish-Bosheth's house, who was still in bed at noon.
They went into the house, as though they wanted to fetch some wheat, and they stabbed him under the fifth rib, but Rechab and his brother Baanah escaped.
When they went into the house, Ish-Bosheth was laying on the bed in his bedroom. They stabbed him and killed him, then they beheaded him and took his head, and traveled through the plains all night.

They brought Ish-Bosheth's head to King David in Hebron. And they said to the king, "Behold the head of your enemy Saul's son Ish-Bosheth who tried to take your life. God has avenged my Lord the king this day against Saul and his descendants."
Then David answered Rimmon the Beerothite's sons Rechab and his brother Baanah and said, "As surely as the Lord lives, who has rescued my soul from all of this adversity.
When someone said to me, 'Behold Saul is dead,' thinking they were bringing me good news, I killed him in Ziklag. For he thought I would give him a reward for his news.
How much more wicked is it when wicked men kill a righteous person in his own house on his own bed? So must I not now require his blood from your hands, and remove you from the earth?"

So David commanded his young men to kill them and cut off their hands and feet. Then he had them hanged over the pool in Hebron. But they took Ish-Bosheth's head and buried it in Abner's tomb in Hebron.
Then all the tribes of Israel came and spoke to David in Hebron and said, "Behold we are your flesh and blood.
In times past while Saul was our king, you were the one who led Israel out and brought us back. And the Lord said to you, "You must feed my people of Israel, and you will be the ruler of Israel."
So all the Israelis elders came to Hebron, where King David made a treaty with them before the Lord, and they anointed David as the king of Israel.
David was 30 years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for 40 years.
David reigned over Judah from Hebron for seven years and six months, and he reigned over Israel and Judah in Jerusalem for 35 more years.

King David and his men marched to attack the Jebusites in Jerusalem who inhabited the land. And they spoke to David and said, "You will never come in here because you cannot even capture the blind and the lame." Because they thought, "David cannot come in here."
But, David captured the stronghold of Zion which is now called the city of David.

On that day David said, "Whoever attacks the Jebusites whose soul I hate will be the top commander, and they must use the gutter to reach to the lame and the blind. That's why they said, "The lame and the blind will never enter the house."
So David lived in the fortress he called the city of David, and he built fortifications all around the inner city.
David continued to grow and he grew to be great because the Lord God of Hosts was with him.
King Hiram of Tyre sent messengers to David along with cedar trees, carpenters, and masons and they built a house for David.
David realized that the Lord had established him as king of Israel, and that he had glorified David's kingdom for the sake of his people of Israel.
David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem after he returned from Hebron, and he had more sons and daughters born to him.
These are the names of those that were born to him in Jerusalem. There was Shammuah, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon.
Also Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, and Japhia.
Then Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphalet.
But when the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king of Israel, they all went looking for him. When David heard about this, he went down to the stronghold.
Then the Philistines came and spread themselves throughout the Valley of Rephaim.

So David prayed to the Lord and asked, "Must I go meet the Philistines? Will you deliver them into my hands?" And the Lord answered David and said, "Go up, because there is no doubt that I will deliver the Philistines into your hands."
David marched to Baal-Perazim where he defeated them and he said, "The Lord has broken my enemies before me, as broken as defenses washed away by flood waters." So he named that place Baal-Perazim.
The Philistines had left their images there and David and his men burned them.
The Philistines marched up and spread themselves all over the Valley of Rephaim again.
Once again, David asked the Lord what he should do, and the Lord said, "You must not go up and confront them, go around behind them and attack them near the mulberry trees.
When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, you must move quickly, because that means the Lord has marched before you to defeat the Philistine armies."
And David did as the Lord had commanded him, and he defeated the Philistines from Geba all the way to Gazer.
Once again, David chose 30,000 men from Israel.
David and everyone with him went to Baale of Judah to bring God's Ark of the Covenant back from there. Whose name is called God by the Lord of Hosts who lives between the cherubim.
They set God's Ark of the Covenant on a new cart, and brought it back from Abinadab's house in Gibeah, and Abinadab's sons Uzzah and Ahio drove the cart.
They brought God's Ark of the Covenant out of Abinadab's house in Gibeah, and Ahio accompanied it as he walked before it.
David and the entire House of Israel played all kinds of musical instruments before the Lord that were made of wood from fir trees including harps, tambourines, maracas, and cymbals.
When they arrived at Nachon's threshing room floor, Uzzah had to grab hold of God's Ark of the Covenant to keep it from falling, because the oxen shook the cart.
The Lord's anger was kindled against Uzzah, so God killed him right there for his error, and he died beside God's Ark of the Covenant.
David was upset, because the Lord had violently attacked and destroyed Uzzah, so he renamed it Perez-Uzzah which remains its name to this very day.
That day David was afraid of the Lord and he said, "How can I bring the Ark of the Covenant back?"
So David refused to bring the Ark of the Covenant back to the city of David, instead he carried it to Obed-Edom the Gittite's house.
The Ark of the Covenant remained in Obed-Edom the Gittite's house for three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-Edom and his entire household.

King David was told about the blessings on Obed-Edom's household and he said, "The Lord has blessed Obed-Edom's entire household because of God's Ark of the Covenant. So he happily brought God's Ark of the Covenant up from Obed-Edom's house into the city of David.
After the people who carried the Ark of the Covenant took six steps, David sacrificed oxen and fatted calves.
Then David wore a linen robe and danced before the Lord with all his might.
So David and all the Israelis brought the Ark of the Covenant back with lots of shouting and the sound of trumpets blowing.
As the Ark of the Covenant was brought into the city of David, Saul's daughter Michal could see King David leaping and dancing before the Lord through her window, and she despised him in her heart.
They brought the Ark of the Covenant to its place in the middle of the tabernacle that David had constructed for it. And David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord.
As soon as David finished offering burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord of Hosts.
Then he distributed a loaf of bread, a piece of meat, and a jug of wine to everyone in Israel, after that they all left and went back home.

Then David returned to bless his own household, and Saul's daughter Michal came out to meet David and she said, "How glorious the king of Israel looked today, when he undressed in front of his housemaids and servants, just as some vain and shameless fellow would undress!"

And David said to Michal, "I danced before the Lord, who chose me to replace your father and his entire household. He appointed me as the ruler over the Lord's people of Israel, so I will continue to celebrate before the Lord.
In fact, I will humble myself and be even more vile than this, and I will be honored by the female servants about whom you have spoken.
So, Saul's daughter Michal never had children before she died.
After king David settled into his house and the Lord gave him rest from all of his enemies.
The king spoke to Nathan the prophet and said, "Look, I live in a house made of cedar, but God's Ark of the Covenant lives in a tent."
And Nathan said to the king, "Go and do whatever is in your heart because the Lord is with you."
And that night, the Lord's word came to Nathan and he said,
"Go and tell my servant David, this is what the Lord says, "Will you build me a house to live in?
Because I have not lived in a house since I brought the Israelis out of Egypt, but I have traveled around with a tabernacle tent as my home.
Wherever I have traveled with the Israelis, have I ever asked their leaders that I command to feed my people and said, "Why have you not built me a cedar house?"
So now you must speak to my servant David and say, "This is what the Lord of Hosts says, 'I took you away from the sheep pen and the life of a shepherd, to become the ruler over my people of Israel.
I went with you wherever you went, and I removed all of your enemies from your sight, and I made your name as great as the names of the great men buried in the earth.

Furthermore, I will appoint a place to plant my people of Israel, so that they may live in their own place where they will no longer have to move. And the children of wickedness will no longer afflict them, as they have in the past.
And just as it has been since I commanded the judges to be over my people of Israel and I gave you to rest from all of your enemies. The Lord also tells you that he will make you a house.
When your days have been fulfilled, and you sleep with your fathers God will say, 'I will raise up your descendants who come from your body, and I will establish their kingdom.
Your descendant will build a house for my name, and I will establish his kingdom's throne forever.
I will be his father, and he will be my son. If your descendant commits immorality, I will punish him with lashes from the staffs of the sons of men.
But my mercy will not leave him as I took it away from Saul, whom I have removed from before you.
Your house and kingdom will be established before you forever, and your throne will also be established forever.'"
So Nathan spoke to David and told him everything the Lord had said to him and what he had seen in his visions.
Then King David went in and sat before the Lord and he said, "O Lord God who am I, and what is my house, that you have brought me until now?

It is as if this was just a small thing in your sight, O Lord God. But you have also spoken of the future of your servant's house for a long time to come. Is this how you deal with all of mankind, O Lord God?
What more can David say to you? For you know your servant, O Lord God.
For the sake of your word and in accordance with what is in your own heart, you have done all these great things, and you have revealed them to me who is your servant.
So you are great, O Lord God, because there is no one like you, and there is no other God besides you, according to everything we have heard with our own ears.

What other nation on earth is like your people of Israel, whom God went to rescue as his own people to establish his name. You do great and terrible things for your people who you rescued from Egypt, because you drove out the other nations and their gods before them.
Because you have established your people of Israel for yourself to be your people forever, and you O Lord, have become their God.
Now O Lord God, establish the words you have spoken about your servant and his household forever, and do what you said you would do.
Let your name be magnified forever when it is said, 'The Lord of Hosts is the God of Israel,' and let the house of your servant David be established before you.
For you O Lord of Hosts, God of Israel have revealed this to your servant when you said, 'I will build you a house.' So that's why your servant has found it in his heart to pray this prayer to you.
Now O Lord God, you are the God whose words are true, and you have promised this goodness to your servant.
So now let it please you to bless your servant's house, so that it may forever continue before you. For you O Lord God, have spoken with your blessing to let your servant's house be forever blessed."
After this David defeated and subdued the Philistines, and he took Metheg-Ammah from the hands of the Philistines.

David also defeated Moab and measured them with a line and made them lie down on the ground. And he to put to death everyone measured within the boundary of two lengths of line, and those within the one length of line was keep alive. So the Moabites became David's servants, and they brought him gifts.
David also defeated King Hadadezer of Zobah, the son of Rehob as he went to recover his border at the Euphrates River.
David captured 1,000 chariots, 700 horsemen, and 20,000 footmen from him and he crippled all the chariot horses, but he saved enough of them for 100 chariots.
When the Syrians of Damascus went to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, David killed 22,000 Syrian men.
Then David put garrisons of soldiers in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians became David's servants and brought him gifts. And the Lord protected David wherever he went.
David took the gold shields from Hadadezer's servants and brought them to Jerusalem.
King David took an exceptionally large amount of brass from Hadadezer's cities of Betah and Berothai.
King Toi of Hamath heard that David had defeated all of Hadadezer's armies.

So King Toi sent his son Joram to King David to salute and bless him because he had fought and defeated Hadadezer. Because Hadadezer had fought wars with Toi, and Joram brought silver, gold, and brass bowls with him as gifts for David.
King David dedicated all the silver and gold that he had taken from all the nations he had subdued to the Lord.
From Syria, Moab, Ammon, Amalek, the Philistines, and all of the spoils from Rehob's son King Hadadezer of Zobah.
So David made a name for himself when he returned after defeating 18,000 Syrian men in the Valley of Salt.
David put garrisons of soldiers throughout all of Edom, and everyone in Edom became his servants, and the Lord protected him wherever he went.
And David reigned and executed judgment and justice to all of his people throughout Israel.
Zeruiah's son Joab was over the army, and Ahilud's son Jehoshaphat was the record keeper.
Ahitub's son Zadok and Abiathar's son Ahimelech were the priests, and Seraiah was the scribe.
Jehoiada's son Benaiah was over both the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David's sons were the ruling priests.
And David asked, "Is there anyone left from the house of Saul that I may show kindness for Jonathan's sake?"
There was a servant named Ziba from Saul's house whom they summoned to King David and asked, "Are you Ziba?" And he answered and said, "Yes, I am your servant."
Then King David asked, "Is there anyone left from the house of Saul that I may show God's kindness to?" And Ziba answered the king and said, "Jonathan's lame son survived."
And King David asked him, "Where is he?" And Ziba answered the king and said, "Behold he is in Ammiel's son Machir's house in Lodebar."
Then King David sent for him and had him brought from Ammiel's son Machir's house in Lodebar.

Jonathan was Saul's son and when Jonathan's son Mephibosheth was brought to David, he bowed facedown out of respect. And David asked, "Are you Mephibosheth?" And he answered, "Behold I am your servant!"

And David said to him, "Fear not, for I will surely show you kindness for your father Jonathan's sake, and I will restore all of your father Saul's land to you, and you will always eat bread at my table."
And he bowed and said, "What am I your servant, that would make you look kindly upon such a dead dog as me?"
Then King David called for Saul's servant Ziba and said to him, "I have given your master's grandson everything that belonged to Saul and his entire household.

You, your sons, and your servants, will work the land for him and you will bring in the harvest, so that your master's grandson may have food to eat. But your master's grandson Mephibosheth will always eat bread at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.

Then Ziba spoke to the king and said, "I am your servant and I will do everything that my Lord the king has commanded." And King David said, "As for Mephibosheth, he will eat at my table as one of my own sons."
Mephibosheth had a young son named Micha, and everyone who lived in Ziba's house were Mephibosheth's servants.
So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king's table and he was lame in both feet.
After this the Ammonite king died, and his son Hanun reigned in his place.

Then David said, "I will show kindness to Nahash's son Hanun, since his father showed kindness to me." So David sent his servants to comfort him for the loss of his father, but when David's servants arrived in the land of the Ammonites.

The Ammonite princes said to their Lord Hanun, "Do you think King David wants to honor your father by sending comforters to you? Do you not think that David has sent his servants to search and spy out the city so he can overthrow it?"
When Hanun heard this, he took David's servants and shaved off half of their beards and cut their garments off at the waist all the way to their buttocks and sent them away.
When David heard this, he sent messengers to meet them because they had been completely humiliated, and the messengers said, "Stay in Jericho until your beards regrow, and then return."

When the Ammonites realized that they had created a stench before David, they hired 20,000 soldiers from the Syrians of Beth-Rehob and Zoba, plus 1,000 men from the king of Maacah, and 12,000 men from Ishtob.
When David heard this, he sent Joab with his entire army of mighty men.
The Ammonites marched out and assembled their battle array at the entrance of the city gate, and the Syrians from Zoba, Rehob, Ishtob, and Maacah were all alone out in the field.
When Joab saw that the front lines of the battlefield were in front of him and behind him, he chose his best men from Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians.
Joab put the rest of his soldiers under the command of his brother Abishai to array them against the Ammonites.
And Joab said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, you must come and help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will come and help you.
Be courageous and let us fight for our people and for the cities of our God. May the Lord do what is good in his sight."
As Joab and his troops drew near, they joined the battle against the Syrians, who fled before them.
When the Ammonites saw that the Syrians had fled, they also fled before Abishai and entered the city. So Joab returned from the battle with the Ammonites and went to Jerusalem.
When the Syrians realized that they had been defeated by Israel, they regrouped their forces.
Then Hadarezer sent messengers to bring more Syrian troops that were beyond the river. So Shobach the commander of Hadarezer's army marched his forces to Helam.
When David heard this, he assembled the entire Israelis army and crossed the Jordan River and marched to Helam, and the Syrians arrayed their soldiers against David and fought him.
Soon the Syrians fled the Israelis, and David killed 700 Syrian chariot men and 40,000 horsemen, and he killed Shobach the Syrian commander, who died on the battlefield.

When all the kings that were Hadarezer's servants realized that Israel had defeated them, they made peace with Israel and served them. After that the Syrians were too fearful to continue helping the Ammonites.

A year after the kings met out on the battlefield, David sent Joab and his servants with the entire Israelis army, and they destroyed the Ammonites, and besieged Rabbah. But David remained in Jerusalem.
One night during the evening tide, David got up from his bed and walked out on the roof of the king's palace, and from the roof he saw a very beautiful woman bathing.
So David inquired about the woman, and someone said, "Her name is Bathsheba, she is the daughter of Eliam, and she is the wife of Uriah the Hittite?
David sent his messengers to bring her to him, and when she came to him, he slept with her, because she had just purified herself from her menstrual period, then she returned home.
She became pregnant and she sent David a message and said, "I am with child."
David summoned Joab and said, "Send Uriah the Hittite to me," and Joab sent Uriah to David.
When Uriah came to David, the king demanded to know how Joab and the troops were doing as the war progressed.
And David said to Uriah, "Go home and wash your feet," and Uriah left the king's palace with a large gift of meat from the king that followed him.
But Uriah slept at the door of the king's palace with all of his Lord's servants, and he did not go home.
When they told King David this, they said, "Uriah did not go home." When David spoke to Uriah he said, "Did you not just return from your journey? Why did you not go home?"

Uriah responded to David and said, "The ark, Israel, and Judah are forced to live in tents. My Lord Joab, and your servants my Lord, are camped in the open fields, Should I go home to eat, drink, and be merry and sleep with my wife? As you and your soul lives, I will not do this thing!"
Then David said to Uriah, "Stay here today and tomorrow, then I will let you leave." So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
Then David asked Uriah to eat and drink with him, and Uriah got drunk. In the evening Uriah went to lie down on his bed with his Lord's servants, but he did not go home.
In the morning, David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it to him with Uriah.
In the letter he wrote, "Put Uriah on the frontline of the hottest battle, and abandon him there, so that he is be defeated and killed."
When Joab looked out over the city, he assigned Uriah to a place where he knew the enemies most courageous men were.
When the men of the city went to fight Joab, some of David's servants were killed and Uriah the Hittite also died.
Then Joab sent messengers to David with a complete account of how the war progressed.
Joab instructed the messenger what to say when he spoke to the king and he said, "When you finish telling the king the state of the war.
If the king is very angry and he says, 'Why did you approach the city so close when you fought? Did you not know you that they would shoot at you from the wall?

Who killed Jerub-Besheth's son Abimelech? Did some woman throw a piece of millstone at him from the wall in Thebez that killed him? Why were you so close to the wall?' Then you must say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.'"
So the messenger went to report to David everything that Joab had sent him to say.
The messenger said to David, "The men from the city came out to attack us in the field, and they prevailed against us, but we managed to drive them back to the city gates.
The archers were shooting at us from the walls, and some of the king's servants were killed, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead."

Then David said to the messenger, "This is what I want you to say to Joab to encourage him, 'Do not be upset by this, because the sword devours one as well as another, reinforce your forces against the city, and overthrow it!'"
When Uriah's wife heard that her husband was dead, she mourned him.
And when the mourning passed, David sent for her and had her brought back to his house, and she became his wife and gave birth to his son. But the Lord was very displeased with what David had done.
The Lord sent Nathan to David who spoke to David and said, "There were two men who lived in one city, one was rich and the other was poor.
The rich man had many very large flocks and herds.

But the poor man had nothing except for one small ewe lamb that he had bought, and he nourished it and it grew up with him and his children. It shared his food and drank from his own cup, and slept in his embrace and it was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to visit the rich man, who decided not to use a lamb from his own flocks and herds to prepare for and feed the traveling man. So the rich man took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for his traveling guest."
When David heard this, he was very angry with the rich man and he said to Nathan, "As surely as the Lord lives, that man must die!
And he must be shown no pity for what he has done, and he must repay the poor man four times what the lamb cost."
Then Nathan said to David, "You are that rich man! This is what the Lord God of Israel says, 'I anointed you king of Israel, and I delivered you from Saul's hand.
I gave your master's house to you, I put your master's wives into your embrace. I gave you the House of Israel and Judah, and if that had not been enough, I would have given you even more.
So why have you despised the Lord's commandment by doing evil in his sight? You killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword and you took his wife as your own. You killed him with Ammonite swords.
And since you have despised me and taken Uriah the Hittite's wife as your own, the sword will never leave your home.'

Furthermore this is what the Lord says, 'I will raise up evil against you from within your own house, and I will take your wives and give them to your neighbor right before your eyes, and he will have sex with them in broad daylight.
You have done this in secret, but I will do this in broad daylight before everyone in Israel.'"
And David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the Lord." Then Nathan said to David, "The Lord has taken away your sin, and you will not die.
But, since you have given the Lord's enemies a great occasion to blaspheme his name, the illegitimate child born to you will surely die."
Then Nathan returned home, but the child born to David and Uriah's wife was struck down by the Lord and became very sick.
So David implored God and begged for the child's life. Then David fasted and went into his house and lay on the ground all night.
Then the elders from David's house and went to him, and they tried to get him up from the ground, but he would not get up, and he would not eat their bread.

But the child died on the seventh day, and David's servants were afraid to tell him. For they said, "We tried to talk to him while the child was alive, and he would not listen to us. How terribly upset will he be with himself, if we tell him that the child is dead?"
When David saw his servants whispering, he knew that the child was dead, so he asked them, "Is the child dead?" And they said, "Yes, he is dead."
Then David got up, washed, anointed himself, changed his clothing, and went into the Lord's house to worship. Then he went to his own house, and at his request they brought him some bread and he ate.
Then David's servants said to him, "What have you done? While the child was alive, you fasted and wept for him, but now that he is dead, you get up and eat bread."
And David said, "While the child was alive, I fasted and wept because I said to myself, 'Who knows whether or not God will be gracious to me and allow my child to live?'
But now he is dead, so why should I fast? Can I bring him back? I can go to him but he will not return to me."
So David comforted his wife Bathsheba and had sex with her, and she gave birth to a son that he named Solomon, and the Lord loved him.
Then the Lord sent word through Nathan the prophet to name him Jedidiah, because the Lord loved him.
At that time Joab fought against the Ammonites in Rabbah and captured the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah and taken the city of waters.
So bring the rest of the army and bivouac outside the city and take it, otherwise I will take it and it will be named after me."
David assembled his entire army together and went to Rabbah, where he fought and took the city.
David took the crown from their king's head. It weighed one gold talent with the precious stones, and it was set on David's head. And David took a great abundance of plunder from the city.

David captured the people there and brought them back as slaves. He put them to work with saws, iron harrows, and axes. and making bricks for the kiln. David did this to all of the Ammonite cities, then David and the entire Israelis army returned to Jerusalem.
Later David's son Absalom had a beautiful sister named Tamar, and his son Amnon loved her.
Amnon felt sick because he was so frustrated over his virgin sister Tamar, and he thought it would be impossible for him to do anything with her.
But Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, who was the son of David's brother Shimeah, and Jonadab was a very cunning and subtle man.
One day Jonadab asked Amnon, "Please tell me, why are you, the king's son so depressed every day?" And Amnon said to him, "I love my brother Absalom's sister Tamar."

And Jonadab said to him, "Lay down on your bed, and act as if you are sick. When your father comes to see you, say to him, "Please let my sister Tamar come and bring me something to eat. And ask her to prepare it in front of me, so that I can watch her and eat it from her hands.'"

So Amnon laid down and pretended to be sick, and when the king came to see him, Amnon said to him, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes for me while I watch, so that I can eat from her hands."
Then David sent word to Tamar back home and said, "Please go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare a meal for him."
So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house where he was laying down. She took some flour and kneaded it, and she made the cakes and baked them as he watched.
Then she brought the pan of bread to Amnon and set it down before him, but he refused to eat and he said, "Send all the men away from me!" And everyone left.
Amnon spoke to Tamar again and said, "Bring the bread into the bedroom, so that I can eat from your hand." So Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into her brother Amnon's bedroom.
When she brought them to him to eat, "He grabbed her and said, "Come to bed with me my sister."
She answered him and said, "No, my brother, please do not force me to do this, because no such thing as this should be done in Israel, do not do this foolish thing.
Where could I ever go with my shame? And you will be like one of the fools in Israel! So I beg you to speak to the king about this, because he will not withhold me from you."
But Amnon would not listen to Tamar, and since he was stronger than her, he forced her onto his bed with him.
Then Amnon hated Tamar so much, that the hatred he had for her was greater than the love he had for her, and Amnon said to Tamar, "Get up and be gone!"
And Tamar said to Amnon, "There is no cause to send me away, sending me away is even more evil than what you have done to me." But Amnon would not listen to her.
Then Amnon called for his servant who ministered to him and said, "Take this woman away from me, and bolt the door when she leaves."
She wore a multi-colored robe, because the king's virgin daughters dressed that way. Then his servant threw her out and bolted the door after her.
Tamar put ashes on her head, and tore the multi-colored robe that she was wearing, and laid her hand on her head and left crying.

Then Tamar's brother Absalom questioned her and asked, "Has your brother Amnon been with you? Stay quiet for the time being my sister, because he is your brother. Do not take this thing to heart." So Tamar remained a desolate woman in her brother Absalom's house.
But when King David heard about these things, he was very angry.
Absalom did not speak to his brother Amnon after that. Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar.
After two full years, Absalom's servants were shearing sheep in Baal-Hazor near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons to come visit.
Absalom went to the king and said, "Behold, your servant has hired sheep shearers. May the king and his servants please come with me?"
The King replied to Absalom and said, "No my son, we should not all go, because we will be large a burden for you." He pressed the king further, but the king would not go, and he blessed his son.
Then Absalom said, "If not, I beg you to let my brother Amnon go with us," and the king said, "Why should he go with you?"
But Absalom pressed him to let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.

Absalom gave his servants an order and said, "Be ready, because when you see that Amnon is drunk with wine, and I say to you, 'Attack Amnon!' Then kill him, and do not be afraid because I have given you this commanded, so be strong and courageous."
Absalom's servants did what he commanded them. Then all the king's sons jumped up and ran to their mule and fled.
While they were on their way back, King David received a report that said, "Absalom has killed all the king's sons, and none of them survived."
The king got up and tore his clothes and laid on the ground, and all of his servants also stood nearby in their torn clothes.

But Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimeah said, "My Lord do not think that they have killed all of your sons, because Amnon is the only one dead. Absalom has been determined from the day that Amnon forced his sister Tamar to do this thing.
So my Lord, do not take this to heart, and do not think that all of the king's sons are dead, because Amnon is the only one dead."
But Absalom fled, and the young man keeping watch looked, and saw many people coming down the hill along the road behind him.
Then Jonadab said to the king, "Behold the king's sons are coming down the road, just as your servant said."
As soon as Jonadab finished speaking, the king's sons began to arrive, and they all cried and wept bitterly, including the king and all of his servants.
But Absalom fled to seek refuge with Ammihud's son King Talmai of Geshur, and David mourned for his son every day.
So Absalom fled to Geshur and stayed there for three years.
King David's soul longed to see his son Absalom, because he had grieved and consoled himself over Amnon's death.
Now Zeruiah's son Joab knew that the king's heart longed to see Absalom.

Joab sent for a wise woman to be brought from Tekoah and he said to her, "I pray you will pretend to be a mourner, and wear mourning clothes, and do not anoint yourself with oil. Act as if you are a woman who has mourned for the dead for a long time."
Then come to the king and speak to him this way. So Joab put the words in her mouth.
When the woman from Tekoah spoke to the king, she fell facedown to the ground, and paid tribute to him and said, "Help me, O king!"
And the king responded to her and asked, "What ails you?" And she answered and said, "My husband is dead and I am a widower.
I am your maidservant and I had two sons. They fought out in the field, and there was no one there to break them up, and one of them killed the other one.

Now the whole family has risen up against me and said, 'Hand over the one that has killed his brother, so that we may kill him for killing his brother. We will also destroy the heir.' So they want to extinguish the last piece of coal that I have left, by not leaving my husband a name or a descendant on this earth."
And the king answered the woman and said, "Go back to your home, and I will give orders about your situation."
But the woman from Tekoah said to the king, "My Lord, O king, may the immorality be on me and my father's house, and may the king and his throne be guiltless."
And the king said, "Bring me whoever speaks to you this way, and they will never trouble you again!"

Then the woman said, "O king, please remember your Lord God and prevent the blood revengers from killing my son!" And the king said, "As the Lord lives, not one hair from your son's head will fall to the ground."
The woman spoke again and said, "My Lord, I pray you will let me speak one more word to the king." And he said, "Speak."

Once again the woman spoke up and said, "So why have you thought such bad things against the people of God? Because when the king says these things, does he not condemn himself for not bringing his own banished son back home?

For we will surely die as if we were just water spilled on the ground which cannot be recovered. Nor does God respect any person above another, but God devises ways to return his banished ones back to himself.

So my Lord, I have come to speak to the king about this very thing because the people have made me afraid. And I thought to myself, 'Now I will speak to the king, and perhaps he will grant his maidservant's request.
Maybe the king will hear me and deliver his maidservant from the hand of the man that would destroy both my inheritance and my son's inheritance from God.'

Then your maidservant said, 'Maybe the words of my Lord the king will make me comfortable, because just like an angel of God, my Lord the king has the ability to recognize the difference between good and evil.' So, may your Lord God will be with you."

Then the king answered the woman and said, "Do not hide anything from me, for I am going to ask you something, and I pray you that you will tell me the truth." And the woman said, "Let my Lord the king speak his mind."

And the king said, "Did Joab put you up to all of this?" And the woman answered and said, "As surely as your soul lives, my Lord the king, no one can turn left or right of anything my Lord the king has spoken. Because your servant Joab, is the one who put me up to this, and he told me exactly what to say.
Joab has done this thing in order to point out the other side of this situation to my Lord. The king is as wise as an angel of God, and he has the wisdom to understand everything on earth."
And the king said to Joab, "Behold, I am guilty of this, so bring my son Absalom back home to me."
And Joab bowed facedown to the ground and thanked the king and said, "My Lord, today I know that I have found grace in your sight. O king, you have satisfied your servant's request."
So Joab went to Geshur and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.
And the king said, "Return him to his own house, but do not bring him to see me." So Absalom returned to his own home, and he did not see his father the king.
But in all of Israel nobody was as praised and handsome as Absalom, because he had no flaws from the soles of his feet to the top of his head.
Absalom had to shave his head at the end of every year because it was so heavy, and the hair weighed about 200 king's shekels when he shaved it every year.
Absalom had three sons and one daughter named Tamar, who was a very beautiful woman.
So Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two years, but he never saw the king during that time.
One day Absalom sent for Joab and asked him to make an appointment for him to see the king, but he would not come, and when he sent for him again, he still would not come.
So he said to his servants, "Go and set Joab's nearby barely field on fire!" And Absalom's servants set the field on fire.
Then Joab went to Absalom's house and asked him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"

Absalom answered Joab and said, "I sent word for you and said, 'Come see me, I want you to go ask the king, why he wanted me to come here from Geshur, it would have been better for me to have stayed there.' So go make an appointment for me see the king, and if there is any immorality in me, he can kill me."
So Joab went to the king and told him what Absalom had said. Then the king summoned him, and he came to see the king, he bowed facedown to the ground and the king kissed him.
After this, Absalom prepared his chariots, horses, and fifty men to run before him.

Sometimes Absalom would get up early and go stand by the roadside near the city gates. Whenever someone brought a problem to the king for him to decide, Absalom would call out to them and say, "What city have you come from?" And if they answered and said, "Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel."
Then Absalom would say, "Look, you have a good and righteous case, but the king has no judge to hear your dispute."
Absalom would also say, "Furthermore, if only someone would make me a judge in the land, then whoever had a lawsuit or cause could come to me, and I would give them justice!"
So, whenever anyone came to show respect to Absalom, he would put out his hand and kiss them.
This was how Absalom treated all of the Israelis who came to the king for judgment, and so Absalom stole the hearts of everyone in Israel.
After forty years, Absalom spoke to the king and said, "I pray that you will let me go and pay what I promised to give the Lord in Hebron.
Because your servant made a promise to God when I lived in Geshur of Syria and I said, "I will serve the Lord if he brings me back to Jerusalem."
And the king said, "Go in peace." So he went to Hebron.
But Absalom sent spies throughout all the tribes of Israel and said, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet you must say, "Absalom reigns in Hebron."
Absalom brought 200 men from Jerusalem with him, and they innocently went with him, but they did not know what he had planned.

Absalom summoned David's counsellor Ahithophel the Gilonite from his city in Giloh. And as Absalom offered sacrifices his conspiracy grew stronger and stronger, and his followers continued to increase in number.
One day a messenger came to David and said, "Absalom has captured the hearts of the Israelis."

David said to all his servants with him in Jerusalem, "We must flee, or we will be unable to escape Absalom. So let us make haste and leave, otherwise Absalom will overtake us and bring evil down upon us and kill everyone in the city!"
Then the king's servants said to the king, "Behold my Lord, we are ready to do whatever the king wants us to do."
So King David left with his entire household, which included ten concubine women who kept the house.
The king left with all of his people and moved to a place far away.
All of his servants marched before the king including the Cherethites, Pelethites, Gittites, and the 600 men who followed him from Gath.
Then the king spoke to Ittai the Gittite and said, "Why are you going with us? Return to your home and stay with the new king, because you are an exiled foreigner there.

In fact you just got here yesterday, so why should I make you wander the countryside with us, since I do not even know where we are going? Return to your brothers and may the Lord's mercy and truth be with you."
Ittai answered the king and said, "My Lord, as surely as the Lord and the king both live, wherever you are is where I will be your servant, whether it is in life or in death!"
And David said to Ittai, "Go and march on." Then Ittai the Gittite and all his men and their children marched by.
The king and his entire country wept very loudly while they crossed the Brook of Kidron, as they marched toward the wilderness.

And behold Zadok and all the Levites were also with him, carrying God's Ark of the Covenant. But they set God's Ark of the Covenant down, and Abiathar offered sacrifices until everyone had left the city.
Then the king said to Zadok, "Carry God's Ark of the Covenant back to the city, if I find favor in his eyes, he will bring me back to the city and show me both the Ark and his home again.
But if he says, 'I am not happy with you,' then I am here, and he can do whatever he thinks is best for me."
The king also said to priest Zadok, "Are you not a prophet? Return to the city in peace and take your two sons Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan with you.
I will wait out on the plains in the wilderness, until I receive word from you."
So Zadok and Abiathar carried God's Ark of the Covenant back to Jerusalem, where they stayed.
David ascended Mount Olive barefooted and with his head covered weeping as he went. All the men covered their heads, and they were all weeping as they went.
Someone spoke to David and said, "Ahithophel is one of the conspirators with Absalom!" And David said, "O Lord, I pray that you will turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness."
When David reached the mountain top he worshipped God, and Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his head covered in dirt, and wearing a torn coat.
And David spoke to Hushai and said, "If I let you come with me, you will only be a burden to me.
But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'O king, I will be your servant just as I have been your father's servant until now,' then maybe you can disrupt Ahithophel's counsel for me.
The priests Zadok and Abiathar will be there also, and you can report whatever you hear to them in the king's palace.
Zadok's son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan will be with them, and you can send me messages of everything you hear in the king's palace through them."
So David's friend Hushai and Absalom both entered Jerusalem at about the same time.

After David was a little past the top of the hill, Mephibosheth's servant Ziba met him with a couple of saddled donkeys carrying 200 loaves of bread, 100 bunches of raisins, 100 summer fruits, and a bottle of wine.

And King David said to Ziba, "Why did you bring all this?" And Ziba said, "The donkeys are for the king's palace to ride, the bread and summer fruit is for the young men to eat, and the wine is for those who grow weary in the wilderness."

The king spoke again and asked, "Where is your master's son?" And Ziba answered the king and said, "He lives in Jerusalem because he said, 'Today the House of Israel will restore my father's kingdom to me.'"
Then the king said to Ziba, "Behold, you now own everything that belongs to Mephibosheth!" And Ziba said, "My lord O king, I humbly beg that I may find grace in your sight."
When King David went to Bahurim, a man from Saul's household named Shimei, who was Gera's son came out cursing as he walked toward the king.
He threw stones at King David and his servants, even though he was surrounded by his troops and all his mighty men.
And as Shimei cursed he said, "Get out, get out of here, you bloody man of Belial.

The Lord has repaid you for all the blood from the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned. The Lord has delivered the kingdom into the hands of your son Absalom. So now your mischief has overtaken you, because you are a bloody man."
Then Zeruiah's son Abishai said to the king, "My lord, why should we let this dead dog curse the king? I pray you will let me go over there and remove his head."
