And the king said, "What does this have to do with you sons of Zeruiah? If the Lord told him to curse me and said, 'Curse David.' Then who can say to him, 'Why did you do this?'"

David spoke to Abishai and all his servants and said, "Behold my son who is my own flesh and blood, seeks to take my life! So why should this Benjamite not want to kill me even more? "Leave him alone and let him curse me, because the Lord has told him to curse me.
Maybe the Lord will see my affliction and repay me with good for all of his cursing today."
As David and his men continued on their way, Shimei followed them along the other side of the hill, and he cursed him as he went, and threw stones and dust at him.
The king and everyone with him arrived there weary, so they stopped and refreshed themselves.
Then Absalom, Ahithophel, and all the Israelis men arrived in Jerusalem.
When David's friend Hushai the Archite went to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "God save the king, God save the king."
And Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this the kindness you show your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?"
And Hushai said to Absalom, "No, but I am with the one chosen by the Lord and by these people, and all the men of Israel, and I will live with him.
So why should I not serve in the presence of his son? So I will serve you the same as I served your father."
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give me your advice, and tell me what you think we should do."

And Ahithophel replied to Absalom and said, "Go sleep with your father's concubines who he left to maintain the house. Then all of Israel will hear that you abhor your father, then the hands of those who are with you will be strengthened."
So they pitched a tent on the house rooftop for Absalom, and he slept with his father's concubines in front of all of Israel.
In those days, the counsel of Ahithophel was as if a man asked the oracle of God for advice. David and Absalom both felt the same way about Ahithophel's advice.
Furthermore, Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose 12,000 men and pursue David tonight.
I will attack him while he is weak and weary, and that should make him very afraid. Everyone with him will flee, and I will only have to kill the king.
Then I will bring all the people back to you, when everyone returns except for the life of the man you want to kill, then all the people will live in peace."
This advice pleased Absalom and all the Israelis elders.
Then Absalom said, "Summon Hushai the Archite, so we can also hear what he has to say."
When Hushai went to Absalom, Absalom spoke to him and said, "Ahithophel has made this proposal, should we do what he says? If not, tell us what you think we should do."
Hushai answered Absalom and said, "Ahithophel's advice is not good for us at this time."

Hushai also said, "Because, as you know your father and his men are mighty men, and their minds are as disturbed as a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Your father is an experienced man of war who will not stay with his troops.

Surely you know by now that your father is hiding in a cave or some other place. And if some of your men are the first to fall in battle, whoever hears about it will say, 'Absalom's followers are being slaughtered.'

You also know that even those who are courageous with the heart of a lion, will completely melt with fear, because everyone in Israel knows that your father is a mighty man and his men are valiant men.
So I advise you to summon all the Israelis armies, all the way from Dan to Beersheba, who are as numerous as the sand on the beach, and you yourself can lead them into battle.
Then we can attack David wherever we find him and we will fall on him as the dew falls on the ground. And there will be no survivors among him or his, not even one will be left!
If he flees into a city, then the Israelis will bring ropes to that city, and pull it into the river, until not even one small stone can be found there."

Absalom and all the Israelis men said, "Hushai the Archite advice is better than Ahithophel advice." Because the Lord decided to oppose Ahithophel's good counsel, since the Lord's intent was to bring evil down on Absalom.
Then Hushai spoke to Zadok and Abiathar the priests and said, "This is what Ahithophel told Absalom and the Israelis elders to do, and this is what I advised them to do.
So send word to David and say, 'Do not stay in the wilderness plains tonight, but quickly cross over the river, otherwise the king and everyone with him could be swallowed up.'"

Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying near En-Rogel, because they did not want to be seen coming into the city. A servant girl would come and pass information to them, and they would go and tell King David.
Nevertheless a boy saw them and told Absalom, but both of them left quickly, and went to a man's house in Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it to hide.
The woman covered the well's mouth with a blanket and spread ground wheat over it, and nobody knew it was there.

When Absalom's servants went to the woman's house they said, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" And the woman said to them, "They went to the brook for water." So after they looked for them and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem.

After the men left, Ahimaaz and Jonathan came up out of the well and went to King David and said, "You must get up and quickly cross over the river, because Ahithophel has given this advice against you."
Then David and everyone with him got up and crossed the Jordan River, and before the morning light they had all crossed over the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that his advice was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went back to his city and went home. He put his household in order and hanged himself and died, and he was buried in his father's tomb.
Then David went to Mahanaim and Absalom crossed the Jordan River, with all the Israelis men.
Absalom made Amasa top military commander instead of Joab. Amasa was Ithra the Israelite's son, and he was married to Nahash's daughter Abigail who was Joab's mother Zeruiah's sister.
So Israel and Absalom camped in the land of Gilead.
When David arrived in Mahanaim, he was met by Nahash of Rabbah's son Shobi the Ammonite, and Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-Debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim.
They brought beds, sinks, clay bowls, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils, and dried beans.
Plus, honey, butter, sheep, and cheese made from cow's milk. All for David and his people to eat because they said, "The people are hungry, weary, and thirsty out in the wilderness."
David counted all the people with him, and he appointed generals to lead thousands, and captains to lead hundreds.

David sent out 1/3rd of the people under Joab's command, 1/3rd of the people under Zeruiah's son Abishai who was Joab's brother, and 1/3rd of the people under Ittai the Gittite's command. And the king said to the people, "I myself, will also surely march out with you."

But the people answered, "You must not go out because if we have to flee, they will not care about us, even if half of us die. But you are worth 10,000 of us, so it is better that you help support us from the city."
Then the king said to them, "Whatever seems best to you is what I will do," so the king stood by the gate, and the people marched out by the hundreds and thousands.
The king gave Joab, Abishai, and Ittai their orders and said, "Deal gently with the young Absalom for my sake." And everyone heard the king's orders to the captains concerning Absalom.
So the people marched into the field against Israel, and the battle was fought in the Ephraim forest.
Where David's servants slaughtered 20,000 Israelis men that day.
Because the battle was scattered all over the whole country, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword.

Absalom was riding a mule when he met David's servants, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak. Absalom's head got caught in the oak's branches, and he was pulled up off the mule, but it continued to walk away.
A certain man saw Absalom hanging in the oak tree and told Joab about it and said, "Behold I saw Absalom hanging in an oak tree."
Joab responded to the man that told him this and said, "Why did you not pull him down on the ground and kill him when you saw him, and I would have given you ten silver shekels and a belt."

Then the man said to Joab, "Even if I had received 1,000 silver shekels, I would not raise my hand against the king's son, because we heard the king charge you, Abishai, and Ittai when he said, 'Do not touch young Absalom for my sake.'
Otherwise, I would jeopardized my own life, because nothing is ever hidden from the king, and you yourself would have turned against me."
Then Joab said, "I am not going to waste my time like you." And he took three spears and shoved them through Absalom's heart while he was still alive hanging from the oak tree.
At the same time ten of Joab's young armor-bearers surrounded Absalom and killed him.
Joab blew the trumpet, and the army turned back from pursuing the Israelis, because that was Joab's signal to recall the troops.
They threw Absalom's body into a great cave in the forest and laid a huge pile of stones on top of him, and all the Israelis fled back to their tents.

While Absalom was still living, he erected a column as a memorial to himself in the King's Valley. He did this because he thought, "I have no son to remember my name," and he named the column after himself, and it is still called Absalom's Place to this very day.
Then Zadok's son Ahimaaz said, "Please let me run and tell the king the good news, that the Lord has avenged him of his enemies."
Joab answered him and said, "You must not give this news to the king today, wait to tell him another day, because the king's son is dead."
Then Joab said to Cushi, "Go tell the king what you have seen." And Cushi bowed to Joab and took off running.

Then Zadok's son Ahimaaz spoke to Joab again and said, "I pray you will let me run with Cushi to deliver the news." And Joab said, "My son, why do you want to run with Cushi since you have no reward waiting for you?"
Then he said, "It doesn't matter, I want to run with him." And Joab said, "Then run with him," so Ahimaaz ran through the plains and overtook Cushi.
David sat between the two gates, and the watchman had climbed up to the roof over the wall's gates, and he looked out and saw a man running toward them all alone.
The watchman cried out to the king. And the king said, "If he is alone, he brings good news," as he quickly came closer.
Then the watchman saw another man running their way, and the watchman called out to the gatekeeper and said, "Behold there is another man running alone." And the king said, "He also brings news."
The watchman said, "The first runner looks like Zadok's son Ahimaaz with the most important news." And the king said, "He is a good man, and he comes with good news."

Then Ahimaaz called out to the king and said, "All is well!" And he bowed facedown to the ground before the king and said, "Blessed be your Lord God, who has delivered the men that lifted up their hand against my Lord the king."
The king asked him and said, "Is young Absalom safe?" And Ahimaaz answered and said, "When Joab sent the king's servant and your servant, I saw a great tumult, but I did not know what was happening."
The king said to him, "Turn away and stand here," so he stepped aside and stood there.
Then Cushi arrived and said, "My Lord, I have good news for the king, because the Lord has avenged you today for all of those who rose up against you."

And the king said to Cushi, "Is young Absalom safe?" And Cushi answered and said, "May the enemies of my Lord the king and anyone who rises up against you and tries to harm you, meet the same fate as that young man."

And the king was so moved, that he went into the room up over the gates and wept. As he walked, he cried out and said, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! If only God would have let me die for you, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
Joab was told that the king wept and mourned for Absalom.
So their victory that day turned into mourning for all the people, because they heard the king was grieved over his son.
So they secretly returned to the city that day as if they had shamefully fled the battle and ran away.
But the king covered his face and cried out loudly, "O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
Then Joab came into the king's palace and said, "You have shamed all of your servants who saved your life today, as well as the lives of your your wives, sons and daughters, and your concubines.

It seems that you love your enemies and hate your friends, because today you have declared that you do not care about your commanders or your servants. Because today I realized that if Absalom had survived and we had all died, then you would be well pleased.

So get up and go out there and comfort your servants, because I swear by the Lord, if you do not go out there, not one of them will stay with you tonight. And that will be worse for you than any other evil that has ever befallen you from your youth until now!"

Then the king got up and sat in the gate, and they told to all the people and said, "Behold the king sits in the gate." So all the people came before the king, because all of the Israelis had fled back to their own tents.

All the Israelis began arguing among themselves and said, "The king saved us from the hands of our enemies, and he delivered us from the hands of the Philistines, but now he has fled the land because of Absalom.
Absalom who was anointed over us has died in battle. So why do you not want to talk about restoring the king?

So King David sent word to Zadok and Abiathar the priests and said, "Speak to the elders of Judah and ask them, 'Why are you the last ones wanting to return the king to his house? This talk all over Israel has even reached the king's palace.
You are my brothers and my own flesh and blood, so why are you the last ones wanting to return the king to his house?'
Then speak to Amasa and say, 'Are you not from my own flesh and blood? May God punish me even more, if you are not made commander of my army instead of Joab.'"
And Amasa convinced the hearts of the men of Judah to unite as one, so that they sent word to the king and said, "Please return with all your servants."
So the king began his trip back home and when he arrived at the Jordan River, the men of Judah came to Gilgal to meet him and carried him across the Jordan.
Gera the Benjamite's son Shimei of Bahurim, hurried down to meet King David with the men of Judah.
Shimei brought a thousand Benjamite men with him, plus Saul's son Ziba, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, and they crossed the Jordan River before the king.
They used a ferry boat to carry the king's palace across the river, and whatever else he thought was good. Gera's son Shimei bowed facedown before the king, as he crossed the Jordan.
And he said to the king, "My Lord, do not take my immorality to heart, or remember the perversity I committed against the king the day that you left Jerusalem.
Because your servant knows that I have sinned, so I am the first one from the house of Joseph to come down to meet my Lord the king."
But Zeruiah's son Abishai answered and said, "Should not Shimei be put to death because he cursed the Lord's anointed?"

David replied and said, "Sons of Zeruiah, why should I be interested in punishing you today for being my adversary? Nobody will be put to death in Israel today. For do I not know for sure that I am the king of Israel today?"
So the king swore an oath to Shimei and said, "You will not die."

Then Saul's grandson Mephibosheth went down to meet the king. And since the day the king left until the day he returned in peace, Mephibosheth had not worn shoes, trimmed his beard, or washed his clothes.
When he went to meet the king in Jerusalem the king said to him, "Mephibosheth, why did you not go with me?"
And Mephibosheth answered and said, "My Lord the king, I spoke to my servant Ziba and said, 'I must saddle a donkey, so that I can ride away with the king, because I am lame.' But Ziba deceived me.
He has slandered me before my Lord the king, who is as wise as an angel of God, so do whatever you think is good.

Because everyone in my grandfather's house deserves death from my Lord the king, but you did set your servant among those who ate at your own table. So what right do I have anymore to cry to the king?"
And the king responded to him and said, "Do you have anything else to say? I hereby declare that you and Ziba must divide the land."
Mephibosheth replied to the king and said, "Yes, let Ziba take it all! Because my Lord the king has returned in peace."
Barzillai from Mount Gilead came down from Rogelim to help the king cross the Jordan River and send him on his way.
Barzillai was an eighty-year-old man who was very wealthy, so he provided nourishment for the king while he stayed in Mahanaim.
The king spoke to Barzillai and said, "Cross over the Jordan River with me and I will feed you in Jerusalem."
But Barzillai replied to the king and said, "How long do I have to live, that I should go to Jerusalem with the king?

I am eighty years old; can I tell the difference between good and evil anymore? Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can I still hear the voices of men and women singing? Why should your servant be an extra burden to my Lord the king?
Your servant can only go a short distance across Jordan with the king. Why should the king compensate me with such a reward?

I pray you will let your servant return, so that I may die in my own city and be buried in the grave by my father and mother. But let your servant Chimham cross the river with my Lord the king and do whatever seems good for him."
The king answered him and said, "Chimham will cross the river with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and I will do for you whatever you require of me."
Everyone crossed the Jordan, and after the king crossed the river, he kissed and blessed Barzillai and returned home.
Then the king and Chimham went on to Gilgal, everyone from Judah and half the Israelis people also escorted the king.
One day all the Israelis men came to King David and asked, "Why did our brothers the men of Judah secretly sneak you, your household, and all of your men away and cross the Jordan River?"

The men of Judah answered the Israelis men and said, "The king is our next of kin and close family. Why are you angry about this? Have we ever eaten at the king's expense, or has he ever given us any gifts?"

And the Israelis men answered them and said, "We have ten parts in the king, and we have more right to King David than you. Why do you despise us? We were the first to advise that the king that he should return!" But the men from Judah spoke more fiercely than the men of Israel.

Bichri's son Sheba the Benjamite a man of Belial happened to be there, and he blew a trumpet and said, "O Israel, we are not interested in David, and we have no inheritance in Jesse's son, so everyone can go back to their own tent."
So all the men of Israel left David, and followed Sheba the son of Bichri, but the men of Judah held loyally to their king, from the Jordan River all the way to Jerusalem.

When David returned home to Jerusalem, he put the ten concubines that he left to maintain his house under guard. He fed them, but he did not sleep with them, and they were confined until the day they died, and they lived as if they were widows.
Then the king spoke to Amasa and said, "Summon the men of Judah here within the next three days, and you must also be here."
So Amasa went to summon the men of Judah, but it took longer than the king wanted.
And David spoke to Abishai and said, "Now Bichri's son Sheba will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, otherwise he will find fortified cities and elude us."
So Joab's men marched out of Jerusalem including the Cherethites, Pelethites, and all the mighty men to pursue Bichri's son Sheba.
When they arrived at the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa joined them. Joab was wearing a military uniform with a sheathed sword strapped to his waist, and as he approached, he pulled it from its sheath.
Joab said to Amasa, "My brother, are you in good health?" And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.

But Amasa did not notice the sword in Joab's hand, so he stabbed him under the fifth rib, and spilled his guts out on the ground. Joab did not have to strike him again because he died. So Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Bichri's son Sheba.
Then one of Joab's men standing near Amasa said, "Whoever favors Joab and David, let him follow Joab."

Amasa wallowed in his own blood in the middle of the highway, and when the man saw that all the troops stopped there to look, he dragged the body from the highway out into the field and threw a blanket over him.
After the body was removed from the highway, all the troops went on with Joab to pursue Bichri's son Sheba.
Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel and finally arrived in Abel-Beth-Maachah, and all the Berites throughout the area joined him and followed him.
Joab's army laid siege to Sheba in Abel of Abel-Beth-Maachah, and they threw a ramp up against the city walls from the trench. And the army battered the wall to knock it down.
Then a wise woman from the city cried out and said, "I pray you will bring Joab here so that I may come out to speak with him."
When Joab approached her, she said, "Are you Joab?" And he answered, "I am." Then she said to him, "Hear what your servant has to say," and he answered her and said, "I hear you."
Then she spoke up and said, "In the old days they used to say, 'We must ask Abel for his advice,' and that's how they settled their disputes.
I am one of the peaceful and faithful people in Israel, and you seek to destroy a city that is like a mother in Israel. Why do you want to destroy the Lord's inheritance?"
Joab answered her and said, "Far be it from me, that I should consume or destroy this city.

That is not my intention, but Bichri's son Sheba from Mount Ephraim, has taken up arms against King David. But if you deliver him to me, I will leave this city alone." And the woman said to Joab, "Behold his head will be thrown over the wall to you."

Then the woman went to speak to everyone in the city with her wisdom, and they cut off Bichri's son Sheba's head, and threw it out to Joab. He blew a trumpet, they left the city and all the men returned to their tents, and Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem.
Joab commanded the entire Israelis military, and Jehoiada's son Benaiah was the general over the Cherethites and Pelethites.
Adoram was over the slaves, and Ahilud's son Jehoshaphat was the record keeper.
Sheva was the scribe, and Zadok and Abiathar were the priests.
Ira the Jairite was David's chief priest.

During King David's reign there was a three-year famine, and David inquired of the Lord and asked, "Why Lord?" And the Lord answered him and said, "It is because of bloody reign of Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites."

So the king summoned the Gibeonites to speak to them. The Gibeonites were not part of the Israelis tribes, but they were the remnants of the Amorites. The Israelis had sworn an oath to them, but Saul tried to kill them in his zeal toward Israel and Judah.
So David spoke to the Gibeonites and asked, "What can I do for you to make an atonement, so that you may bless the Lord's inheritance?"

And the Gibeonites answered David and said, "We will accept no silver or gold from Saul or his house, and we do not want you to kill anyone in Israel for us." And David said, "Whatever you ask, I will do for you."
They answered the king and said, "As for the man who planned to destroy us and leave us with nothing within the borders of Israel.
Deliver seven of his sons into our hands, and we will hang them before the Lord at Gibeah of Saul, whom the Lord had chosen." And the king said, "I will give them to you."
The king spared Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, because of the Lord's oath between David and Jonathan. Jonathan was Saul's son.
But the king took Saul and Aiah's daughter Rizpah's two sons Armoni and Mephibosheth, and Barzillai the Meholathite's son Adriel and Saul's daughter Michal's five sons.

And he delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the hill before the Lord. All seven of them were put to death during the first harvest days, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Then Aiah's daughter Rizpah spread a sackcloth for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until a rain from heaven fell on the bodies, and she kept the birds away from them by day and the wild field animals at night.
David was told what Saul's concubine Aiah's daughter Rizpah had done.

David took the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the men in Jabesh-Gilead, which they had stolen from the streets of Beth-Shan. The Philistines had hung them there after they killed Saul in Gilboa.
David brought Saul and his son Jonathan's bones back from there, and they also gathered the bones of those that had been hanged.

So they buried Saul and his son Jonathan's bones in his father Kish's tomb, in the country of Benjamin of Zelah. They did everything that the king commanded, and after that God answered their prayers for the land.
Once again the Philistines decided to wage war against Israel. So David went down with his army and fought against the Philistines, but David was soon exhausted.
Ishbi-Benob, who was a descendant of Rapha the giant and carried a spear that weighed 300 brass shekels was wearing a new sword, and he decided to kill David.

But Zeruiah's son Abishai helped him kill the Philistine. Then David's men swore an oath to him and said, "You must not go into battle with us anymore, you are the light of Israel which must not be quenched."
After this, there was another battle with the Philistines at Gob, then Sibbechai the Hushathite killed Saph, who was also a descendant of Rapha the giant.
Then once again there was another battle with the Philistines at Gob, where Jaare-Oregim's son Elhanan of Bethlehem killed Goliath the Gittite's brother, whose spear was as thick as a weaver's beam.

And there was yet another battle at Gath, where a man of great stature with six fingers on each hand, and six toes on each foot, with twenty-four fingers and toes altogether, who was also a descendant of Rapha the giant.
When the man defied Israel, Shimeah's son Jonathan the brother of David killed him.
These were Rapha's four descendants in Gath that fell by the hands of David and his servants.
David sang this song to the Lord on the day that the Lord delivered him from the hands of Saul and all his enemies.
And he said, "The Lord is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.
I will trust in the God of my rock, he is my shield, the horn of my salvation, my high tower, my refuge, and my savior. You save me from violence.
I will call on the Lord, who is worthy to be praised, so I shall be saved from my enemies
When the waves of death surrounded me, the floods of ungodly men made me afraid.
The sorrows of hell surrounded me, and the snares of death confronted me.
In my distress I called upon the Lord and cried out to my God. And God heard my voice from his temple, and my cries entered his ears.
Then the earth shook and trembled, the foundations of heaven were shaken because God burned with anger.
Smoke rose from the Lord's nostrils, and a devouring fire came from his mouth which kindled glowing coals.
He also parted the heavens and descended with darkness under his feet.
He rode a cherub and flew, and he was seen soaring on the wings of the wind.
He made darkness into a pavilion all around him, with dark waters and thick clouds in the skies.
Through the brightness before him coals of fire were kindled.
The Lord thundered from heaven, and the voice of the Most High was heard.
He sent his arrows and scattered his foes; he hurled lightning and embarrassed them.
The ocean's channels appeared, and the foundations of the world were discovered at the Lord's rebuke, and the blast of breath from his nostrils.
He sent for me from above and pulled me out of many deep waters.
He delivered me from my strong enemies, and from those who hated me for they were too strong for me.
They confronted me on my day of disaster, but the Lord protected me.
He also brought me out into an open place; he delivered me because he delighted in me.
The Lord rewarded me based on my righteousness, and he repaid me according to the cleanliness of my hands.
Because I have kept the Lord's ways and I have not wickedly abandoned my God.
For all of his judgments were before me and I did not depart from his statutes.
I was also honest before him, and I have kept myself from immorality.
So the Lord has compensated me according to my righteousness and my cleanliness in his sight.
You show yourself merciful with the merciful, and with honest men you show your honesty.
You show yourself pure with the pure, and you show your unsavory character with the fraudulent.
You save the afflicted people, but your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down.
For you, O Lord, are my lamp and the Lord will lighten up my darkness.
For in you I have run through the troops, by my God I can leap over a wall.
As for God, his way is perfect and his word is tried and true, he is a shield to all who trust in him.
For who is God except the Lord? And who is a rock except our God?
God is my strength and power, and he makes my way perfect.
He makes my feet feel like deer's feet and sets me on high places.
He teaches my hands to make war, so my arms can bend and break a steel bow.
You have also given me your shield of salvation, and your gentleness makes me great.
You have enlarged my steps beneath me, so that my feet do not slip.
I have pursued my enemies and destroyed them; I did not turn away until they were consumed.
I have consumed and wounded them so that they could not rise; they have fallen under my feet.
For you have surrounded me with strength in battle; you have subdued those who rose up against me.
You have routed my enemies before me, so that I could destroy those who hate me.
They looked, but there was no one to save them, and even the Lord did not answer them.
Then I ground them up as small as the dust of the earth, I trampled them like the mud in the street and spread them abroad.
You have delivered me from my people's strife, you have preserved me as the head of the heathen, a people whom I did not think would serve me.
Foreigners submit themselves before me, and when they hear me, they obey me.
Foreigners fade away, and they are afraid to come from their hiding places.
The Lord lives and blessed is my rock! May my God, the rock of my salvation be glorified.
God avenges me and brings the nations down beneath me.
My God frees me from my enemies! You lift me up on high places above my foes who rose up against me; you have delivered me from violent men.
So I will give thanks to you among the heathen O Lord, and I will sing praises to your name.
God is the tower of salvation for his king and shows mercy to his anointed one David and his descendants forever."
Now these are the last words of David, "Jesse's son David was raised up on high as the anointed one of the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel.
The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and his word was in my tongue.
The God of Israel said, "The Rock of Israel spoke to me and said, 'He who rules over men must be just, and rule in the fear of God.
He will be as the morning light when the sun rises in the cloudless clear skies, like the glistening rain on the tender grass after a spring rain.'"
My house has been with God; yet he has made an everlasting, detailed, and guaranteed covenant with me. For this is my salvation and everything I desire, although he does not make it grow.
But the sons of Belial are as worthless as thorns raked aside, because they cannot be taken with hands.
But the man who touches them must be armed with an iron spear or sword, and the fire completely burns them in the same place."

These are the names of David's mighty men: first there was Adino the Tachmonite who sat in the chief captain's chair. He was also known as Adino the Eznite. He raised his spear against 800 men, whom he killed all at one time.
After him was Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite. He was one of the three mighty men with David, when they defied the Philistines who had gathered for battle after the Israelis retreated.
Eleazar arose and killed Philistines until his hand grew weary and stuck to his sword. The Lord worked a great victory that day. Then the troops returned but only to plunder the spoils.
After him was Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite. When the Philistines gathered together near a field full of lentils, and the Israelis army fled from the Philistines.
But Shammah stood his ground in the middle of the field, and defended it and killed the Philistines, and the Lord worked a great victory.
At harvest time, three of the thirty chiefs went down to meet David at the Adullam cave, when the Philistine troops were camped in the Valley of Rephaim.
And David was in one of his strongholds, and the Philistine garrison was stationed in Bethlehem at that time.
David longed for water and said, "Oh I wish someone would bring me a drink of water from the Bethlehem well near the city gates!"

So the three mighty men broke through the Philistine lines and drew water from the Bethlehem well near the city gates. They brought it back to David, but he refused to drink it and poured it out on the ground to the Lord.

And David said, "Far be it from me, O Lord to drink this, is this not the blood of the men who jeopardized their lives." So David would not drink it, and these are some of the things done by these three mighty men.
Joab's brother Abishai son of Zeruiah was the commander of the three, and he lifted up his spear and killed 300 men and made a name for himself among the three.
Was he not the most honorable of all three? So he was their captain, even though he was not among the first three.
Jehoiada's son Benaiah was a man of valor from Kabzeel, who had done many things. He killed two lionlike men from Moab, and he also went down and killed a lion in a pit in the snow.

He killed a very large Egyptian man who had a spear in his hand, but Benaiah went down to meet him with nothing but a staff. Then he took the spear from the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear.
These are the things that Jehoiada's son Benaiah did to make a name for himself among three mighty men.
He was more honorable than the thirty, but he was not one of the first three. And David put him over his bodyguards.
Included among the thirty were Joab's brother Asahel, and Dodo son of Elhanan of Bethlehem.
Then Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite,
Helez the Paltite, Ikkesh the Tekoite's son Ira,
Abiezer the Anethothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite,
Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite,
Baanah the Netophathite's son Heleb, Ribai's son Ittai from Gibeah of Benjamin,
Benaiah the Pirathonite, Hiddai from the brooks of Gaash,
Abialbon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite,
Eliahba the Sha-Albonite, Jashen's sons Jonathan,
Shammah the Hararite, Sharar the Hararite's son Ahiam,
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai, son of the Maachathite, Ahithophel the Gilonite's son Eliam,
Hezrai the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite,
Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite,
Zelek the Ammonite, Nahari the Beerothite, Joab's armor-bearer and the son of Zeruiah,
Ira and Gareb the Ithrites,
And Uriah the Hittite, which is a total of thirty-seven in all.
Once again the Lord's anger was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them when he spoke to his leaders and said, "Go and take a census of Israel and Judah."

For the king spoke to Joab who was his top military commander and said, "Go throughout the tribes of Israel, all the way from Dan to Beersheba and count the people, so that I know how many people there are."
Joab answered the king and said, "May your Lord God multiply the people a hundred times over, and may my Lord the king's eyes see it. But why does my Lord the king want to do this thing?"
But the king's word prevailed against Joab, and the commanders of the military, and Joab and the commanders left the king's presence to count the Israelis people.
They crossed the Jordan River and camped in Aroer, on the right side of the city that lies in the middle of the valley of Gad toward Jazer.
Then they arrived in Gilead and the land of Tahtim-Hodshi, and they went to Danjaan then around to Zidon.
And they came to the stronghold of Tyre and all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites. Then they turned south and went to Judah, then on to Beersheba.
So after they had gone through the entire land in nine months and twenty days, they returned to Jerusalem.
Joab reported the total number of people to the king, and there were 800,000 men of valor who drew the sword in Israel, and there were 500,000 men in Judah.

After David had numbered the people, his heart distressed him and he said to the Lord, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done, and now O Lord, I beg you to take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have been very foolish."
When David got up in the morning, the Lord's word had come to his prophet Gad,
So the Lord told Gad to go see David and say, "This is what the Lord says, 'I offer you three options, choose you one as your punishment.'"

So Gad went to David and told him what the Lord said, "You may choose between three years of famine in your land, or you can flee from your enemies for three months while they pursue you, or would you rather have three days of pestilence in your land? Think it over and decide what answer I should return to the one who sent me."
And David answered Gad and said, "I am in great distress, please let us fall into the Lord's hands because his mercies are great, but do not let me fall into the hands of man."
So the Lord sent a plague against Israel that morning for the appointed time, and 70,000 men died among the Israelis people from Dan to Beersheba.

But when the angel stretched out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, the Lord relented and said to the angel, "That is enough evil, stay your hand!" At that time the Lord's angel was near Araunah the Jebusite's threshing room.

When David saw the angel destroying the people he spoke to the Lord and said, "Look, I am the one who has sinned and acted wickedly. But what have these sheep done? I pray that you will let your hand be against me and my father's house."
And that day Gad came to David and said, "Go and build an altar to the Lord on Araunah the Jebusite's threshing room floor."
So David did what Gad said, and he went where the Lord commanded.
Araunah saw the king and his servants coming toward him and he went and bowed facedown on the ground before the king.

And Araunah said, "Why has my Lord the king come to see his servant?" And David said, "I came to buy your threshing room floor from you and to build an altar to the Lord there, so that the plague against the people may be stopped."

Then Araunah said to David, "Let my Lord the king take it and offer whatever seems good to him. Behold there are also oxen to offer for a burnt sacrifice, and the wooden threshing instruments and other wooden instruments and wood from the ox yokes.
O king, I give all these things to the king! May your Lord God accept you."

And King David said to Araunah, "No, but I will surely buy it from you at a fair price. I will not make burnt offerings to my Lord God that cost me nothing!" So David bought the threshing room floor and the oxen for fifty silver shekels.
So David built an altar to the Lord there, and he made burnt offerings and peace offerings. After David pleaded for the land; the Lord ended the plague that was upon Israel.
Now King David was very old and even when his servants covered him with blankets, he could not stay warm.
So David's servants said to him, "Please allow my Lord the king's servants to find a young virgin for the king to cherish and lie in your embrace, so that she may keep you warm."
They searched throughout all of Israel for a beautiful young girl, and they found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king.
Abishag was very beautiful and she loved the king and ministered to him, but David did not have sexual relations with her.
Then Adonijah, the son of King David and Haggith began to glorify himself and he said, "I will be king!" And Adonijah prepared chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.
Adonijah's father had never at any time expressed displeasure with him or said, "Why are you doing this?" Adonijah was also very handsome, and his mother gave birth to him after Absalom.
Adonijah was advised by Joab, son of Zeruiah and Abiathar the priest, and they helped support him.
But Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and the mighty men all remained loyal to David not Adonijah.
Adonijah killed sheep, oxen, and fat cattle by the stone of Zoheleth near En-Rogel. He invited all his brothers the king's sons, and all of the king's servants from Judah.
But Benaiah, Nathan the prophet, the mighty men, and Adonijah's brother Solomon was not invited.
So Nathan spoke to Solomon's mother Bathsheba and said, "Have you not heard that Adonijah the son of King David and Haggith has appointed himself king, and our Lord King David has not heard about it?
I pray that you will let me come and advise you on how to save your life and your son Solomon's life.

Go now to King David and say to him, 'My Lord, O king, did you not swear to your maidservant and say that your son Solomon will surely reign after you, and sit on your throne? So why does Adonijah reign in your place?'
Then, while you are talking with the king, I will come in and confirm your words."
Then Bathsheba went into the king's chambers, and since the king was very old Abishag the Shunammite ministered to him.
Bathsheba bowed and paid tribute to the king who asked, "What would you like?"
And Bathsheba said to him, "My Lord, you swore by your Lord God to your maidservant and said, 'Your son Solomon will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne.'
And now, behold Adonijah reigns in your place, and my Lord the king does not even know it.
He has killed oxen, fat cattle, and sheep in abundance, and he has summoned all of the king's sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the army commander, but your servant Solomon was not invited.
And you, my Lord, O king, the eyes of all of Israel are on you, waiting for you to tell them who will sit on my Lord's throne after the king.
Otherwise, when my Lord the king sleeps with his fathers, my son Solomon and I will be counted among the criminals."
While she was still talking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in.
They told the king that Nathan the prophet was there, and when he came into the room he bowed facedown before the king.
And Nathan said, "My Lord, O king, have you said that Adonijah will reign after you and sit on your throne?

Because he has killed an abundance of oxen, fat cattle, and sheep and he summoned all of the king's sons, military commanders, and priest Abiathar the priest and they are all eating and drinking with him while he says, 'God save King Adonijah!'
But he did not invite me your servant, Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, or your servant Solomon.
Is this something my Lord the king has done that you have not revealed to your servant? Have you decided who should sit on my Lord the king's throne after him?"
Then King David answered and said, "Send Bathsheba to me." So she entered the king's chambers and stood before him.
And the king swore an oath and said, "As the Lord lives who has rescued my soul from all distress.
I will certainly do this day what I swore to you by the Lord God of Israel when I said, "Your son Solomon will surely reign after me, and he will sit on my throne in my place."
Then Bathsheba bowed facedown to the ground and showed her respect for the king and said, "Let my Lord King David live forever!"
And King David said, "Send Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Jehoiada's son Benaiah to me," and they all went to the king.
The king also said to them, "Take my servants and put my son Solomon on a mule, and bring him down to the Gihon River.
Then let priest Zadok and Nathan the prophet anoint him king of Israel, and blow your trumpet and say, 'God save King Solomon!'
After that bring him here so that he may come and sit on my throne and he will be king instead of me. Because I have appointed him as the ruler of Israel and Judah."
Jehoiada's son Benaiah answered the king and said, "Amen, this is what the Lord God of my Lord the king also declares.
As the Lord has been with my Lord the king, he will also be with Solomon, and he will make his throne greater than the throne of my Lord King David."
So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Jehoiada's son Benaiah, the Cherethites, and the Pelethites made Solomon ride King David's mule down to the Gihon River.
Priest Zadok took a horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon, then they blew the trumpet and all the people said, "God save King Solomon!"
Then all the people followed him around playing flutes and rejoicing with great joy, so that the earth was torn open by their noise.
Adonijah and all his guests heard all the noise as they were eating. When Joab heard the trumpet, he asked, "What is causing all that noise and uproar in the city?"
While Joab was still speaking, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest went to Adonijah who said to him, "Come in, for you are a valiant man bringing good news."
Jonathan answered Adonijah and said, "Truly, our Lord King David has just made Solomon the new king.
The king has also sent Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Jehoiada's son Benaiah, the Cherethites, and the Pelethites with Solomon and they made him ride on the king's mule.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed Soloman king in Gihon. The noise that you heard ringing throughout the city is everyone there rejoicing over the news.
And King Solomon also sits on the kingdom's throne.

Furthermore, the king's servants came to bless our Lord King David and said, 'God make the name of Solomon greater than your name, and make his throne greater than your throne,' and the king himself bowed down on his bed.
And the king also said, 'Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because my eyes have seen the chosen one who he has been given to sit on my throne today.'
All of Adonijah's guests were immediately afraid and they all got up and left.
But Adonijah was afraid of King Solomon, and he got up and went and took hold of the horns on the altar.

Someone reported this to Solomon and said, "Behold Adonijah is so afraid of King Solomon, that he has taken hold of the horns on the altar and he said, 'Let King Solomon swear to me today that he will not kill his servant with the sword.'"
And Solomon said, "If Adonijah shows himself to be a worthy man, not one hair on his head will fall to the ground, but if wickedness is found in him, he will die."
So King Solomon sent for him, and they brought him down from the altar and he went and bowed to King Solomon, and Solomon said, "Go to your home."
David was old and as the day of his death drew near, he spoke to his son Solomon and said,
"I am going back to the earth soon, so you must be strong and show them that you are a man.

Keep your Lord God's commandments and walk in his ways, keep his laws, commandments, judgments, and testimonies as they are written in the Law of Moses, so that you may prosper in everything that you do and wherever you turn.

So that the Lord will continue the word that he spoke to me and said, 'If your descendants take heed of their ways and walk truthfully before me with all their heart and soul, you will never fail to have a descendant on the throne of Israel.'

Furthermore, you know what Zeruiah's son Joab did to me and to Ner's son Abner, and Jether's son Amasa who were Israel's two top army commanders. He murdered them, and shed the blood of war during peace time, and smeared the blood of war on his belt and his shoes and feet.
So use your wisdom in everything that you do, and do not let his gray head go down peacefully to the grave.
But show kindness the Sons of Barzillai from Mount Gilead and let them be among those who eat at your table, because they came to me when I fled from your brother Absalom.

Never forget Shimei the son of Gera the Benjamite from Bahurim who grievously cursed me the day I went to Mahanaim. But, when he came down to meet me at the Jordan River, I swore to him by the Lord and said, 'I will not kill you with the sword.'
So do not hold him guiltless, because you are a wise man and you know what you should to do to him. So send his gray head down to a bloody grave."
Then David died and slept with his fathers, and he was buried in the city of David.
King David reigned over Israel for forty years, he ruled from Hebron for seven years, and from Jerusalem for thirty-three years.
After that King Solomon sat on his father David's throne, and he established a great kingdom.
Haggith's son Adonijah went to Solomon's mother Bathsheba and she asked, "Do you come in peace?" And Adonijah said, "I come in peace."
And Adonijah said, "Furthermore, I have something to say to you." And Bathsheba said, "Speak up."

And Adonijah said, "You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all of Israel wanted me to reign, but the kingdom was turned upside down and was given to my brother, because it was what the Lord wanted.
Now I ask you for just one petition, and please do not deny me." And Bathsheba said to Adonijah, "Speak your mind."
Then Adonijah said, "I pray that you will speak to King Solomon because he will not say no to you and ask him if he will give Abishag the Shunammite to me as my wife."
Bathsheba answered him and said, "Well, I will speak to the king for you."

So Bathsheba went to talk to King Solomon for Adonijah. The king stood up to meet her as he bowed before her and sat back down on his throne. Then the king had a seat brought in for his mother, and she sat at his right hand.
Then Bathsheba said, "I have one small petition to ask of you, and I pray you will not say no." And the king said to her, "Make your question mother, because you know that I will not say no to you."
Bathsheba spoke up and said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to your brother Adonijah as his wife."

And King Solomon answered his mother and said, "Why are you asking me to give Abishag the Shunammite to Adonijah? You know he is my older brother, and you may as well ask me to give him the kingdom along with Abiathar the priest, and Zeruiah's son Joab because they are with him in this."
Then King Solomon swore by the Lord and said, "May God punish me even more severely, if Adonijah's words do not cost him his very own life.
Therefore, as surely as the Lord lives who established me and set me on my father David's throne and made me the leader of a house as he promised, Adonijah will be put to death today!"
So King Solomon sent Jehoiada's son Benaiah to Adonijah, and he killed him.

Then the king spoke to Abiathar the priest and said, "Go back to your fields in Anathoth. Because even though you deserve to die, I will not put you to death at this time, because you carried the God's Ark of the Covenant before my father David, and you have been afflicted by everything that my afflicted father."
So Solomon banned Abiathar from being the Lord's priest, so that he could fulfill what the Lord said when he spoke in Shiloh about the house of Eli.
Then news came to Joab, and because he had followed Adonijah instead of Absalom, he fled to the Lord's tabernacle and grabbed hold of the altar's horns.
King Solomon was told that Joab had fled to the Lord's tabernacle, and he was near the altar. Then Solomon sent Jehoiada's son Benaiah to Joab and said, "Go, and kill him."

Benaiah went to the Lord's tabernacle and said to Joab, "The king says, 'Come out!" And Joab answered him and said, "No, I will die here." And Benaiah sent word back to the king and said, "This is how Joab answered me."
King Solomon answered Benaiah and said, "Do just as Joab says. Kill him and bury him, to remove the innocent blood that Joab has shed from me and my father's house.

The Lord will return Joab's bloodshed back on his own head, because he killed two men who were more righteous than him, without my father David's knowledge. And with the sword, he killed Ner's son Abner commander of the Israelis military, and Jether's son Amasa commander of Judah's military.
Their blood will be on the heads of Joab and his descendants forever. But as for David and his descendants, his house, and his throne there will be peace from the Lord forever."
So Jehoiada's son Benaiah went and killed Joab, and he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.
Then the king replaced Joab with Jehoiada's son Benaiah as his commander over the military, and he replaced Abiathar with priest Zadok.
Then the king summoned Shimei and said to him, "Build your house in Jerusalem and live there, but do not go anywhere else.
For on the day that you go out and cross over the Kidron Brook, you will surely die and your blood will be on your own head."
Shimei replied to the king and said, "This sounds good to me. I will do as my Lord the king has said," and Shimei lived in Jerusalem for many years.
After three years, two of Shimei's servants ran away to Maachah's son King Achish son of Gath. Someone told Shimei this and they said, "Behold your servants are in Gath."
And Shimei got up and saddled his donkey and went to King Achish in Gath looking for his servants, and he brought his servants home from Gath.
King Solomon was told that Shimei had left Jerusalem and gone to Gath, and that he had returned.

The king sent for Shimei and when he arrived Solomon said to him, "Did I not make you to swear by the Lord and warn you, that on the day you leave Jerusalem and go anywhere else that you will surely die? And you said to me, 'That sounds good to me.'
Why have you not kept the Lord's oath and the command that I have given you?"

Then the king said to Shimei, "Furthermore, you know in your heart all of the wickedness that you did to my father David. Therefore, the Lord will return all of your wickedness back onto your own head.
But King Solomon will be blessed, and the throne of David will be established before the Lord forever.
So the king gave Jehoiada's son Benaiah an order, and he went and killed Shimei. Thus, the kingdom was firmly established in King Solomon's hands.

Solomon had an affinity for Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he married Pharaoh's daughter and brought her to live in the city of David until he finished building his own house, the Lord's house, and the walls around Jerusalem.
But the people had to offer their sacrifices in high places because the Lord's house had not been built yet.
Solomon loved the Lord and he walked in the statutes of his father David; except he only sacrificed and burned incense in high places.
The king went to sacrifice in Gibeon because it was the great high place, and Solomon offered 1,000 burnt offerings on that altar.
The Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream one night in Gibeon and God said, "Whatever you ask I will give you."

And Solomon said, "You showed great mercy to your servant my father David, because he walked before you with an honest heart in truth and righteousness. And you have kept this great kindness for him, because you have given him a son to sit on his throne to this very day.
Now O Lord my God, you have made your servant king instead of my father David, and I am like a little child, who does not know how to come in or go out.
Your servant is here in the midst of your chosen people who are a great people too numerous to count.
Therefore give your servant an understanding heart to judge your people, so that I may recognize the difference between good and evil. For who can govern your great people?"
When the Lord heard Solomon's speech, he was pleased that he had asked such a thing.

So God said to him, "Because you have asked this, and you have not asked for long life, or riches for yourself, or for the life of your enemies, but you have asked for understanding for yourself to recognize good judgment.
Behold, I have done everything you asked! I have given you a wise and understanding heart, and there was no one like you before nor will there be anyone as wise as you rise up again.
I have also given you things which you have not asked for. I have given you both riches and honor, so that there will be no other kings like you as long as you live.
If you walk in my ways and keep my laws and commandments, as your father David did, then I will lengthen your days.

Solomon woke up and knew that it was a dream, and he went to Jerusalem and stood before the Lord's Ark of the Covenant and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings and made a feast for all of his servants.
Then two women who were prostitutes came and stood before the king.
One of the women said, "O my Lord, this woman I and live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was there.
The third day after I delivered the baby, this woman also gave birth to a child and we were alone together in the house, and no one else was there.
This woman's child died in the night because she had laid on top of it.
She got up at midnight and took my son from me as I slept, and she embraced my child and laid her dead child beside me.
When I got up the next morning to feed my child, it was dead, but when I had time to think about it that morning, I realized that the dead child in my arms was not the son I had given birth to."

And the other woman said, "No, the living child is my son and the dead child is your son." Then the first woman said, "No, the dead child is your son, and the living child is my son." And this was what they told the king.
Then King Solomon said, "This one says, 'My son lives and your son is dead.' And the other one says, 'No, your son is dead and my son lives.'"
Then the king said, "Bring me a sword!" And they brought the king a sword.
And King Solomon said, "Cut the living child in half. Then give half the child to one woman and half to the other."

Then the woman whose son was alive spoke to the king because she feared for her son and she said, "O my Lord, give her the living child and do not kill it." But the other woman said, "Cut it in half and it will not be mine or hers."
Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to her, and do not kill it because she is his mother."
All of Israel heard about the judgment that the king had made, and they were afraid of the king because they could see that God's wisdom to judge the truth was in him.
So King Solomon ruled over all of Israel.
The following is a list of King Solomon's top officials: Zadok's son Azariah was the priest.
Shisha's sons Elihoreph and Ahiah were the scribes, Ahilud's son Jehoshaphat was the record keeper.
Jehoiada's son Benaiah was the top military commander, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Nathan's son Azariah was over the government officials, and Nathan's son Zabud was the king's friend and his principal officer.
Ahishar ran the king's household, and Abda's son Adoniram supervised the tax collectors.
And Solomon had twelve Israelis officers, who provided food for the king and his household, each one supplied provisions for one month out of the year.
These are the names of Solomon's twelve officers: The son of Hur on Mount Ephraim.
Dekar's son in Makaz, Sha-Albim, Beth-Shemesh, and Elon-Beth-Hanan.
Hesed's son in Aruboth governed Sochoh and the entire land of Hepher.
Abinadab's son governed the entire region of Dor, and Solomon's daughter Taphath was his wife.
Ahilud's son Baana governed Taanach and Megiddo, all of Beth-Shean near Zartanah beneath Jezreel from Beth-Shean to Abel-Meholah, and further beyond Jokneam.
Geber's son in Ramoth-Gilead governed Manasseh's son Jair's towns in Gilead, he also governed the region of Argob in Bashan with its sixty great walled cities with brass bars.
Iddo's son Ahinadab governed Mahanaim.
Ahimaaz governed Naphtali, and Solomon's daughter Basmath was his wife.
Hushai's son Baanah governed Asher and Aloth.
Paruah's son Jehoshaphat governed Issachar.
Shimei the son of Elah, in Benjamin.
Uri's son Geber governed Gilead, and the entire Amorite country of King Sihon, and King Og of Bashan, who was the only officer in the land.
The people of Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand on the beach, and they were eating, drinking, and making merry.
King Solomon reigned over all kingdoms from the river to the land of the Philistines to the Egyptian border. They brought presents and served Solomon all the days of his life.
One day of provisions for King Solomon's household required 30 measures of fine flour, and 60 measures of meal.
Ten fat oxen, 20 oxen from the pastures, 100 sheep, deer, fawns, antelope, and fat birds.

For Solomon had authority over the entire region on his side the river, from Tiphsah all the way to Gaza. He reigned over all the kings on his side the river, and there was peace on all the borders around him.
Judah and Israel lived safely, everyone had their own vines and fig trees, from Dan all the way to Beersheba, all the days of King Solomon's life.
Solomon had 4,000 stalls for his horses and chariots and 12,000 horses.
Each month those officers took turns providing food for King Solomon and everyone who ate at his table, and they lacked nothing.
The officers also brought their quotas of barley and straw for the horses and camels to the designated place.
And God gave Solomon extreme wisdom and understanding and a large heart as abundant as the sands on the beach.
Solomon's wisdom far excelled that of all the inhabitants of the east, and greater than all the wisdom of Egypt.
Because he was wiser than all men including Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Chalcol, Darda, and Mahol's sons, and he was famous in all the nations everywhere.
Solomon wrote 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs.
He spoke of the trees, from the cedar trees in Lebanon to the hyssop that grow on the wall, he also taught about the animals, birds, reptiles, and fish.
People came to hear Solomon's wisdom, sent by all kings on earth who had heard of his wisdom.
King Hiram of Tyre had always loved David, and he sent his servants to Solomon, because he had heard that Solomon had been anointed king in his father's throne room.
And Solomon sent this message to Hiram which said,
"You know that my father David could not build a house to the name of his Lord God because of the wars that surrounded him on every side, until the Lord had trampled them under his feet.
But now my Lord God has given me peace on every side, and there are no adversaries nor evil crises.

And behold, I propose to build a house to the name of my Lord God, for the Lord spoke to my father David and said, 'Your son, whom I will seat on your throne in your throne room will build a house to my name.'

Now I ask you to cut the cedar trees of Lebanon for me and my servants will work with your servants. I will hire your servants from you and pay you whatever you think is fair, for you know that we have no one with the skills to carve timber like the Sidonians."
When Hiram heard Solomon's words he rejoiced and said, "Blessed be the Lord this day, who has given David a wise son to rule over these great people."
Hiram sent word back to Solomon and said, "I have considered everything that you have asked of me, and I will do as you desire concerning the cedar and fir timber.

My servants will bring them from Lebanon down to the sea, and I will ship them by sea to wherever you designate. They will be discharged to you there and you can take possession of them, and all I ask is that you supply food for my household."
So Hiram gave Solomon all the cedar and fir trees that he desired.
And Solomon gave Hiram 20,000 measures of wheat and 20 measures of pure oil as food for his household year after year.
The Lord gave Solomon all the wisdom that he was promised, and there was a peace treaty and peace between Hiram and Solomon.
King Solomon conscripted 30,000 laborers from all of Israel.
He sent 10,000 of them per month to Lebanon, and they stayed in Lebanon for one month and they were home for two month, and Adoniram supervised the laborers.
Solomon had 70,000 workers transporting heavy loads and 80,000 stone carvers in the mountains.
This did not include Solomon's 3,300 officers supervising the workers.
And the king ordered great and costly carved stones, that they brought to lay the house foundation.
Solomon's and Hiram's builders and stone quarriers carved them, so they prepared stone and timber to build the house.
It was 480 years after the Israelis left Egypt, that Solomon started building the Lord's house. It was his fourth year as king of Israel, and it was during Zif which was the second month of the year.
The temple that King Solomon built for the Lord was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.
The temple's front entrance hall was twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide, and it stretched across the front of the temple.
Solomon had windows made for the temple with narrow lights.
Solomon built floors all around and against the temple walls of both the temple and the inner sanctuary.

The bottom floor was five cubits wide, the middle floor was six cubits wide, and the third floor was seven cubits wide. Solomon also built narrow ledges all around the outside of the temple, so that the beams would not be fastened to the walls of the temple.
The temple was constructed using finished stones cut at the quarry, so that no hammers, axes, or any iron tools were heard in the temple while it was being built.
The door for the middle floor was on the right side of the temple, and a winding staircase was built from the bottom floor up to the middle floor, and from the middle floor to the third floor.
So Solomon finished building the temple with beams and cedar boards.
Then Solomon built floors all along the temple that were five cubits high, and they were attached to the temple with cedar timbers.
And the Lord's word came to Solomon and said,
"About this temple you are building, if you walk in my laws, execute my judgments, and keep and all of my commandments, then I will keep my promise that I made to your father David.
I will live among the Israelis, and I will not forsake my people of Israel."
So Solomon finished building the temple.
Solomon built the temple's walls with cedar boards including the floor and ceiling, and he covered the inside walls with wood, and he covered the temple floors with fir planks.
Solomon partitioned off twenty cubits along the back side of the temple, and he covered both the floor and walls with cedar boards, to form an inner sanctuary and a place for the Most Holy Place.
The front of the temple before the inner sanctuary was forty cubits long.
The inner temple's cedar was carved with knobs and blooming flowers, it was all covered with cedar, and there was no stone visible.
Solomon prepared the inner sanctuary as a place to keep the Lord's Ark of the Covenant.
The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high, and he overlaid it with pure gold, and covered the altar with cedar.
So Solomon overlaid the inside of the temple with pure gold, and he partitioned it off with gold chains before the inner sanctuary which was also overlaid with gold.
Solomon overlaid the whole inner temple with gold, until the temple was completely finished. He also overlaid the whole altar near the inner sanctuary with gold.
Solomon made two ten cubit high cherubim inside the inner sanctuary from olive tree wood.
One of the cherub's wings was five cubits long and the cherub's other wing was also five cubits long. So the cherub's full wingspan from the farthest tips of each wing measured ten cubits.
The other cherub was also ten cubits wide, so that both cherubim were the same shape and size.
Both cherubim were ten cubits tall.

Solomon placed the cherubim in the inner sanctuary, where the first cherub's wing touched one wall, while the other cherub's wing touched the other wall, and their wingtips touched in the middle of the room.
Solomon overlaid the cherubim with gold.
Solomon carved all the temple walls inside and out, and all around with carved cherubim figures, palm trees, and blooming flowers.
Solomon overlaid all the temple floors with gold inside and out.
At the inner sanctuary entrance Solomon made olive wood doors, with five-sided lintels and doorposts.
The two doors were made of olive wood, and he carved cherubim, palm trees, and blooming flowers on them, and overlaid the cherubim and palm trees with gold.
He also made the temple's four-sided doorposts from olive wood.
Two doors were made of fir, and each one had folding panels.
After that he carved cherubim, palm trees, and blooming flowers and overlaid the carved work with gold.
Solomon built the inner court with three rows of carved stone, and a row of cedar beams.
The Lord's temple foundation was laid in the fourth year in the month of Zif.
In the eighth month of Bul of the eleventh year of King Solomon's reign, every detail of the temple was completely finished. So he built the temple in seven years.
But before he was finished it took King Solomon thirteen years to build his own palace.

He also built the palace with wood from the forest of Lebanon. It was a hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. It was built on four rows of cedar columns, with cedar beams on top of the columns.
The palace roof was covered with cedar shingles above on the beams that rested on forty-five columns, and there were three rows of fifteen columns in each row.
There were three rows of windows each with three windows facing each other.
All the doors and posts were rectangular, with the windows facing each other in three groups.

Solomon built columns for an entrance hall that was fifty cubits long, thirty cubits wide, and the front entrance hall was built along the front of the building, and it had a canopy supported by other columns and thick beams.
Then he built a great hall for the throne where he could sit in judgement called the Hall of Justice, and it was covered with cedar from floor to ceiling.
The palace where King Solomon lived had an inner court inside the entrance hall of similar construction. Solomon also built a palace similar to this for his wife who was Pharaoh's daughter.
These were all built of costly carved stones inside and out, everything from the foundation to the coping, and so were its outer walls toward the great court.
The foundation was laid with great costly stones that were ten cubits by ten cubits or eight cubits by eight cubits.
Above the foundation were costly carved stones of similar size, and cedar beams.
All around the great court were three rows of carved stones, and a row of cedar beams, both were used for the inner court of the Lord's temple and the temple entrance hall.
King Solomon sent for Hiram and brought him from Tyre.

Hiram was a widow's son from Naphtali's tribe, and his father was from Tyre. He was a brass worker, and he was filled with wisdom and understanding. He skillfully made all types of brass items, and he came to King Solomon to do all of his brass work.
Hiram cast two circular brass columns each eighteen cubits high and measured twelve cubits around.
He made two ornamental capitals of molten brass to set on the tops of the columns; both capitals were five cubits high.
He made lattice grating with seven wreaths made of chain for each ornamental capital that were set atop the columns.
He made the columns with two rows of carved pomegranates around each grate to cover each capital atop both columns.
The ornamental capitals atop the columns were shaped like the carved lilies on the entrance hall, and they were four cubits high.
The ornamental capitals of both columns also had pomegranates above, next to the rounded protrusion near the lattice grate, and there were rows with two hundred pomegranates encircling each capital.
Hiram constructed the columns for the temple entrance hall, and he named the column on the right Jachin, and the column on the left he named Boaz.
After they carved lilies above the columns, work on the columns was finished.
He built a pool of molten metal that looked like the ocean, it was round with a diameter of ten cubits from one rim to the other. It was five cubits high, with a circumference of thirty cubits.
It was encircled by two rows of ten cast ornamental flower buds per cubit beneath the ocean pool's rim.
It stood on twelve oxen, three looking north, three looking west, three south, and three looking east, and the ocean pool was set atop of them, and their rear parts faced inward.
It was as thick as the width of a hand, and its rim was worked like the rim of a cup with cast lily flowers, and it held as much water as 2,000 bathtubs.
Hiram made ten brass foundations, and each base was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.
The foundations were designed with panels that had ledges between them.
There were lions, oxen, and cherubim carved on the panels between the ledges. There were bases above the ledges, and beneath the lions and oxen were wreaths that were beveled downward.
Each base had four brass axels and wheels, and a brass sink underpinned by four corners underpinned by a molten support.

The round opening at the top inside the ornamental capital was a cubit deep, and like the design of the base it was a cubit and a half wide. There were engravings around the openings, but they were square, not round.
There were four wheels under the panels, and the wheel's axle were attached to the base, and each wheel was a cubit and half a cubit in diameter.
The wheels were designed to look like chariot wheels, and their axles, hubs, rims, and spokes were all cast of molten metal.
There were four underpinnings attached directly to the four corners of each base.
There was a ring around the top of the base that was half a cubit high, and the panels and ledges on top of the base were all the same.
Because on the plates of its ledges and its borders, he engraved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, in accordance with the proportions of each one and additions all around.
He built the ten foundations with this same design, all of them were cast with the same dimensions and shape.
Then Hiram made ten brass basins and each one contained as much water as forty baths, and every basin measured four cubits across, and each basin was supported by ten foundations.
He built five foundations on both the right side and left side of the temple, and he installed the cast ocean pool on the eastern right side of the temple near the southside.
So after Hiram also made the pots, shovels, and basins and he was finished doing all the work for King Solomon's palace and the Lord's temple.
The two columns and the two ornamental capitals shaped like bowls sitting on top of the columns, and the two lattice grates covering the capitals on the top of the columns.
And the two rows of 400 pomegranates for each of the two lattice grates, even two rows of pomegranates for one network that covered the capitals on top of the columns.
And the ten foundations, and ten basins on the foundations.
And one ocean pool, and twelve oxen under the ocean pool.
And the pots, shovels, basins, and vessels that Hiram made for King Solomon for the Lord's temple, were all made of bright brass.
King Solomon had all of these things cast in clay molds on the plains of Jordan between Succoth and Zarethan.
Solomon did not weigh the brass vessels, because there were so many of them, and the total weight of brass used is unknown.
Solomon had all the vessells, the altar, and the table where the priests offered bread for the Lord's temple made of gold.
The five lampstands on the right side and the five lampstands on the left side before the inner sanctuary plus the flowers, lamps, and tongs were all made of pure gold.
And the vessels, candle snuffers, basins, spoons, censers, and hinges for both doors of the inner temple, the doors of the Most Holy Place, and the temple doors were all made of pure gold.

So King Solomon's work on the Lord's temple was finished, and he also brought all the things his father David dedicated to the Lord including the silver and gold vessels and he put them among the treasures of the Lord's temple.
Then King Solomon summoned all the Israelis elders, tribal leaders, and the leading Israelis fathers to Jerusalem, to bring the Lord's Ark of the Covenant with them from Zion, the city of David.
All the Israelis men assembled before King Solomon at the feast in the seventh month called Ethanim.
All the Israelis elders came with the priests and brought the ark.
The priests and Levites came and brought the Ark of the Covenant, the congregation's tabernacle, and all the tabernacle's Holy vessels with them.
King Solomon and the entire Israelis congregation assembled with him before the ark, and they sacrificed so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted.
The priests brought the Lord's Ark of the Covenant to the Most Holy Place in the temple's inner sanctuary under the cherub's wings.
The cherubim 's wings were spread over the ark and covered it and its poles.

Then they pulled the poles out that were so long, that the ends of the poles could be seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen outside. They are there to this day.
There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses put there in Horeb, when the brought the Israelis out of Egypt and made a covenant with them.
Then the priests left the Holy Place, and a cloud filled the Lord's temple.
When the cloud filled the room, the priests could not stand there and minister, because the Lord's glory filled his Temple.
Then Solomon spoke and said, "The Lord said that he would live in the thick darkness.
I have surely built you a temple to live in, a secure place where you can live forever."
Then the king turned around and blessed the entire Israelis congregation as they stood before him.
And he said, "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who has fulfilled everything that he promised when he spoke to my father David and said,

'Since the day I brought my people of Israel out of Egypt, I have not chosen any city from all the Israelis tribes to build a temple in my name where I might live. But I have chosen David to rule over my people Israel.'
And it was in my father David's heart to build a temple in the name of the Lord God of Israel.
And the Lord spoke to my father David and said, 'It is a good thing that you have it in your heart to build a temple in my name.
But you must not build the temple, because your son who comes from your own flesh and blood will build the temple in my name.'

The Lord has fulfilled the promise he made, and I have risen to take my father David's place and sit on the throne of Israel. And as the Lord promised, I have built a temple in the name of the Lord God of Israel.
And I have provided a place for the ark, which contains the Lord's covenant that he made with our fathers when he brought them out of Egypt."
Solomon stood before the Lord's altar in the presence of the entire Israelis congregation, and spread out his hands toward heaven.
